no-territory-conceptual.essay:
Some declared countries exist only as an idea, an artwork or an organisation. Nothing is claimed on the ground, or the claim is carried with a person or an object. People do this for several reasons, including protest, art, religion, study and amusement. The law's response is simple, because nothing happens to the legal position of anyone involved. Nothing is owned, and the people remain under the law of the place where they stand.

To see why, it helps to know what a state is in law. The usual checklist comes from the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty, which asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries. A conceptual country has no population living in a place under its rule and no territory. Its government governs only those who agree to it, and other countries do not deal with it as a state. There is no treaty, office or court that a declaration needs to pass through, so anyone can make one and no authority needs to refuse it. Nobody has to raid a place that does not exist, which is why these projects tend to survive for a long time, and also why governments do not trouble to answer them.

Two real situations come close, and they show what the law actually asks. The Sovereign Order of Malta, a Catholic order, has no national territory and is still treated as a sovereign entity under international law. It keeps diplomatic relations with about 115 states, signs treaties and has been an observer at the UN General Assembly since 1994. That standing comes from centuries of history and from governments choosing to deal with it, and a new group cannot declare its way into it. The other situation concerns states losing land. In its climate opinion of July 2025, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, said that "once a State is established, the disappearance of one of its constituent elements would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". Low-lying island states pressed this point because of rising seas. The sentence protects a state that already exists, it did not mention sea level rise in terms, and how far it reaches is still argued by scholars. It gives nothing to a project that never was a state.

The best-known example is Nutopia, announced by John Lennon and Yoko Ono at a New York press conference on 2 April 1973. Its declaration says it has no land, no boundaries, no passports, only people, and no laws other than cosmic ones. Anyone could become a citizen by declaring awareness of it. Its flag was a white handkerchief, and its anthem is four seconds of silence. There was a practical side. Lennon had just received an order to leave the United States, and all citizens were to be ambassadors, with a request for diplomatic immunity, the legal protection foreign diplomats have from a host country's courts, and for recognition by the United Nations. No government is known to have granted the immunity. His home-country problem was solved by ordinary US immigration law, when the deportation order was overturned in 1975 and he received a green card in 1976.

That case shows the first and most common misunderstanding. A declaration does not reach the legal problem the person already has. Immunity comes from an agreement between a receiving state and a sending state, so naming yourself an ambassador has no effect on a court or an immigration officer. Your home country's law continues to apply to your income, your debts, your marriage and any charge against you.

The cases differ in how seriously they organise. Nova Roma, formed in 1998 and later incorporated in the US state of Maine, aims to restore the religion, culture and values of ancient Rome. It calls itself a sovereign nation and has a senate, elected officials and laws passed by members' votes, with Latin as its official language. It minted coins in 2000 and 2005. Its most recent dated activity is a twentieth-anniversary celebration in Rome, and what it does now has not been confirmed. The Ambulatory Free States of Obsidia, founded in 2015 by Karo Yagjian, is a feminist micronation and art project whose territory is two book-sized slabs of obsidian, a volcanic glass, carried in a briefcase usually based in Oakland, California. Huck magazine estimated about 250 citizens in 2021, roughly 50 with passports. Its present activity has not been confirmed. The obsidian itself is personal property under the law of wherever the briefcase is.

Passports are the first real pitfall. Printing a booklet for fun is one thing, but using it at a border is another. Border officers check documents against lists of real issuers, and a document from an unrecognised body is at best refused. Members who treat one as real can face questions or charges, so the sensible use of such a passport is as a keepsake. A real passport stays necessary for every actual trip.

Money comes next, and it is where a harmless project can turn into a legal problem. Selling coins, stamps and certificates as souvenirs is ordinary trade, and the seller owes ordinary tax. Atlantium, founded in Sydney in 1981 by three teenagers, sold coins, stamps and banknotes in its imperial solidus and had almost 3,000 citizens as of 2015, most of whom signed up online and never visited. Selling titles or promises of future value raises other questions. The Global Country of World Peace, launched by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi on 7 October 2000 and incorporated in Iowa in 2002, is run by initiates called rajas, and reports say that title cost $1 million or more. It also issued a currency, the raam, accepted by some businesses in Iowa and the Netherlands.

The same group shows what happens when a project of this kind goes looking for land under its own authority. It offered Suriname $1.3 billion over three years for a 200-year lease of 3,500 acres, and no deal followed. Tuvalu rejected a proposed city-state in 2001, and Rota in the Northern Mariana Islands declined a request for 100 acres in 2002. Costa Rica expelled its representative in 2002 after officials said to be acting for the group allegedly offered Talamanca families payments to appoint a king. It did buy ordinary private property, including a 30-acre island in Ireland and more than 1,000 acres in Kansas, all of it under the law of the country concerned.

Land also does not change the legal position when a project buys it privately. Slowjamastan is a patch of California desert that the DJ Randy Williams bought in 2021, 11.07 acres for $19,000, and declared independent that December. More than 25,000 citizens had applied online by March 2026, while nobody lived there as of February 2025. Williams cites the Montevideo Convention as the basis of its legitimacy, and the convention's tests do not make a declaration effective on their own, since other countries must still be willing to deal with it. The project has no legal recognition. Atlantium's plots in Australia likewise stay under Australian law.

Another misunderstanding is that a long life or a large roll means growing legal status. Several of these projects have lasted decades as organisations, and Nutopia has taken citizens through a website since April 2024. None is reported to have gained recognition from any country.

The safest form is exactly what it appears to be. It is an artwork, a society or a nonprofit that openly calls its country an idea, registers as a normal organisation if it holds money, pays ordinary taxes on sales and never asks anyone to rely on its documents. It can carry a message for decades at very little cost, and it carries little risk as long as no one is misled. The limit is that it gives its members no legal protection, tax status, travel right or land, because nothing in law has changed.

inland-waters.essay:
An island in a lake or river can seem to sit between countries, especially on a border. The water around it belongs to the countries on its shores, and a newcomer gets no share. The ocean has a stretch that belongs to no one, the high seas. Lakes and rivers have nothing equivalent, because land under some country's control encloses them.

To understand how these borders work, start with a river. When two countries agree that a river is their border, they usually sign a treaty. A treaty that names only the river normally means the line follows the thalweg, the deepest channel, since that is the part boats use. Rivers shift and split, though, so the treaty may fail to say which channel it meant. Sedudu, called Kasikili in Namibia, is an island of about 5 km² in the Chobe River that floods for several months each year. An 1890 treaty between Germany and Britain put the line in the "main channel" without saying which one. In 1996 Botswana and Namibia asked the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, to decide. In 1999 it studied the river and held that the northern channel was the main one, so the island fell on the Botswana side. Nobody lives there permanently, and it is now one of the main tourist attractions in the Chobe area. The case asked only which of the two countries held the island.

Lakes work the same way, with lines drawn by treaty or by old colonial orders. Migingo is a rock of about 2,000 m² in Lake Victoria, valued for the Nile perch in the waters around it. A colonial order, the Kenya Colony and Protectorate Order in Council of 1926, draws the Kenya-Uganda line across the lake by straight lines between named islands, and it is copied into the Ugandan constitution. Two Kenyan fishermen say they settled the rock in 1991, a Ugandan fisherman says he arrived in 2004, and Kenya says Ugandan marine police raised a flag in June 2004. In February 2009 Kenyans there were told to buy special Ugandan permits. By then the rock held homes of corrugated metal, four pubs, a pharmacy and an open-air casino, with 131 people reported, while Ugandan police estimated about 500. Ministers agreed that Uganda would withdraw its 48 police officers, and they stayed. A 2009 survey placed the rock 510 metres on the Kenyan side, and its report was still unpublished in January 2025. Wikipedia says the results were announced and Uganda withdrew, while a Kenya News Agency report says surveyors disagreed and the joint work stopped. In January 2025 residents petitioned Kenya's president over harassment by Ugandan police, and that August fishermen said Ugandan officials were still seizing their gear. Settling first or raising a flag did not decide the matter.

Some waters have no agreed line at all. Lake Constance, where Germany, Switzerland and Austria meet, has no binding agreement fixing the borders in its deep part. Areas under 25 metres deep go to the nearest country, and shipping and fishing have treaties of their own. Switzerland holds that the line runs down the middle. Austria says the deep part belongs to all the shore states together, an arrangement called a condominium, meaning shared rule. Germany has kept its opinion ambiguous. Under every one of those views, the deep water belongs to one or more of the shore countries, so an outsider has no claim.

The Caspian Sea, at 389,000 km², is the largest case. Its five shore countries argued for decades over whether it counts as a sea or a lake, because the law of the sea applies only to seas. The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea was signed on 12 August 2018 at Aktau, Kazakhstan. It would give each shore country 15 nautical miles (about 28 km) of territorial water and a further 10 nautical miles (about 19 km) of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface would be a common space open to the five members, and the seabed is left to agreements between the countries concerned. It was not in force as of September 2026, because all five must ratify it, meaning formally approve it. Four have. Iran's cabinet approved it on 22 July 2026 and sent it to parliament, which had not ratified it. Even the open middle is for the five named countries, so an outsider has none of the freedoms found on the ocean. Iranian patrol boats have at times fired on vessels Azerbaijan sent to explore disputed oil fields.

A treaty can also give an island to two countries at once. Pheasant Island, in the Bidasoa river, stays a condominium of France and Spain under the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659, and each governs it for six months in turn. In January 2018 it measured about 200 metres by 40 metres. It is uninhabited and eroding, and access is forbidden apart from rare heritage days. Naval personnel check it every five days.

A river island can also be overlooked for a time. Ada Kaleh, in the Danube, was forgotten at the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and stayed Ottoman in law, with other countries on both banks. Its residents paid no tax or customs and were not drafted, and it became known as a free port and a smugglers' nest. Austria-Hungary declared sovereignty in 1913, Romania occupied it in 1919, and the Treaty of Lausanne, which the residents did not sign, made it Romanian in 1923. In 1970 the Iron Gates dam flooded it. Ada Kaleh had a legal owner throughout, and its residents had no say in the treaty or the dam.

New land raises a fresher problem. Santa Rosa is an island in the Amazon where Brazil, Colombia and Peru meet, with about 3,000 people under Peruvian administration. In June 2025 Peru's Congress made it a district of its Loreto region. Colombia's president said in August that Peru had "appropriated it by law". Colombia argues that the island had not formed when the 1922 and 1929 treaties were signed, so they cannot have assigned it. Peru treats it as an extension of an older island. Land that a river newly creates may fall outside a treaty's words, and the competition for it still runs between the neighbouring countries. The Chamizal dispute between the United States and Mexico shows a rule used for moving rivers. An 1884 treaty accepted that a river border moves with the river only when the change is gradual, and that a sudden shift leaves the border where it was. The Rio Grande shifted at El Paso, a 1911 tribunal recommended splitting the land, and the United States rejected that. A treaty signed in 1963 largely followed the recommendation, and the land passed to Mexico in October 1967, with more than 5,600 residents of El Paso displaced. Whether anything like that rule decides Santa Rosa depends on the words of the 1922 and 1929 treaties, which Colombia and Peru read differently.

Suppose a group floats a platform onto a large lake and declares a state. Lake police and customs officers from the nearest shore are a short boat ride away, and they are the practical limit. Every supply run ends at a dock in one of the shore countries. There is no high-seas freedom to argue from. Banks, tax, courts and building permits are those of the shore country.

The common misunderstanding treats a gap in a line as a gap in ownership. A border argument, a missing treaty, a shifting channel and a forgotten island have each been resolved or left open among the countries on the shore.

The realistic version is ordinary. A floating home, lodge or tourist concession can be built on lakes and rivers with the permission of the country that holds the spot, under that country's law. Building is easier than at sea, and supply and medical care are close. It gives no new status, since it is one more property in an existing country, and on a contested border it may bring officials from two countries, as on Migingo.

moon.essay:
The Moon is the natural body that circles Earth, about 385,000 kilometres away, with a radius of about 1,740 kilometres. Its gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, and its very thin atmosphere gives no protection from the Sun's radiation or from falling rocks. The ground reaches about 127 C in full sun and falls to about -173 C in darkness. Ice lies in permanently shadowed craters near the poles. It is the only other world people have walked on, although no one has stayed longer than a few days, so the legal questions are closest to being tested here.

The basic rules come from the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Everyone has free access to all areas (Article I). No country may take over the Moon by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means (Article II). The Moon may be used for peaceful purposes only, with no military bases, weapons tests or military exercises (Article IV). Private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, which answers for it (Article VI).

The treaty also separates things from ground. An object that a country has registered stays the property of its owner, and the registering country keeps legal power over the object and its staff, on the surface as well (Article VIII). Countries must avoid harmful contamination and pay due attention to the interests of others (Article IX). Stations are open to visits by representatives of other members, on a reciprocal basis and with advance notice (Article XII).

The result resembles a tent on a public campsite, where the tent is yours and the ground never becomes yours. The Soviet probe Luna 2 scattered metal pennants marked "USSR" when it crashed in 1959, and they gave no claim. The descent stage and flag of Apollo 11, and the rover of Apollo 17, remain American property on ground that is not American. The same holds for China's Chang'e 4 and Chang'e 6, India's Vikram lander at the place India calls Shiv Shakti point, and Japan's silent SLIM lander. The wreck of Russia's Luna 25 is still Russian property. Firefly's Blue Ghost lander belongs to a private company, and the United States still answers for it.

A second treaty, the Moon Agreement, took effect in July 1984 after Austria became the fifth country to join. It calls the Moon the "common heritage of mankind", meaning it belongs to humanity as a whole, and says its surface cannot become the property of any country, organization or person (Article 11). A future set of rules is to govern commercial use of its resources, and those rules have never been written. Countries may build stations using only the area they need, and they must tell the UN (Article 9). As of 1 January 2026 it had 17 members and 4 countries that signed without joining, and no leading space power is a member. American campaigners fought it in 1979 and 1980, and the United States stayed out. Saudi Arabia left with effect from 5 January 2024. A country that has not joined is not bound by it.

The newer approach is the Artemis Accords, a US-led set of principles first signed by eight countries in October 2020. They describe themselves as a political commitment and not a treaty, so they create no duty that a court could enforce. NASA counts 78 signers, the latest Vietnam on 28 October 2026. China and Russia are not among them. The Accords say that extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body (Section 10). They also create "safety zones", areas where signers give notice of their work and coordinate to avoid interference, with a size that follows the work done there and an end when the work stops (Section 11). NASA says this respects free access. It is the most debated part of the Accords, because critics fear that a zone others must keep clear of could work in practice like a claim, and no court has tested it. A US law, 51 USC 51303, lets American citizens own and sell space resources they recover, subject to the country's international obligations. China and Russia lead a rival project, the International Lunar Research Station, with construction planned from 2031. Both camps want the area around Shackleton crater at the south pole because of its ice, and the Outer Space Treaty bars either from claiming it.

Private deeds sit apart from all this. A. Dean Lindsay of Georgia claimed space objects before a notary in the 1930s, and Robert Coles later sold Moon lots at a dollar an acre. James Mangan's Nation of Celestial Space claimed all of space in 1949 and applied to join the UN. Jenaro Gajardo Vera, a Chilean lawyer, declared himself owner of the Moon in 1954, partly to meet a social club's rule that members own property. The property registry has no record of the deed. Dennis Hope filed a claim in 1980, told the UN, treats its silence as approval, and sells deeds through his Lunar Embassy. Discover magazine reported 4.25 million buyers and over $9 million in sales. The Official Lunar Registry charges about $20 an acre. Virgiliu Pop, a Romanian space lawyer, traced these claims in his book Unreal Estate and took apart Hope's legal argument. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, warned that such deeds raise the chance that individuals will be misled. No government or court is known to back one, and a buyer receives a printed paper.

Suppose a group wants its own settlement. The first bump is permission. In the United States a launch needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), with insurance for harm to others of up to $500 million. Radio frequencies are assigned through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a UN agency, and only member countries can file. The Moon Express case shows how unformed this still is. In 2016 no US agency was clearly in charge of a private landing, so the company asked the FAA, which issued a favourable review. Lawyers at the group TechFreedom doubted that one letter met the treaty's demand for continuing oversight, and the mission never flew. Lonestar's small data centre, marketed as beyond national data rules, reached the Moon on the Athena lander in 2025. The lander fell on its side, the mission ended in about 13 hours, and the United States answers for that hardware too.

Money comes next. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, and the Moon is much farther. Food at 2.77 kilograms a day comes to about 1,000 kilograms a person each year, which would be about $3.3 million even at the low-orbit rate. The International Space Station costs about $3 billion a year to run.

On site, no one can lawfully keep others out, because access is free to all, though safety zones may limit access in practice. For All Moonkind, a nonprofit, helped pass a US law in 2020 protecting old landing sites, which binds only companies working with NASA, and the Accords commit signers to preserve such sites (Section 9). In an emergency, astronauts of member countries must help each other (Article V), and specialist care means going home. Crime stays under outside law, since the registering country has power over the base and US law reaches offences by or against US nationals outside any nation. American settlers would still owe US tax returns, under a 1924 Supreme Court case, Cook v. Tait.

Declaring independence would change little. The usual test of statehood, from the Montevideo Convention of 1933, requires a defined territory, and the ban on national claims leaves no land on the Moon for a new state to hold. UN membership requires a Security Council recommendation and two-thirds of the General Assembly.

The form the law allows is a licensed base under a cooperating country, with residents' own rules made by contract and with a safety zone announced around the work. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, put building even that at about 5 percent, and the chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower. Whoever arrives first with a state's support gains practical influence over a site, which lasts only as long as the work and carries no title. Residents stay subject to the licensing country.

digital-no-territory.essay:
A digital country is a group of people who organise online and call themselves a nation, with no land of their own. Founders like the idea because the projects that held land are the ones that met arrests and raids. Anyone can found one for the cost of a website.

The difficulty lies in where the members and machines actually are. Each participant stays under the law of the place they live, and each server sits under the law of the place it stands. A person in Ohio who joins an online nation still pays US taxes and still needs a US passport to travel. John Perry Barlow's Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, published on 8 February 1996, told governments they had no sovereignty, meaning legal authority, online. It created no institutions, and governments have since acted against its claim, because servers and the people who run them are within their reach.

The legal test comes from the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist. It asks for a defined territory (Article 1). It also says statehood does not depend on recognition (Article 3), and reading the two together appears to keep the territory test in place. A project with no land therefore fails one of the four tests, and it can still function as an association, a company or a club.

Suppose a group now tries to act like a country. A web domain ending in a country code follows the ISO 3166 list, the international list of country codes, under a 1994 document called RFC 1591, and IANA, the body that manages these domains, says it does not decide what is a country. Passports follow the standard of the International Civil Aviation Organization, the UN agency for civil flying, and its Doc 9303 takes issuer codes from the ISO 3166 agency or from separately listed organisations. A project on neither list has no code for a border machine to read. In 2002 a group travelling on passports of Elgaland-Vargaland, a Swedish art project in the form of a country, was detained in Estonia and sent back to Sweden the next day.

The next bump is money. Selling citizenship, land or tokens to the public brings securities law, the law on investments sold to the public, along with fraud law. Moving money brings the rules set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that writes anti-money-laundering standards. Banks and crypto exchanges apply those rules to members at the point where tokens turn into ordinary money. A project also needs a real company to hold its bank account, which puts it under that company's home law. CityDAO, which bought 40 acres in Wyoming for about $100,000 in 2021, chose Wyoming because it was then the only state letting a group run through software on a blockchain, a shared public ledger, hold property as a company. Its 6,500 or so citizens in June 2022 were token holders, zoning may allow only one house on each 40-acre lot, and in May 2023 the land was undeveloped.

A country with no location is also easy to fake. The Dominion of Melchizedek, declared in 1990 by Mark Pedley, claimed a Colombian island, a shoal that appears to have been invented and part of Antarctica, among other places. About 300 bank licences were claimed to have been sold by the end of the 1990s, and one scheme took over $4 million from at least 1,400 people. The Marshall Islands condemned its claims in 1998, and Pedley pleaded guilty to share manipulation in 2010.

Other projects fade or stay small. Bitnation, founded in 2014, offered blockchain ID cards and had about 25 volunteer embassies in 2016. With no recognition, an embassy could do little for an asylum seeker, and by August 2022 its domain had been sold. Wirtland, founded in 2008, claimed about 700 citizens and proposed asking Nauru for territory, and no land is known to have changed hands. Afropolitan raised $2.1 million as a digital nation for the African diaspora and, according to a critical 2025 article, was running a podcast and three services three years on. Asgardia reported more than 290,000 citizens in March 2019, and its only territory, a 2.8-kilogram satellite under US authority, burned up in 2022. A list of free sign-ups differs from the permanent population the test asks for, since those people live and pay tax elsewhere.

Virtual land is a separate misunderstanding. Decentraland sold plots as tokens, with one sale of $2.43 million in 2021, and fewer than 1,000 users a day were making transactions in October 2022. A token gives no authority over any place on Earth. A virtual city designed in 2022 for Liberland, a self-declared country on the Danube, gave it no access to the real land, which Croatia controls. Real governments have tried the same idea without any change in law. Sweden spent 400,000 kronor, about $57,000, on a Second Life embassy in 2007, which added nothing to its legal status, and it is not known whether the metaverse embassy Barbados planned in 2021 ever opened.

Balaji Srinivasan's 2022 book on the network state proposes an online community that buys scattered land and eventually seeks diplomatic recognition. Its test site was the Network School, in a hotel in Johor, Malaysia. Officers checked 266 foreigners there on 14 July 2026 and found all documents valid. On 21 July the city council revoked its business licence, and it moved to Astana, Kazakhstan, under a non-binding memorandum. Praxis, a New York company, reported $525 million, of which $500 million is conditional on listing tokens, and it has looked at Greenland, a California base and Uruguay. No Praxis city has been built. A group that holds a building holds it under a local licence, and that licence can be withdrawn.

The cases that succeed have a real state or a long history behind them. Estonia's e-Residency gives foreigners a digital identity for running Estonian companies, with over 144,000 e-residents from 187 countries. It gives no citizenship or right to live there, and it relies on Estonia's territory, law, courts and banks. Estonia's data embassy is a Tier 4 (highest-reliability grade) data centre in Luxembourg holding state databases, by agreement between the two countries, drawing on the treaty on embassies, the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. Tuvalu, a recognised country of about 10,000 people, has asked other countries to agree in advance that it stays a state if the sea takes its land. Twenty-six had reportedly done so by December 2023, and in 2025 the International Court of Justice said the loss of one part of a state "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". The question has not been tested. The Nansen passport of 1922, a travel paper for refugees, worked because governments agreed in advance to honour it. Garry Davis's World Passport, issued from 1953 for a fee, had no such agreement, and he was regularly arrested and expelled.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is often cited as proof that land is unnecessary. It lost Malta to Napoleon in 1798, kept its status, and reports relations with 118 countries. It began in the 11th century and was already treated as sovereign when it lost its land, a history a new group cannot copy.

Borrowing a real state's protection has also failed. In 2010 the Swedish Pirate Party offered to host The Pirate Bay inside parliament for legal cover, and it won no seats.

A project that stays within the law is candid about what it is. It is a company, nonprofit or membership club registered in a real country, with no securities sold, no passports for border use, ordinary tax compliance by members and a clear statement that citizenship is membership. It can last, with culture, voting and shared funds, and there is no single place for a government to raid. It holds no land, its members and servers remain under local law, and recognition as a state remains close to nil.

combo-network-plots.essay:
The network state is an idea set out by Balaji Srinivasan in a 2022 book. A community forms online around shared values, pools its money, buys land in many places, and later seeks diplomatic recognition from real governments. It reverses the usual order, in which land comes first. On a map, the result would look like an archipelago, with houses and buildings scattered among other countries and joined by the internet. This combines an online nation, private land purchase and a later claim to statehood.

The most important settled point is the difference between owning land and ruling it. A deed gives a person rights under the law of the country where the land lies. It gives no authority to make law there. Kiribati, a full UN member, paid $8.6 million in 2014 for the Natoavatu estate in Fiji, and the land stayed under Fiji's law. If a sovereign state buying land gets no sovereignty with the deed, a private group gets none. Each plot therefore has its own government. A plot in Wyoming follows county zoning and state law, as CityDAO found when it bought 40 acres near Cody and learned that zoning may allow only one house on each 40-acre lot. A plot in Portugal follows Portuguese law, tax and building rules. Many countries also limit land purchases by foreigners or foreign companies, so a single community may have to buy through a different local company in each country.

Follow one plot. The community's foundation buys a farm through a local company and builds cabins. A local council asks whether the use is residential or commercial. If members come from abroad, each needs a visa and a right to stay. If they work there, a permit. Rent and profit are taxed locally. If someone is hurt, a local court hears the case. If a neighbour complains, or if politics turn, the licence can go. The Network School shows how fast. It ran from a hotel in Forest City in Malaysia as an ordinary business with a council licence. After a row in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council revoked the licence on 21 July and ordered it to stop the next day. Within hours Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a memorandum to host a campus, which opened in Astana on 2 September. The two facts belong together. A host can end a site quickly, and a mobile community can find another host.

Scattered holdings do give something. Risk is spread, since one country's decision touches only one plot. Money and members can flow to whichever site is working. A site also gives a physical place to meet, which an online nation lacks. Praxis has spent years looking for such a site, and each candidate has needed a host government's agreement.

The history people cite most often as a precedent is contested and differs in important ways. The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, raised money from a worldwide diaspora to buy land in Ottoman and then British-ruled Palestine, and it was incorporated in London in 1907. By 1948 it held about 54 percent of the land in Jewish hands, a bit under 4 percent of Mandatory Palestine. Statehood in 1948 came through UN debate, war and displacement that the land purchases did not decide, and the legitimacy of later land transfers has been questioned. So the case shows that a diaspora can buy land for a national goal for decades, and it does not show that purchases produce a state.

What is genuinely open is recognition of a state with no contiguous land. The Montevideo Convention's test asks for a "defined territory", and it says nothing about the land being in one piece. Reading the text, it seems that scattered territory could in principle count, as states with enclaves and islands show. That helps only if those pieces have been given up by their current sovereign, and private title does not do that. The theory's answer is that a large enough community would have the numbers and money to bargain for recognition or for special zones. Srinivasan and his supporters argue this. Critics in Malaysia and elsewhere object to the sovereignty aims themselves. No such recognition has ever been granted, so no one can say what number of members or what level of money would matter. Article 3 of the Convention says statehood does not depend on recognition, yet it does not remove the territory test.

There is a further indirect limit. A community with thousands of members and a treasury is a target for securities law if it sold tokens with hope of profit, and for tax authorities and banks, which look at who controls the money. Founders stay under the law of their own nationality. Praxis's reported $500 million facility depended on listing tokens on a public exchange, which puts it in regulated hands.

As a network of real places, this has more practical potential than others in the digital family, and its chance of giving a group its own territory under its own laws is low. The strongest version is a foundation that buys only where the law allows, follows every zoning and visa rule, negotiates with willing governments for campus status, and treats recognition as a distant goal. It could produce real towns with a shared culture and a shared legal contract among members. In 25 years it may hold a good deal of land, each plot under a different flag, with a real chance at a special economic zone somewhere. The members would remain citizens of their own countries unless a state chose to do otherwise.

combo-treaty-cession-new-body.essay:
On paper, the cleanest legal route to title over a new territory would be this, although the chance of it happening is very small. An existing state signs a treaty handing a piece of its land to a new body, gives up all claim to it, and the new body becomes its government. Title would then come from the one party entitled to give it. This combines buying from a state, an agreement between governments, and the attempt to become a state.

Some of this is clear. States can transfer territory to each other. Egypt announced in 2016 that it would hand Tiran and Sanafir to Saudi Arabia and ratified the treaty in 2017, although the handover has stalled and sources differ on where it stands. Sovereignty over Vatican City was recognised to the Holy See by Italy in the Lateran Treaty of 1929, creating a state of 44 hectares. It is also clear that treaties are made between entities with capacity. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, in Article 6, says every state has the capacity to make them. It says nothing that helps a company or club. And it is clear that a transfer from one state does not bind other states to recognise the result. South Africa declared four homelands independent from 1976, starting with Transkei, and apart from South Africa and the four themselves, which recognised one another, no government accepted them.

The hard part is the recipient. The Holy See was an old international body with diplomatic ties before 1929, and its case is not a pattern for a new group. The closest modern parallel is the 1998 treaty by which Malta gave the Order of Malta, another old body with diplomatic ties, use of part of Fort St Angelo for 99 years. It gave the Order use with listed privileges and it did not give sovereignty. What is open, and has not been tested, is whether a brand-new private body could receive sovereignty directly by treaty. Nothing in the Vienna Convention says that it could never hold title, since a place may become a state by meeting the usual tests of territory, population and government. Reading the text, it seems that a treaty signed with a body that is not yet a state would at first count as a domestic act of the giving state or as a private contract, and that the new place's status would depend on other governments' responses. That reasoning is a reading and no court has ruled on it.

Politics makes the transfer far harder than the law. In the Tiran and Sanafir case, a transfer between two friendly states set off the largest protests against the government since 2014, with hundreds arrested. The Chagos treaty shows how slow it can be, even when a court has spoken. In 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that Britain should end its rule of the islands. On 22 May 2025 Britain and Mauritius signed a treaty transferring sovereignty and letting Britain exercise rights on Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years, for annual payments. Then a change in the American position stalled it, the British bill lapsed in April 2026, and as of October 2026 it was not in force. The same opinion shows a further limit. The court held that Mauritius's agreement to give up the islands in 1965 could not be treated as an international agreement, because it came while Britain ruled Mauritius, and that land cannot be split off without the free and genuine will of the people concerned. Reading that reasoning, a founder would have to expect the people on any ceded land to have a say, and a deal that ignored them would be open to attack.

Follow the steps. A government must first want this, which means something large in exchange and few voters who object. Its constitution may forbid giving up land, as the Honduran Supreme Court said of an earlier special zone plan on grounds of sovereignty. A parliament must vote, and a later government may attack the treaty. Neighbours with interests in the area would then respond. If it all succeeded, the new place would hold land and would need everything else, including a passport other states accept, a country code, a bank that will deal with it and recognition. The founders would remain citizens of their home countries, with those countries' tax and criminal laws still following them, until they gave up that nationality.

It has potential only as a very rare event. The strongest version would be a state already willing to give up a remote, unpopulated and undisputed piece of land, to a body with real backing from other governments, perhaps as part of a settlement of a bigger problem. No such transfer to a new private body has taken place in modern times. If one did, the title would be strong, which explains the high legal and holding figures, and those figures assume the transfer has already happened.

combo-private-currency-treasury.essay:
A country usually has its own money and a central bank. A private project can try to copy this by combining a private currency, printed or digital, with a treasury kept somewhere outside its home government's easy reach. That treasury might be an account at an offshore bank, a bank the project charters for itself, or crypto held in wallets the project controls. The hope is that members can trade among themselves, that the project can pay for things, and that no government can freeze the money. Each piece has a history, and most of the history is of prosecutions.

Some of this is settled. Inside a country, that country's criminal law applies to anyone who issues money-like things there. Bernard von NotHaus minted Liberty Dollars in the United States, coins worth about $7 million in total according to the FBI. On 18 March 2011 a federal jury in North Carolina convicted him of making coins resembling US coins, of issuing and passing them as current money, and of conspiracy. The government's release said it is a federal violation to create private coin or currency systems to compete with the official coinage. Its prosecutor called such attempts a form of domestic terrorism. That case turned on metal coins resembling US money, so its reach over a clearly different token is less certain.

Digital private money met the same fate through a different law. Liberty Reserve, based in Costa Rica, let users move money with only a name, an email address and a birth date, and made no effort to verify identities. Costa Rica told it in 2009 that it needed a licence, and refused one in 2011. In May 2013 US prosecutors shut it down under the Patriot Act after an investigation across 17 countries, alleging more than $6 billion in laundering, and charged its founder Arthur Budovsky and six others. Moving offshore did not put it out of reach, because its customers and its dollars passed through places the United States could reach.

An offshore bank does not solve this. A bank in the ordinary sense needs a licence from a supervisor other banks trust, a correspondent bank to reach the world, and access to SWIFT, the messaging network banks use. A self-chartered bank has none of these. The Dominion of Melchizedek claimed to have sold about 300 bank licences, and that history is one reason compliance officers treat such licences with suspicion. A licensed bank in a low-tax country is available, and it reports account holders under the Common Reporting Standard and FATCA.

Currency codes are a smaller, real obstacle. Banks book payments using the ISO 4217 list of three-letter codes, and a new currency has no listed code. Even unrecognised governments with real economies run into exchange problems. The Somaliland shilling cannot easily be exchanged outside Somaliland, and the Transnistrian ruble can be exchanged only inside the territory. A state does not guarantee its way out of this either. The Marshall Islands passed a Sovereign Currency Act in 2018 for a national digital currency called SOV, and the International Monetary Fund opposed it. The plan later wound down. That was a recognised state, and it still could not make the idea work.

Crypto is where the law is most unsettled. Holding a token in a wallet needs no bank. Nothing about the software requires anyone's permission, and a court order has to be aimed at a person. In August 2022 the US Treasury sanctioned the mixing software Tornado Cash. On 26 November 2024 the Fifth Circuit appeals court in Van Loon held that its immutable smart contracts do not qualify as "property" under federal law, so the sanctions office lacked authority to sanction the software as such. In March 2025 the Treasury lifted those sanctions. The people were treated differently. A Dutch court sentenced developer Alexey Pertsev to 5 years and 4 months in 2024, and in 2025 a US jury found Roman Storm guilty of conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, on one of three charges. The jury could not agree on the other two charges. A retrial on those is set for 26 April 2027, and as of August 2026 he had not been sentenced and his request for acquittal was undecided. So what remains open is how far software that no one controls is beyond sanctions in other courts and under other laws, and how far writing such software makes a person a money transmitter. One appeals court's reading of one statute does not answer those questions worldwide.

Follow a treasury through a real month. Suppose a community holds $20 million in stablecoins, tokens tied to the dollar, and wants to buy diesel. The fuel supplier wants dollars in a bank. A regulated exchange must identify the sender and the recipient under the Travel Rule, the international standard on money transfers, and must check sanctions lists. Stablecoin issuers can often freeze tokens at a regulator's request, and in the United States issuers now fall under the GENIUS Act of 2025. If tokens were sold to members with hope of profit, the regulators who sued over New Utopia's bonds can come back in, and EU buyers bring in the MiCA rules. Any American running the accounts is bound by US sanctions wherever they sit. Reading the money transmission cases, it seems that if the community's treasury moves funds on behalf of members, the person doing it could be treated as an unlicensed transmitter in the places members live, though the result would vary by country and has not been tested for a self-described national treasury.

The potential as a members' token is modest and real. The raam, issued by the Global Country of World Peace, was accepted by some businesses in Iowa and the Netherlands. A closed token that works as membership credit or a local exchange unit is a common idea, kept small and not represented as legal money. The strongest version has a token used only among members for goods and services, no promise of profit, and a reserve of ordinary money in a licensed bank or regulated custodian, with honest tax reporting by members. This gives a community an internal economy. Outside its circle, every payment still crosses into a system run by states, and the community would be a customer of that system.

territorial-sea.essay:
The territorial sea is the belt of water next to a coast. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a country may set it at up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 km) from its baselines, the lines from which sea zones are measured (Article 3). The normal baseline is the low-water line on the country's official charts (Article 5).

Inside this belt the coastal country has full authority over the water, the seabed under it and the air above it, the same as over its land (Article 2). The main limit is innocent passage, the right of foreign ships to pass through peacefully and without delay (Articles 17 to 19). A private road that the owner must let travellers use is similar, since a traveller may drive through and may not stop and build a house. Passage has to be continuous, and stopping is allowed only for ordinary navigation, emergencies or helping people in danger (Article 18), so settling in one spot falls outside it.

A further belt, the contiguous zone, can reach out to 24 nautical miles if the country declares one. There the country may act to prevent or punish customs, tax, immigration and health offences committed in its territory or territorial sea (Article 33).

The practical result is that a structure here is a domestic building project. Suppose a group anchors a platform 5 nautical miles off a coast and declares independence. The group is inside the country, in the same legal position as someone who puts up an unapproved building on land and announces that it is a new state. Harbour, building, tax and police officials all have ordinary powers. A nearby officer can visit, and the group's boats have to land at that country's docks.

Giorgio Rosa's Rose Island shows how little room there is even near the line. His 400-square-metre platform stood nearly 12 km off Rimini, a few hundred metres outside Italian waters as they were then measured. The Rimini harbour office asked him to stop in late 1966. He declared independence on 1 May 1968, and police and tax officers took control on 26 June, about eight weeks later. A project inside the limit would not even have the argument about position that Rosa made.

The line itself is less simple than it looks, and two British cases teach this. Roy Bates ran a pirate radio station on Knock John, a wartime fort about 16 km off Essex, where British broadcasting law could reach him only if the fort lay inside the three-mile limit then used. Distance is measured from a line set by law, which need not follow the shore. Magistrates fined him £100 in 1966, and his appeal failed when the court held that the fort lay on the landward side of that line. Radio 390, on Red Sands fort, lost in the High Court in December 1966, two judges to one, because the distance could be measured from a sandbank that shows only at low water. UNCLOS keeps the same idea today. Land that shows only at low tide can serve as a baseline if it lies within the territorial sea's width of the coast (Article 13). Neither fort had moved. A person therefore cannot judge the limit with a map and a ruler from the beach.

A country can also move the line. Bates went on to Roughs Tower, which he declared to be Sealand in 1967. The fort sits about 6 to 7 nautical miles off the English coast, or about 11 to 13 km, and at that time it was outside British waters. A British court said so in 1968, when it held that it could not try his son on firearms charges there. In 1987 the UK extended its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles, which put the fort in waters recognized as British. Offshore installations and artificial islands, for their part, do not count as harbour works and cannot push the boundary out in the builder's favour (Article 11). So the limit can grow toward a project, and a project cannot grow the limit.

Three real projects show what is possible when the country's law is accepted from the start. The Seasteading Institute of San Francisco chose French Polynesia, a self-governing French territory, for its calm lagoons. In January 2017 the territory's government signed a memorandum of understanding with the institute, a document that records intentions and is usually weaker than a contract. It opened the way to studies of "seazones" with a special governing framework, and the institute formed a company, Blue Frontiers. Residents objected and opposition politician Valentina Cross protested. On 28 February 2018 it was reported that the government considered the deal to have no legal force and to have expired at the end of 2017. Nothing was built. The memorandum had bound the government to very little, so it could simply let the plan lapse.

SeaPods came from Ocean Builders, the same company whose cabin off Phuket was raided by the Thai navy in 2019. It turned to homes at Linton Bay Marina in Panama, with $100 deposits and prices from about $295,000 to $1.5 million. Each home stands above the water on a float tethered to the seabed by anchors. At the unveiling on 22 September 2022, in front of an audience that included Panama's president, the prototype tipped over with people inside. The company blamed a failed bilge pump, the pump that clears water from a hull, and denied that it sank, and no injuries were reported. Guests were staying in one by June 2023. The company claims no independence, and the number of permanent residents is not known.

Oceanix Busan is the largest of the three. On 18 November 2021 the city of Busan in South Korea, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX agreed to build a prototype floating district, with about $200 million anticipated as the cost, and they unveiled the design at UN Headquarters in April 2022. At the developers' later figure of $10,000 per square metre, its 15.5 acres would come to about $627 million. A conference in October 2023 gave no concrete financing or construction plans, construction is not known to have started, and no one is known to live there. This project attempts to build on the sea while staying fully inside South Korean law.

The ordinary bumps follow from being inside a country. Permits come first, and residents can stop them, as in French Polynesia. Ocean Builders' cruise ship plan outside national waters collapsed in 2020 when no insurer would give liability cover, which shows how much depends on insurance anywhere at sea. Tax on residents stays as it was. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income, and the host country may tax local income too. Medical care, schooling, inheritance and birth records run through the country's normal systems, which is an advantage for families. Police and courts have the same reach as on the shore, so a dispute over a floating home would go to an ordinary local court.

The common misunderstandings come from treating water as different from land. A boat's flag does not take a settled home out of the coastal country's law, since passage rights do not cover staying. A declaration does not change the zone either. Stuart Hill, who declared a Shetland islet the state of Forvik in 2008, was still charged with motoring offences in a Scottish court. Recognition is as far away as it is anywhere else, since UN membership needs nine of 15 Security Council votes with no veto and two-thirds of the General Assembly.

What can be built here is a licensed floating neighbourhood or marina, or at most a special zone written into the host country's law by its legislature. Calm water, short supply lines and a nearby hospital make building here among the easier options at sea, and holding out against the coastal country close to impossible. Any self-government lasts only as long as that country's politics allow, and a memorandum alone gives no protection.

buffer-zones.essay:
When two armies stop fighting, they often agree to pull back from each other and leave a strip of land between them, so that a stray shot or a patrol does not restart the war. That strip is a buffer zone. Because no army is meant to hold it, it can look on a map like land that belongs to nobody, and people interested in empty places sometimes wonder whether a new territory could be set up there. It cannot, and the reasons say a good deal about how ceasefires work. The surrounding countries, or the parties to the ceasefire, keep their claims. A peacekeeping force or a ceasefire body controls entry. The strip is an arrangement between the two sides, and the land inside still belongs to someone in law.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone is the most guarded example. It was created by the armistice, or ceasefire agreement, of 27 July 1953. Under it, each side moved back 2,000 metres from the front line, leaving a zone about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. Only two villages are allowed to remain inside. Daeseong-dong, also called Tae Sung Dong or Freedom Village, is on the southern side, governed and protected by the United Nations Command. It had 218 people in 2008, descended from those who owned the land before the war. They must generally spend at least 240 nights a year there to keep their residency. They count as South Korean citizens and do not pay tax or do military service. Kijŏng-dong, or Peace Village, is on the northern side. Only North Korea or the UN Command can give access. In January 2026 the UN Command strongly opposed South Korean bills that would give Seoul authority over non-military entry, calling them completely at odds with the armistice and stressing its role as the zone's administrator. If South Korea's own lawmakers meet that response, a private founder has little room. Those villagers' special position comes from the armistice and from their families' earlier ownership of the land. A newcomer has no route in, and the edges of the zone are among the most heavily armed borders in the world.

The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, also called the Green Line, shows a much more lived-in version. It began in 1964 and was extended after the ceasefire of 16 August 1974, which followed the Turkish invasion and split the island. It runs 180 kilometres across the island and covers 346 square kilometres, ranging from under 20 metres wide in places to over 7 kilometres, and it cuts through the capital, Nicosia. The UN force in Cyprus patrols it. Four villages lie inside it. Their listed populations in 2021 were Athienou 9,721, Pyla 2,771, Troulloi 1,175 and Deneia 373, about 14,000 people in all. Pyla is the only village, by the UN force's account, where Greek and Turkish Cypriots live side by side. The UN divides the zone into two kinds of ground. In the Civil Use Areas, which include these villages, people may enter freely. Everywhere else, civilian activity needs specific authorisation from the UN force, which weighs security, ownership and its own operations when dealing with civilian building. It handles about 1,000 incidents a year. These are people who were already there, or their descendants, and they remain citizens of an existing country. Crossing was very limited until April 2003, when the Turkish Cypriot administration eased its restrictions after nearly 30 years.

A person might assume that such a mixed village, in a place neither side fully governs, would be a good place to declare something new. No one has been reported trying to declare a separate state in the zone, and small events show how closely the ground is watched. In 2009 UN troops stopped villagers in Mammari, a Civil Use Area, from gathering wild asparagus in nearby fields, saying the fields were in a restricted area near Turkish military outposts. Access to restricted ground required a request to the UN. In August 2023 de facto Turkish security forces attacked UN peacekeepers near Pyla in a dispute over unauthorised construction, seriously injuring three, and the Security Council called it a violation of the status quo, meaning the existing situation that is meant to stay unchanged. In 1996 two Greek Cypriot protesters were killed during protests against the division, one beaten and one shot while climbing a flagpole. A newcomer's building or flag would land in that setting, and it would need authorisation from a force whose job is to prevent changes.

The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone is a different kind of no-go strip. It was emptied because of radiation, with no army line involved. The 30-kilometre zone in Ukraine and Belarus was evacuated after the 1986 nuclear disaster, about 100,000 people in all. About 1,200 people returned in 1986. They are called samosely, meaning self-settlers. Most were elderly people who had lived there before the disaster. Many had been told they could go home in a few days, and they then faced discrimination in the areas where they were resettled. Some outsiders came too. Ukraine's government has not legalised their settlements, because living in the zone remains prohibited. A bill backed by Ukraine's parliament at first reading in July 2021 proposed fines of 17,000 to 42,500 hryvnia or restriction of freedom for illegal entry, and whether it passed in that form is not known. A minister said in 2013 that they receive full social support, and local officials have unofficially let elderly settlers stay.

The samosely show what tolerance looks like. Officials look away because the people are old, few and doing no harm, and because the state already pays them social support. They depend on the same state for help, which leaves them far from independent. Their number has fallen mainly through old age, from 314 in a 2007 census to 135 in 2017, and a Ukrainian report in April 2026 put the number left at about 25. Russian forces occupied the area in 2022, and residents have described that time as frightening. None of them has declared a separate state, and they remain residents of the countries that run the zone.

Several misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that a ceasefire strip is a gap in sovereignty, the legal right to rule a place. A ceasefire only pauses a fight, and the claims remain in place on both sides. The UN General Assembly's Friendly Relations Declaration of 1970 says this in its own way. States must not use force to violate international lines of demarcation such as armistice lines, and that duty does not affect the parties' positions on the status of those lines. Another is that peacekeepers are a kind of government that could be persuaded to let a project go ahead. Their job is to keep the two sides apart under the terms given to them, and they have no power to give away land. A third is that a place with no tax, like the Korean village, is free of the state. Its residents hold those exemptions because of special rules from an armistice, and they are still South Korean citizens. A fourth is that physical emptiness means legal emptiness. Chernobyl has been sealed for 40 years, and two governments still run it.

The risks of trying are serious. In the Korean zone, entry without permission means walking into a military frontier. In Cyprus, unauthorised activity outside the Civil Use Areas meets UN patrols, and the 2023 clash at Pyla shows how quickly construction can involve armed forces. At Chernobyl, living in the zone is prohibited, and the radiation that emptied it remains a health issue for anyone new.

There is no way to set up a self-governing territory here. The realistic options are to study or visit where that is allowed, and to work with those trying to reduce tension, such as the bicommunal life of Pyla. People do live in these zones, under peacekeepers or military authorities, and that leaves no room for a new government. For that reason the chances of building something are put at about 10 percent, law and holding at the same low level, and recognition at a tenth of a percent, and the chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower. Nothing in the known record gives a legal basis for self-rule in such a place.

lagrange-cislunar.essay:
The space between Earth and the Moon is sometimes called cislunar space, meaning "on this side of the Moon". It has no ground. Anything placed there is a craft that keeps moving, and the Moon itself, about 385,000 kilometres from Earth, is the far edge of the region. Within it, and in the wider neighbourhood of Earth's path around the Sun, are special positions called Lagrange points. They are named after a mathematician, and they are places where the pull of two large bodies, such as the Earth and the Sun or the Earth and the Moon, balances in a way that lets an object keep its position relative to them while using little fuel.

NASA describes five such points for any pair of large bodies. Three of the five, called L1, L2 and L3, are like a ball balanced on the top of a steep hill. Any small push moves an object away, so a craft there needs constant small adjustments to stay in place. The other two, L4 and L5, are like a ball in a bowl. If an object there is pushed a little, it tends to return. L4 and L5 sit 60 degrees ahead of and behind the smaller body along its orbit. A point is a mathematical position, and nothing about it can be fenced or occupied the way a piece of land can. For the Earth and the Sun, NASA puts the first and second points about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, which is roughly four times the distance to the Moon.

The law here is the ordinary law of outer space, and no separate treaty covers this region. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, makes space free for all to use in Article I and bars any country from taking it over in Article II. Article VI makes countries responsible for space activity, including private activity, which needs their permission and continuing oversight. Article VIII gives legal power over a craft, and over the people aboard, to the country that registered it. Being at a Lagrange point changes none of that, so a craft at L5 is in the same legal position as a craft in low orbit. Two operators who both want to be near L5 have only the general duty of Article IX, which asks each country to pay due attention to the interests of others.

Two further documents add detail for some countries. The Moon Agreement, a treaty on the Moon and other bodies in the solar system, says in Article 1(2) that references to the Moon include orbits and paths around it. Its rules, including its treatment of the Moon as the common heritage of mankind, therefore reach parts of this space, but only for the 17 countries that have joined it. The Artemis Accords, a set of principles for space activity, ask signing countries to register their objects (Section 7), release scientific data (Section 8), and give notice of operations inside "safety zones" to avoid harmful interference (Section 11). Section 1 names "the Lagrangian points for the Earth-Moon system" among the places they cover, and it limits them to civil activities of the signers' space agencies. The Accords describe themselves as a political commitment, so they do not create rights that a court could enforce.

The idea of living at these points has a real history. In September 1974 the physicist Gerard O'Neill published "The Colonization of Space" in the magazine Physics Today, describing colonies at Lagrange points. Keith Henson and Carolyn Meinel of Tucson, Arizona, read it and wrote to him, and in August 1975 they incorporated the L5 Society, named after the point. Its first newsletter set the long-range goal of disbanding at a mass meeting at L5. O'Neill's book The High Frontier followed in 1977. No hardware was ever built, and critics said transport costs were far too high for individuals to pay. The society's real effect was political. In 1979 and 1980 it campaigned against the Moon Agreement, arguing that treating the Moon's resources as the shared property of humanity would make space colonies impossible, and the United States never ratified that treaty. In 1987 it merged with the National Space Institute to form the National Space Society, which still operates. Later work on a design called Kalpana One reflects a change of view. The Moon's L4 and L5 points are now thought too far from the Moon and Earth, and a settlement there would spend about two-thirds of its time outside the protection of Earth's magnetic field.

Suppose a private group wants to put a small habitat at the Earth-Moon L5 point. The group needs a launching country and an entry on that country's register, in the same way as a station in low orbit. In the United States, a launch needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. Whichever country registers the habitat then holds legal power over it and everyone inside.

The second step is radio. The habitat must talk to Earth, and the frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. A national authority must file on the group's behalf, and that gives that country's regulator a say over the project. Supplies are the third step. The habitat depends on Earth for radio frequencies and for deliveries, and supply runs here would be harder than to low orbit. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit alone, and a person needs about 2.77 kilograms of food and 0.84 kilograms of oxygen each day. Even the International Space Station, which has reached 98 percent water recovery, relies on deliveries. It costs about $3 billion a year to run.

The fourth set of bumps concerns people. A resident needing a surgeon faces a trip of days to reach Earth. The Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, requires members to help spacecraft crews who land in distress and return them to the launching authority, which means a country or a qualifying international organization. A self-declared state appears to have no standing under it. Crime would fall under the law of the registering country, and US citizens would still owe US tax returns. A child born aboard would take nationality from whatever the parents' countries provide, because the Outer Space Treaty does not mention birth. One operator's debris endangers everyone nearby, and no one can fence off the surroundings.

A common misunderstanding is that a point with no ground and no neighbours must be free of law. In fact the law travels with the craft through its register. Another is that being first at a Lagrange point gives a right to stay there alone. Article I keeps it open to others, and a safety zone under the Accords lasts only as long as the work and binds only those who signed. A third is that declaring a nation at L5 could meet the usual test of statehood, the Montevideo Convention of 1933, which asks for a defined territory. A position in empty space that no one may claim does not provide one.

What could be built lawfully here is a licensed, registered station at or near one of these points, operated by a company under the supervision of a cooperating country. Residents could agree among themselves by contract how daily life is run, within that country's law. No published plan for a private settlement here is known. The chance of building one is estimated at about 3 percent, and the chance of holding on against outside control at about 20 percent, because supply lines to Earth and the registering country's authority stay in place the whole time. The chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower.

combo-platform-with-sinking-state.essay:
Several low-lying Pacific countries expect rising seas to make their land hard to live on. They are real states with UN seats, large sea zones and few resources for adaptation. A founder might propose a partnership. The founder would finance floating or raised platforms in the state's own sea zone, and the state would grant a charter and its legal cover. If the land one day disappears, the platforms might be part of how the state continues. This combines a coastal zone, a host's grant and the idea of a state without ordinary territory. It has never been done.

The sea-zone part is settled. Article 60 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives a coastal state the exclusive right to authorise artificial islands in its exclusive economic zone, and sole legal power over them. So a small island state could lawfully permit a platform in its own waters. Article 60(8) also says such a platform is not an island and has no territorial sea of its own. In 2011 Kiribati's president Anote Tong mentioned floating islands, comparing them to oil rigs, at a cost of about $2 billion, and his government went on to buy land in Fiji instead.

The question of what happens to the state is moving quickly and is not closed. The usual test for statehood, in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, includes a defined territory. Pacific states have argued that a state continues even if its land is fully inundated, and that its zones continue. The Pacific Islands Forum issued a declaration on statehood in 2023. In its 2025 advisory opinion on climate change, the International Court of Justice said that loss of territory "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood", and that UNCLOS does not require states to update baselines once they are established. Judge Peter Tomka wrote separately that "territory has been indispensable to the concept of a State". On 24 September 2026 all 193 UN members adopted by consensus a political declaration that states a presumption in favour of continued statehood despite sea-level rise, and says that states may keep their maritime zones once baselines are set. Harry Aitken, an Australian diplomat who led negotiations on the declaration's legal elements and who writes in his personal capacity, describes this as a beginning, and the declaration's legal force and working details remain to be shown through what states do. Australia and Tuvalu signed the Falepili Union treaty on 9 November 2023, and it entered into force on 28 August 2024. Australia's foreign ministry says it is the first legally binding treaty to recognise that a state continues despite sea-level rise.

The reported texts do not address platforms. Reading them, it seems that continued statehood is grounded in the state's existing legal identity and in other states' agreement to keep treating it as a state. A platform would be useful for housing people and would not itself supply the missing territory, since Article 60(8) denies it island status. Whether a state whose only physical presence is a set of platforms in its own zone would be treated as the same state is an open question. The presumption in the 2026 declaration would help it. Tomka's view would count against it, and no court has decided.

Follow how the partnership might go. The first problem is consent. The declaration speaks of "mobility with dignity" and says that relocation must be voluntary. A foreign investor offering to build the future home of a nation, in exchange for a charter, is asking a small state and its voters to give up something sensitive, and the French Polynesia case shows that local opposition can end such a plan even when ministers agree. The second is money. Kiribati's figure of $2 billion came with the remark that other countries would have to pay. It appears that aid of that kind would reach the state first, so a private founder would depend on the government for it. The third is control. Article 60(2) gives the host fiscal and immigration power, and the host could revoke a charter later, as Honduras's court ended its zones in 2024. For the founder, the state's recognition is the main asset, and the founder cannot own it. The state's UN seat, passports, bank links and treaties are the state's own. The founder's residents would need to be the state's citizens or permitted foreigners, so the state's nationality law would decide who may live there. Tuvalu's own plan so far has been a digital archive of its land and culture and agreements with other countries that it stays a state, which suggests where its priorities lie.

The potential for a lawful platform is higher than for other platform routes, in one specific sense. This is the one situation in which a platform would stand under a recognised state that has a strong reason to want it and whose continued existence other states have just promised to presume. Banks, insurers and ports would be dealing with a real government. The strongest version is led by the state itself, with outside finance on ordinary commercial or aid terms, with residents' consent, under the state's own law. What it cannot offer is a new country for the founder. The sovereignty would be that of the existing state. A founder seeking control would be asking that state to give up what it is working to keep, and the French Polynesia case suggests how local voters may respond. The recognition figure below refers to a new separate entity. The host itself already has recognition.

combo-eez-permit-own-charter.essay:
Most attempts to live beyond a state's reach have ended with a raid or a lack of money. This idea takes the opposite approach. A group asks a coastal country for permission to build a platform in that country's sea zone, and it also asks for a special law that gives the platform its own courts, tax rules or internal government. It combines the exclusive economic zone, which reaches up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, with the zones that countries have carved out on land, such as the Dubai International Financial Centre.

The sea part of the law is clear. Article 60 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives the coastal state the exclusive right to build and to authorise artificial islands and certain structures in this zone. It also says that the coastal state "shall have exclusive jurisdiction" over them, including "customs, fiscal, health, safety and immigration laws". Artificial islands have no territorial sea and change no boundary (Article 60(8)). The state may set a safety zone of up to 500 metres around them (Article 60(5)). Beyond that, other countries' ships remain free to pass (Article 58). So a platform with a permit is entirely legal, and it remains within that country's authority.

The land part is also clear in principle. A country may pass a law setting up a zone with its own rules. Dubai's financial centre has had its own common-law courts since 2006. Próspera in Honduras ran on its own regulations, and it shows the danger. On 20 September 2024 the Honduran Supreme Court declared the zone laws unconstitutional with retroactive effect, and the company is now pursuing an investment claim against the state at a World Bank tribunal.

The open question lies where the two meet. Article 60 says the coastal state "shall have" exclusive jurisdiction. Reading the text, it seems that this is a statement of who holds power against other countries, and that nothing in it stops the state from using its own law to delegate daily functions to a local body, as it might for a port authority or a free zone. It is less clear whether a coastal state could promise never to apply its own criminal or immigration law to the platform. UNCLOS does not say, and no case has tested a charter of this kind at sea. A second open matter is classification. UNCLOS does not define "artificial island", so it is uncertain whether a moored floating platform falls under Article 60(1)(a) in every case or only under the rule for structures with an economic purpose. For a project with permission this hardly matters, because the state has authorised it either way. It matters if the state later revokes the permit and the operator argues that a registered vessel should be free to remain.

The nearest real attempt was planned for a lagoon, closer to shore than the offshore zone discussed here.
