On 13 January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the Seasteading Institute, and it cleared the way for studies of "seazones" with a special governing framework, which would have needed legislation. Local residents objected and an opposition politician asked the government to withdraw. In February 2018 the government's position was reported to be that the deal had no legal force and had expired. Nothing was built. Oceanix Busan, a floating neighbourhood proposed off a South Korean port with the city and UN-Habitat behind it, claims no independence and had no residents reported, with about $200 million anticipated in 2021. Kiribati's president raised floating islands in 2011 and his government instead bought land in Fiji. XLII off Phuket in 2019 is the reverse case, a home placed without permission and raided by the Thai navy, with its occupants charged under a law carrying life in prison or death.

Follow how this would actually go. The founder needs a government willing to pass a law, and a law of this kind is usually a political fight, because voters ask what is being given up. Then come an environmental review, a construction permit, and rules on maritime safety for a structure that the classification societies may not have standards for. The host's own tax and immigration laws apply until the special law displaces them. Banks would look at the host's banking regulator, and this is a real advantage over any independent project, since correspondent banks, the banks that connect others internationally, have someone to rely on. Insurers can price a permitted structure. Staff and residents hold visas under the host's rules. Their home countries still reach them, and a host that has extradition treaties can hand them over. Children born there would take nationality under the host's law and the parents' law.

The largest risk is political. A later government can repeal the law, and a court can strike it down, as in Honduras. Investment treaties may pay compensation, though they do not bring the zone back. Article 60 leaves no neutral fallback, since sole legal power belongs to that same state, and a platform is easier to tow away or close than a town. Reading the text, it seems that a founder would be better protected by a treaty between the host and another state than by a contract alone, but a treaty needs a second government to care.

There is real potential here for a lawful platform with special rules, more than in most sea routes, and it comes from giving up independence at the start. The strongest version would have a stable host with a tradition of special zones, a statute and constitutional change passed with broad local support, an arbitration clause and an investment treaty behind it, and local people sharing in the benefit, which French Polynesia lacked. It would have separate rules in many areas and remain part of the host country. That makes recognition as a separate state very unlikely, and it is not the goal of such a project.

buy-from-a-state.essay:
Buying a house and buying a country sound like larger and smaller versions of the same act. In law they are two different things. When someone buys land, they get ownership, which is the right to use it, fence it and sell it. The right to make the laws on that land, run its courts and collect its taxes is a separate thing called sovereignty, and it stays with the government. A person who owns a whole island still pays that country's taxes. The two can move separately. A classic American Journal of International Law article by Sayre explains that when a territory changes rulers, private owners generally keep their land while political authority passes to the new ruler. Sovereignty moves only when one government agrees to hand it to another, normally by treaty. So the selling country keeps authority until a treaty moves it to the buyer.

Countries have done this many times. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about 2,140,000 square kilometres. It paid Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about 1,717,856 square kilometres. It paid Denmark $25 million in 1916 for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies. Pakistan bought Gwadar from Muscat and Oman in 1958, at a price given as about £3 million or 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees. The most recent sale on Wikipedia's list of such purchases came in 1963, when West Germany paid the Netherlands 280 million Deutsche Marks for Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick. Every buyer and seller on that list is a country or a country-like ruler, and the list leaves out leases. A private buyer has no treaty partner, because a treaty is an agreement between states.

The first obstacle is that a government has to be willing to sell, and governments almost always refuse. The United States has tried to buy Greenland several times, including a secret offer of $100 million in gold in 1946, which Denmark rejected. When President Trump raised it in 2019, the Danish prime minister called the idea absurd. Under section 21 of Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum, so the decision does not rest with one government alone. A September 2026 security agreement involved no sale. Sultan Abdul Hamid II told Theodor Herzl in 1896 that he could not sell a foot of land.

Private attempts have gone the same way. The founders of Minerva and Operation Atlantis looked for a government willing to sell and found none. Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman whose Romanov Empire project issued passports online, talked with several countries, and as of 2017 his talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Freedonia tried to lease land in Somaliland in 2001 and was rejected. No private purchase in the 20th or 21st century is known to have produced sovereignty.

Readers often point out that private buyers did get ruling rights in the past, and this is true. The Liechtenstein family paid 115,000 guilders for Schellenberg and 290,000 for Vaduz because it needed land directly under the emperor to earn a seat in the Imperial Diet. The emperor joined them into a principality in 1719, and it became sovereign in 1806 when Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine took it out of the empire. The Sultan of Brunei's representative granted James Brooke land in Sarawak in 1841, the sultan confirmed the appointment by July 1842, and the family ruled as Rajahs until 1946. The British North Borneo Company bought concessions from the Sultans of Brunei and Sulu in 1877 and 1878, issued laws and set up courts, and handed the territory to Britain in 1946. King Leopold II of Belgium held the Congo Free State as a personal possession from 1885 to 1908, a regime of forced labour and mass death that ended when an international campaign led Belgium to annex it. Each of these rested on an emperor, sultan, king or great power willing to agree, and on an age when empires gave such grants. The International Court of Justice's Western Sahara opinion of 1975 explains how the law saw deals of this kind. Agreements with local rulers were treated as derivative roots of title, meaning that the buyer's title came from the ruler who gave it up. The land was not treated as empty and free to take. The North Borneo Company still needed a British royal charter, and it sold out to Britain for £860,000 in 1946. The Hudson's Bay Company held Rupert's Land, about a third of present-day Canada, under a 1670 charter, granted Lord Selkirk 300,000 square kilometres of it in 1811, and sold it through the Crown for £300,000 in 1869, while sovereignty lay with the Crown throughout. The Knights of Malta bought four Caribbean islands in 1651 with the French king keeping the final right to rule, and sold them in 1665. Jacques du Parquet bought Martinique in 1650, and the king revoked such sales in 1664. The Duchess of Atholl sold the lordship of Man to the Crown for £70,000 in 1765, which took an Act of Parliament. Sark's fief was sold in 1852 with the Queen's permission.

That earlier era also shows who was left out. Many of these purchases were made from peoples who did not understand the terms or who were later told they had no right to sell. Adolf Lüderitz bought coastal land in what is now Namibia in 1883, describing its width in German miles of about 7.4 kilometres to a chief who understood the English mile of 1.6, and Germans called it the Mile Swindle. Lobengula signed the Rudd Concession in 1888 and spent the next years trying to disown it. In Johnson v. M'Intosh in 1823, the US Supreme Court ruled that private buyers could not get good title from the Piankeshaw, because only the government holding sovereignty could buy out Native occupants. In 1835 the Governor of New South Wales declared John Batman's deal with Aboriginal elders for 600,000 acres near today's Melbourne void against the Crown. Virginia and North Carolina cancelled Richard Henderson's purchase from the Cherokee and paid him in land grants.

Today the normal result of buying land is ordinary ownership, and sometimes a very long lease. The Clunies-Ross family owned the Cocos Islands under an 1886 Crown grant while Britain and then Australia ruled them, and Australia paid A$6.25 million for most of their property in 1978. Firestone took up to a million acres of Liberia for 99 years in 1926, and the Golden Triangle zone in Laos runs on a 99-year lease in Lao territory. Kiribati, an actual country, paid $8.6 million in 2014 for about 22 square kilometres of Fiji, and it holds the land as an ordinary owner under Fijian law. Larry Ellison bought 98 percent of Lānaʻi in 2012 for $300 million, and it remains part of Hawaii. The Robinson family keeps Niʻihau closed to most outsiders, and it is still counted within Kauaʻi County. Palmyra Atoll shows how strong private title can be and where it stops. The US government sued the Fullard-Leo family, claiming the atoll had never been private, and the family won at the Supreme Court in 1947, yet the atoll was under US sovereignty the whole time. Martin Coles Harman, owner of Lundy, issued his own coins in 1929 and was convicted, and the High Court upheld that in 1931 because Lundy was part of England.

Even plain ownership can meet resistance if the purchase is large or held by foreigners. Iceland's law bars big purchases by outsiders, and its minister refused Huang Nubo an exemption in 2011 for about 300 square kilometres. Douglas Tompkins's Pumalín Park in Chile ran from the Pacific to the Argentine border, and parliament debated whether he was undermining sovereignty. Madagascar's new leader cancelled Daewoo's 99-year farm deal in 2009 after the protests that helped bring down his predecessor. The Solomon Islands Attorney-General declared a provincial lease of Tulagi unlawful in 2019. Satoshi Island's token sale in Vanuatu collapsed in 2025 because of a breach of the land lease, and Vanuatu had already said that a token gave no right of residence.

Selling is itself a legal hazard for a founder. Gregor MacGregor sold land and bonds in a country called Poyais that did not exist, and at least 180 of the roughly 250 settlers who sailed there in 1822 and 1823 died. Selling shares in a future country can count as selling securities, as Lazarus Long's New Utopia found when the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued him in 1999 over a $350 million bond offering that had raised $24,000.

The workable version is modest. A person can buy an island or a ranch, pay the taxes, run it privately under the rules of the host country and write whatever charter they please for their own members. Reading these rules, it seems that if a government did give up land by treaty to a new government, the title would be strong and hard to undo, and a treaty handover would answer the usual objection to a new state. Since a treaty needs a state on each side, the seller would in effect first have to accept the buyer as a state, as Italy did for the Holy See in the Lateran Treaty of 1929. No private buyer has been offered this. That is why the estimates for legal standing and for holding such land, which assume the handover has already happened, are high in this route, while the chance of it happening at all stays near one percent and the chance of a private group getting its own territory under its own laws is lower still. No such deal is known, and a government would need a reason to give one that outweighs the anger seen in Egypt in 2016, when the announced transfer of Tiran and Sanafir to Saudi Arabia set off the largest protests against the government since 2014.

combo-colony-declares-independence.essay:
Most routes to independence in space try to escape states before leaving Earth. This one accepts every licence and register on the way out, then declares independence once the settlers have arrived. It combines settling a distant body with the law on breaking away, and it has some of the historical logic of a colony that outgrows its parent. Since nobody lives off Earth permanently yet, all of it rests on reading rules made for other purposes.

Some things are clear. Issuing a declaration is not itself against international law. The International Court of Justice said so in 2010 about Kosovo, by 10 votes to 4. That opinion was narrow, and it does not mean that a declaration creates a state or that others must accept it. Self-determination, the right of a people to decide its political status, is recognised in the UN Charter and in later UN instruments, and it applies clearly to colonial peoples and those under foreign occupation. The Supreme Court of Canada's 1998 opinion on Quebec held that international law gives no general right to break away from a state that governs all its people without discrimination. The usual tests for statehood come from Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries.

Space law adds its own rules. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, says the state of registry keeps jurisdiction and control over registered objects and any personnel in space or on a body. Article VI makes states answer for national activities. It does not end when a group of nationals stops listening. Neither article has any time limit or distance limit. Article II says bodies in space cannot be appropriated by claim of sovereignty, use, occupation or any other means. All this binds states.

The open part is large. The first question is whether a new state can come into being on a body where the treaty bars appropriation. The prohibition speaks of "national appropriation". A writer in Völkerrechtsblog, citing others, holds that it applies to anyone acting under state authority, and that exercising jurisdiction would count as a sovereign claim. Settlers who had broken away from their state would say they no longer act under it. Reading the text, it seems that the new body, not being a party, would not be bound by the treaty except through custom, while all parties would remain barred from treating any part of Mars as national territory, and that includes recognising it as such. Whether recognising a new state on Mars counts as appropriation by the recognising state has never been discussed by any court. A second question is the meaning of "defined territory". A settlement could say its buildings are the territory, since Article VIII protects ownership of objects, but objects are not territory. The third is whether settlers would be "a people" for self-determination. They would be a small voluntary group of various nationalities in the first generation. Children born there, and later generations, would have a far stronger claim on any reading. The Mars Society has run a design contest for a Martian city state of one million people, and how a settlement could move to self-rule under the treaty has not been settled.

Follow the events. A settlement of some thousands, under the register of one state, passes a resolution of independence. That state's first response is legal. It announces that its law still applies under Article VIII, and that it remains responsible under Article VI. It would be under pressure to show it is supervising, because the treaty requires it. It holds powerful tools, since supply ships, launch licences, spare parts, data links and the settlers' bank accounts all depend on Earth. A Mars transit window comes only every 26 months or so, so a cut-off would take effect slowly and be hard to reverse. Settlers' relatives and property stay on Earth, and the home state can act against them where they are in its reach, and against any settler who returns. The settlers' own treaties, passports and currency would have no standing without a recognising state. The rescue treaty speaks of returning astronauts to the launching authority, which then is the state they broke from.

Force is unlikely, and that is what makes this different from other routes. No navy reaches Mars in less than months. The home state might prefer to negotiate, and Canada's opinion about the duty to negotiate, though about a very different case, shows how law might respond to a clear vote. If a settlement can feed itself, the leverage falls year by year. Other states' interests also matter. A rival power could recognise it for its own reasons, as Russia did for Abkhazia and South Ossetia in 2008, which brought few followers and much dependence.

This route addresses independence more directly than most space routes, while the chance of getting a territory under the settlers' own laws is very low, and it can only arrive late. The strongest version has a large, self-sufficient, multi-generation population, a negotiated transition with the state of registry, a new treaty among interested states revising Article VIII for this case, and a government that has been running its own affairs for decades. Nobody can say when this could happen, and it lies well beyond a 25-year horizon. The route also tends to work best when the parent is willing, in which case the outcome looks like ordinary decolonisation.

orbital-megastructures.essay:
A megastructure, in this context, means a human-made object in space far larger than any spacecraft flown so far. Two kinds have been proposed as places to live or work. The first is the giant space habitat, a spinning wheel or cylinder in which the spin presses people against the inner wall and imitates gravity. The second is the space elevator, a cable running from the ground up into orbit, with climbing machines carrying people and cargo along it. None has been built. They raise the same legal question as any spacecraft, and the elevator raises an extra one because it touches Earth.

The Stanford torus came from a NASA summer study at Stanford University in 1975. It is a ring 1.8 kilometres across, turning once a minute, for 10,000 residents, with a total mass of about 10 million metric tons. About 95 percent of that would be a radiation shield of raw soil from the Moon, and the site would be the Earth-Moon L5 point, a stable spot in the Moon's orbit. Kalpana One, a design revised by Al Globus in 2007, is a cylinder with a 250-metre radius and a length of 325 metres for 3,000 people. The McKendree cylinder of 1995 has a 460-kilometre radius and a length of 4,600 kilometres. The Bishop Ring of 1997 has a 1,000-kilometre radius and about 3 million square kilometres of land, close to the size of India, held in by walls about 200 kilometres high and needing carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms. All remain on paper.

The cost problem is simplest to see through mass. At the Falcon 9 rocket's price of about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, lifting the 10 million tons of a Stanford torus from Earth would cost about $32 trillion, by simple arithmetic, before any construction. That is why the design relies on Moon soil, and using it would require an industry on the Moon that does not exist. Even the 5 percent not made of soil would come to about $1.6 trillion at that rate. For comparison, the International Space Station costs about $3 billion a year to run. Large colonies have been designed since 1975 and have never been funded, so the chance of building one is estimated at about 2 percent.

The law for the habitat is short, and it does not change with size. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 is the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty member. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space. Article VII makes countries liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage caused by their space objects. Under the Liability Convention, a later treaty on that subject, a launching country pays without any need to prove fault for damage on Earth or to aircraft, and pays for damage in space if it was at fault. A launching country includes one that launches, pays for the launch, or whose territory is used. A ring with 10,000 residents would legally be the same as a small satellite with a very large crew, under one country's register. Nothing in the treaty turns an object into territory because people live on it.

A habitat built in parts by different countries could follow the International Space Station. A 1998 treaty among its partners leaves each with legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens on board, and no single legal authority covers the whole station.

The elevator adds a physical link to Earth. The cable is held taut by a counterweight far out in space. The stated technical obstacle is the cable material. Google X, Google's research lab, froze its project in 2014 after finding that no one had made a flawless carbon nanotube strand longer than a metre. A 2016 study by Feng Ding's team suggested small flaws could sharply cut the strength of nanotubes. Obayashi, a Japanese builder, announced in 2012 that it could build one by 2050 with an 8-day climber trip to geosynchronous orbit, where a satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation. Nothing has been built.

Bradley Edwards worked from 2000 on a version with a thin ribbon, supported by NASA's advanced concepts institute. Construction would begin with a seed cable of 19,800 kilograms, and 207 climbers would add material until the ribbon reached about 750 tons and could lift 20 tons per climber. He proposed anchoring it on a movable sea platform in the western equatorial Pacific, to avoid lightning and hurricanes and to shift the ribbon out of the way of space debris large enough to track.

The sea anchor brings in ocean law. Ocean sites are usually in international waters, which could make talks over territory simpler. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, lists building artificial islands among the freedoms of the high seas, says no country may claim any part of the high seas, and says artificial islands get no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has. So an anchor at sea creates no territory. A floating platform registered as a ship flies one country's flag, and a warship may board a ship with no nationality. A land anchor would sit under the law of the country that hosts it. Above the anchor, the cable passes through the air, then space. Over a country, the air belongs to that country under the Chicago Convention, with no stated height limit, and the boundary between air and space has never been agreed. The treaties do not mention elevators at all. Whether a cable fixed to Earth counts as a "space object" is therefore uncertain, and that affects who pays if it falls. Sunao Kai of Nihon University argued in a 2012 conference paper that because an elevator runs from Earth into space, it cannot be analysed under space law alone and has to be read together with the law of the sea and the law of the air. No court or treaty body has ruled on the point. Philip Ragan, co-author of a book on space elevators, said the first country to deploy one could control most space activities.

Fundraising has been its own hazard. LiftPort Group, founded in Washington state in 2003, announced a nanotube plant in New Jersey and a goal of launching an elevator in 2010. The plant was never built, though the company did test a 1,000-foot ribbon held up by a balloon. It faced a state penalty over an alleged illegal share offering and settled without a fine in February 2010. A 2012 Kickstarter campaign raised $110,353 from 3,468 backers, and many have reportedly asked what happened and received no reply. In April 2019 its founder admitted little progress despite more than $200,000 in seed funding.

The common misunderstanding is that size eventually creates a country. A habitat with thousands of residents could meet the population test of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist of statehood, yet it would still have no land the law allows anyone to hold, and it would still be on a government's register. Another misunderstanding is that an elevator in international waters escapes all states. Its platform would need a flag, and launching countries would answer for damage. Everyone aboard either structure stays within reach of the registering country and their home country, and one operator's debris endangers all the others.

A more modest form is a small licensed station registered by a cooperating country, growing in stages. Voyager Station, a proposed wheel-shaped hotel in orbit covered in its own entry, shows how far such plans have got, with no funding announced as of 2024 and no construction begun. The chance of holding out against outside control is estimated at about 12 percent, because launch licensing, liability rules and, for an elevator, the anchor all stay within a state's reach. The chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower.

combo-low-tide-with-claimant.essay:
In disputed seas such as the South China Sea, several countries claim the same reefs. A private founder could not hold such a place alone, since rival navies are close by. The idea here is to approach one of the claimants and offer to develop a reef that dries at low tide, in return for a charter or a concession. The claimant gets a presence that supports its position, and the founder gets a protector. This combines reef law, a territorial dispute and a host government's grant.

Start with what the law says about the reef. A low-tide elevation is natural land that is above water at low tide and under water at high tide (UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, Article 13). The International Court of Justice said in Qatar v Bahrain in 2001 that treaty law is silent on whether such features can be considered territory, and that state practice does not clearly allow or exclude taking them. In 2008, in the Pedra Branca case between Malaysia and Singapore, it held that sovereignty over South Ledge, a low-tide elevation, "belongs to the State in whose territorial waters it lies". In the South China Sea arbitration, decided in 2016, the Philippines asked the panel to find that Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and "not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise". The panel agreed that all three were submerged at high tide in their natural condition, and it said that a feature is judged by its natural state before any building. Its reasoning keeps treating Mischief Reef as a low-tide elevation for the purpose of appropriation even after China built on it. China took no part and rejects the award, and an award binds only the parties, so its reach as a rule is argued over, though its reasoning is widely cited. Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, which has no territorial sea (Article 60(8)).

Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore summarises the working position. A low-tide elevation within a territorial sea comes under the coastal state's sovereignty through its rights over the seabed. One beyond the territorial sea is part of the shelf, where the coastal state has rights over resources. In overlapping zones no state can claim sovereignty over such a feature, and which state holds the rights must wait for a boundary agreement. In the meantime states should make provisional arrangements and avoid unilateral acts.

So the founder's partner may not own what it is offering. The open question is what a permit from one claimant is worth while the zone is undelimited. Article 60 says the coastal state alone may authorise artificial islands in its zone. Reading the text, it seems that the permit is good if that claimant proves to be the coastal state and worthless, or a wrongful act, if it does not, and that nobody can say which until a boundary is agreed. The other claimants would treat the work as a violation at once. How a tribunal would treat a private investor who relied on one claimant's permit has not been tested in this setting.

A real example of a partnership of this kind is Layang-Layang, or Swallow Reef, in the Spratly Islands. Malaysian special forces put up a plaque in 1980 and built an encampment in 1983. Malaysia reclaimed land, raising the area from 6.2 to 35 hectares, and built a runway of 1,367 metres and a navy station. A dive resort operated there under Malaysian licence. China, Taiwan and Vietnam also claim the reef. On 6 January 2025 Malaysia revoked the resort's operating licence and it closed. The investor's position rested on one government's decision, and that government changed it. The example shows the business pattern. It says nothing about the reef's status in law, which would depend on its natural state before reclamation.

Tomás Cloma's Freedomland shows the private version of the idea going badly. He claimed part of the Spratlys in 1956 and asked the Philippine government for support. Taiwan's navy burned buildings there, and in 1974 the Philippines arrested him and made him sign over his rights. The partner he had courted took what he had claimed. The Minerva group in the South Pacific sought no partner, and Tonga annexed the reef in 1972.

Follow how the partnership would work. The claimant's law would apply, because that is the only source of the charter. Its navy decides who may land, and it may want the site for a garrison. Banks and insurers look at sanctions risk and war risk, and they would have to consider that a rival claimant regards the project as illegal. Other governments may warn their nationals off, since a home country's laws can reach its citizens. Workers need visas from the claimant, and their goods come through its ports. If shooting starts, the founder has no standing to negotiate. Under the South China Sea award's reasoning, a rival could later argue that the project sits on its seabed and demand its removal.

The potential for a permitted base is real but narrow. A founder could gain a physical base, a garrison next door and a commercial licence, as the Layang-Layang resort had until 2025. The strongest version would be a place where two claimants agree to joint development, so that the permit comes from both and the dispute is set aside, along the lines Beckman describes as a provisional arrangement. The Mauritius and Seychelles joint shelf is a peaceful model of two states sharing a seabed, though it is not a dispute over a reef. Independence is not on offer in any version, because the only thing that protects the project is a state's claim, and that state's interest is in strengthening its own position.

interstellar-ships.essay:
The nearest star system beyond the Sun, Alpha Centauri, is 4.34 to 4.37 light-years away. A light-year is the distance light covers in a year, so a radio message would take more than four years to get there and the same to come back. A ship that could carry people there would have to travel for a very long time. Designers therefore describe a generation ship, also called a worldship, in which people would live and die during the trip and their descendants would arrive. One report on a recent design competition describes a voyage of 250 years. No such ship exists. Crewed ships exist only as studies and paper designs.

Anyone hoping such a ship could leave every country behind first needs to understand how the law treats a ship once it has left. A ship built to travel to another star would stay under the legal control of the country that lists it on its official register of space objects. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, took effect on 10 October 1967, and 118 countries had joined it as of October 2025. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it "while in outer space" or on a natural body in space. It gives no distance at which this ends.

Read literally, that means the ship carries its registering country's law with it for as long as the voyage lasts. A person born aboard, a century out, would appear to come under the authority of a government that person had never seen. The treaty speaks of "personnel", which is an odd word for a child born on a ship, and it does not mention birth, so whether the word covers such a child is uncertain. The meaning of the word is unclear even for ordinary visitors. One commentary on whose law applies in a lunar habitat suggests that personnel may mean the operator's employees, so that paying visitors may fall outside the article and would have to be bound to the rules by contract. On that narrow reading, a child born aboard would be even less clearly covered. No court or government agency is known to have applied these articles to a voyage between stars, and no one has ruled on what happens to law on a voyage lasting many generations.

Two other articles apply before and during the trip. Article VI says private space activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and that the country answers internationally for that activity. Article VII says countries are liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage their space objects cause. These rules explain why the obstacle comes before departure. A private launch needs a country's approval. In the United States, that means a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million and the power to block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. A group wanting to leave all governments must therefore first persuade one government to approve, register and take responsibility for it. No known project has reached that stage.

The real projects are studies. Project Hyperion was started by the researcher Andreas Hein in December 2011 from a student group at the Technical University of Munich. Its team published a study in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 2012. In 2014 the researcher Cameron Smith used its data to estimate how large a population must be to stay genetically healthy over the trip. A design competition opened in 2024, with results in July 2025, and first place went to the Italian team Chrysalis. Reports do not say how such a ship would be governed.

Icarus Interstellar, a volunteer nonprofit registered in Alaska in February 2011, aims at interstellar flight before the year 2100. Its project Persephone is a design concept for a worldship 20 kilometres long and 5 kilometres across, housing 50 to 500 people. Its activity after 2015 is not known, and it has built no ship.

The 100 Year Starship began in 2010 at DARPA, the US military's research agency, which gave it $1 million, with $100,000 from NASA's Ames center. A workshop in January 2011 listed intellectual property, credibility and governance as immediate problems. In 2012 a group led by the foundation of the former astronaut Mae Jemison won a $500,000 grant and took over the name, moving the project from government to private hands. That year Senator Tom Coburn listed it among the 100 most wasteful federal spending projects. The last activity reported was a symposium in Nairobi in 2023.

Breakthrough Starshot, the one funded plan, carries no people. The investor Yuri Milner announced it in 2016. About 1,000 probes of a few grams each would ride on sails pushed by lasers on the ground, reaching 15 to 20 percent of the speed of light and arriving in 20 to 30 years. It began with US$100 million, with the final cost put at $5 billion to $10 billion. In September 2025 Scientific American reported it was on hold indefinitely, and the physicist Philip Lubin estimated that about $4.5 million had been spent. No formal cancellation has been reported. That final cost estimate is for probes of a few grams each.

Suppose a crewed ship were somehow funded and approved. The questions then follow in order. Before departure come the licence, the register, the radio frequencies coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries, and the question of who insures a craft that never returns. During the trip, no rescue is possible. Article V of the treaty asks astronauts to help each other, and no one else would be near. Everything must be made and recycled aboard. Even the International Space Station, which has reached 98 percent water recovery, still relies on deliveries. The population must be large enough to stay healthy. The researchers F. Marin and C. Beluffi calculated in 2018 that 98 people gave a 100 percent success rate in their simulations of a 6,300-year trip to the planet Proxima Centauri b. Those aboard would need doctors, engineers and teachers from among themselves in every generation.

Governance is where the legal theory and practical reality separate. The ship's officers would be under the registering country's law, and a crime aboard would in theory fall under that country's courts. In practice, no police could reach them, and a message asking for instructions would take years once the ship neared another star. This is why the chance of holding off outside control once under way is estimated as high, about 50 percent, although the chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower. It reflects distance alone. Children aboard would be subject to a law they never chose, though no outside authority could enforce it. The treaty's Article XVI lets a country withdraw on one year's notice, and countries can change or cease over a period of centuries. What would happen to a ship's legal status in such a case has not been addressed.

A common misunderstanding is that leaving the solar system means leaving the law. On paper it does not. Another is that a ship's company could become a nation on departure. The Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist of statehood, asks for a defined territory, and a ship in motion has none. Recognition is estimated at about 0.1 percent, as is the chance of building a crewed ship at all.

What can be done today is what is already happening, namely research papers, design contests and small probes on paper, carried out under ordinary law on Earth. A crewed voyage would need a sponsoring country, which would keep legal control for as long as it and the treaty last.

combo-treaty-organisation.essay:
An international organisation is a body set up by a treaty among states, such as a UN agency. It is treated in international law as a legal person, separate from its members, and it usually gets immunities from the host country in a headquarters agreement. The idea here is a shortcut. A private community or foundation persuades a few friendly small states to sign a treaty creating an organisation around it. The result would be neither a state nor a company. It would be an international body with immunity for its premises and staff, a legal standing that private bodies lack, and a place in diplomatic life. This combines a private project, a host deal and a small treaty.

This has actually happened in a limited way, and the example shows both what works and what it takes. The Global Green Growth Institute began as a think tank in 2010, started by the then President of South Korea, Lee Myung-bak. In 2012 it was turned into a treaty-based international organisation, a change formalised at the Rio+20 summit in Brazil. It has an Assembly of member countries and a Council. Membership is open to any UN member state that shares its aims. So a body that started as a non-state institute did convert into an international organisation, and it took a sitting head of government and a group of states willing to sign.

What is settled is that treaties are made by states. Article 6 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties says every state can make them, and Article 3 notes that international agreements can also exist with other subjects of international law. A private group cannot give itself this status by signing with itself. Any treaty needs at least two real governments, and each one's constitution decides who may sign and whether parliament must approve. Nothing in general international law limits how small those states may be. Small states already earn money from legal services. Tonga rents satellite slots, Nauru sponsored a mining company at the International Seabed Authority, and the Marshall Islands runs a registry.

What such a body gets is defined by its treaty and its host agreement. The Red Cross's agreement with Switzerland shows the kind of thing a host might offer, with immunity for staff, protected premises, tax exemption and secure communications. A UN headquarters district shows the limit, since most local law still applies inside. Host agreements usually cover official acts, so a resident who commits a theft or owes tax would remain under ordinary law.

Follow the steps. Suppose a foundation persuades two small states to sign a treaty, with one hosting. The first challenge is the parties' own politics, since opposition parties can attack a deal that looks like selling sovereignty. Honduras's reversal of its zones, and the $10.8 billion claim that followed, would be on every minister's mind. Next is outside recognition. Other states are not bound by a treaty they did not sign, so a third country need not grant immunity, accept the body's documents or treat its staff as officials. Banks ask who regulates it, and an international organisation with no known member states will look to them like the Melchizedek licences of the 1990s. The International Civil Aviation Organization's passport standard does list codes for certain organisations, such as the UN, but a new body would have to be added, and no state must honour its papers. Sanctions and money laundering rules apply through the banks, and a founder's own nationality can keep them under home law for crimes abroad.

The open questions are real. No treaty sets a minimum number of members for an organisation to count as a true international person. It is not settled whether third states owe any respect to a body created by only two tiny states to house a private community. No court has ruled on such a design, since none has been built. Whether a state may in effect hand its treaty power to a private sponsor by signing whatever it brings is also unsettled. Reading the Vienna Convention, it seems that a treaty is valid so long as states freely consent, and it does not ask why they want it. A later government could still withdraw under the treaty's terms, and if the host withdraws, the body has nowhere to stand.

Fake versions are a known hazard. The Dominion of Melchizedek sold passports and bank licences on the strength of claims to standing, and the Marshall Islands publicly condemned those claims in 1998. A real treaty is ratified by named governments, and that can be checked.

There is potential here, and it is probably the most legally solid way for a paper project to gain standing as an organisation, short of a state's own act. The strongest version is an honest public-interest mission such as ocean rescue, climate records or stateless people's documents, with several states of different regions as members, a public treaty and a real budget. It might gain immunity for its site, an observer seat at some forums and the right to sign agreements. It would have a purpose defined by treaty and be answerable to its member states, so a community that wanted to live by its own rules would have exchanged a government above it for a council of governments above it.

combo-small-state-station.essay:
Ships can fly the flag of a small country with light rules, so people ask whether a station can do the same. A group would launch from some site, then have a tiny state enter the station on its register, and live under that state's nearly empty space law. This is a combination of orbit and the flag-of-convenience practice in shipping. Tonga's history with orbital slots makes it the obvious reference.

Start with what Tonga actually did. In 1987 a businessman named Matt Nilson, who had moved to Tonga, persuaded its king that even a tiny country could apply for positions in geostationary orbit, the ring above the equator where a satellite seems to hold one spot. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates radio use, accepts applications from member countries only. Tonga eventually held nine slots and leased them out, and a company called Tongasat ran the business. In 2018 Tonga's Lord Chief Justice ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. So the small state's right to apply was real, and it stayed the state's right, while disputes grew over who got the benefit. Later filings of a similar kind came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. In September 2021 Rwanda filed for two constellations totalling 327,320 satellites, which shows that a small state can still file for very large systems. Filing for frequencies is a separate act from registering an object, and neither of these cases registered a home.

Registration has a condition the shipping system lacks. Under Article II of the Registration Convention, only a launching state can register an object. A launching state is one that launches or procures the launch, or whose territory or facility is used. So a small country cannot accept any object offered to it. To qualify it would have to procure the launch, which it could do on paper by buying the launch itself or on the group's behalf. Tonga's position also shows a further difficulty. According to the UN's table of 1 January 2026, Tonga has joined the Outer Space Treaty and the Rescue Agreement but not the Liability Convention or the Registration Convention. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty speaks of a "State Party" on whose registry an object is carried. Reading the text, it seems that Tonga could fill that role under the treaty it has joined, with a registry it creates under its own law, and that small states that have joined nothing could not, since the article applies to State Parties.

What is open is whether a country that buys a launch only on paper really counts as procuring it. The treaty does not define "procures". It is also unanswered whether the state of registry must have a real connection to the object. Shipping law has a genuine link requirement (UNCLOS Article 91), although the same treaty does not say what happens if the link is missing, and space law has no such phrase at all. Adrian Taghdiri, writing in 2013, predicted that some countries would write loose rules to attract private space firms, and he warned of debris and of danger to passengers. A presentation to the UN's legal subcommittee in 2016 asked how the shipping concept would fit space objects. No court has ruled on any of this. Reading the text, it seems that a small state could lawfully be the state of registry if it has a real part in the launch, and that registration by a state with no part in it would be open to challenge by others.

What the registry changes is limited. The registering state holds jurisdiction and control over the object and everyone aboard. It is the law of that state that applies, so the founders move from one sovereign to another, and they gain only to the degree that the second one leaves them alone. Article VI still requires authorisation and continuing supervision by the appropriate state. If a small state does none of that, it breaches its treaty duty, and the state in which the founders actually live remains free to enforce its own laws against its own citizens. A US citizen who launches still needs a US licence wherever the launch happens (51 USC 50904), and British founders are subject to the Outer Space Act. The launch site's own country remains a launching state and liable whichever register is chosen, and that country will impose its conditions first. So the launch provider's government decides whether the plan goes ahead at all.

The next steps are as follows. The group pays for a launch from a licensed provider, and the provider's state requires details of who will supervise the payload. A small state with no regulator offers little comfort to that licensing office, and it may refuse if the payload's oversight is unclear. Radio frequencies then need the small state's filing at the ITU, which it has the right to make. Banks would look at the small state's record. Insurers would want a clear legal system. If the station later injures someone or is in trouble, that small country has to answer, and a country with a tiny budget has good reason to set limits. Its law may also change with its politics, and the Tongasat litigation shows that local courts do hear such disputes.

The potential for a station under a friendly flag is real but limited. A small state's register gives a station a lawful home, with fewer rules and a more friendly regulator than a large power would provide. The strongest version is a contract between the group and a small state that has joined the Outer Space Treaty, since a private group cannot be a party to a treaty. Under that contract the state actually procures the launch, sets up a small agency and gets paid for it. That produces a privately run station under a friendly flag, with no independence. The state can still change the deal, and the station would have to live with that risk.

reefs-low-tide-elevations.essay:
A reef is shallow and often far from any town, so founders have often chosen one as a place to start a country. The law treats it according to two facts, whether the feature stays dry at high tide and which legal zone of the sea it lies in.

The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, sorts features by what the sea does to them. An island is naturally formed land, surrounded by water and above water at high tide. A rock is an island that cannot support human habitation or an economic life of its own. It gets a territorial sea, a belt of coastal water of up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 km), and no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf, the wider belts of resource and seabed rights (Articles 3 and 121). A low-tide elevation is natural land that is above water only at low tide. More than 12 nautical miles from land, it has no territorial sea of its own (Article 13). A bank that stays under water at all times, such as Cortes Bank or the Saya de Malha Bank, is simply part of the seabed. Many of the reefs and banks that founders have chosen fall into these last two groups.

In 2016 a panel of judges set up under UNCLOS, in a case the Philippines brought against China over the South China Sea, ruled on this. It found that Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and "not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise". It also held that a feature's status depends on its natural condition, before any building. It found that no feature in the Spratly Islands can generate an exclusive economic zone, and that they cannot do so collectively as a unit. China took no part in the case and rejects the ruling, which formally binds only those two countries. On the panel's reasoning, a low-tide reef cannot be claimed by moving onto it, and it belongs to whichever legal zone it lies in.

That reasoning closes the most natural idea, which is to dump sand until the reef stays dry. Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, and an artificial island generates no territorial sea (Article 60(8)). Building is physically possible, as Minerva's founders showed in 1971 by barging sand from Australia. If the reef is inside a country's exclusive economic zone, the belt up to 200 nautical miles from its coast, that country must authorize the work and sets any safety zone around it (Article 60).

Suppose a group finds a reef 100 nautical miles from a country's coast and starts to build. The first question is whose zone it is in, and a reef that far out normally answers to that country. United States v. Ray shows what happens next. In the 1960s two rival groups, the Grand Capri Republic and Atlantis, Isle of Gold, planned countries on Triumph and Long Reefs, about four and a half miles off southeast Florida, in what were then international waters. The US Army Corps of Engineers refused a permit in 1964, and Louis Ray dredged anyway. A trial court barred building in 1969 and rejected a trespass claim, since the government did not own the reefs. In 1970 the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that the reefs were part of the outer continental shelf, where US law and the Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf give the country exclusive rights to resources, and it ordered a full permanent ban, noting harm to corals and shipping.

The Republic of Minerva shows the other route, which is annexation, meaning a country formally adding the place to its territory. Michael Oliver, a Nevada real estate developer, raised money from about 2,000 investors, and his group declared independence on the reefs between Fiji and Tonga on 19 January 1972. Tonga had not included them in its 1887 claim. At a conference on 24 February 1972, about five weeks later, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed a Tongan claim. Tonga proclaimed the reefs and the waters within 12 miles on 15 June, and an expedition arrived on 18 June. The king came with a convict work party, and the platform was dismantled within hours. In 1982 a group led by Morris Davis, Minerva's former provisional president, tried again, and Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks. Annexing the reef then left two states arguing. Fiji rejected Tonga's sea claims from the reefs in 2005, its navy destroyed navigation equipment there in 2010 and 2011, and the dispute is not known to have been settled. How the 2016 reasoning would apply to Tonga's older claim has not been tested in court.

Other projects ended earlier. Operation Atlantis, begun by the soap executive Werner Stiefel in 1968, lost a concrete boat to capsizing and then to a storm. At Silver Shoals, described in accounts of the project as claimed by both Haiti and the Bahamas, gunboats ordered his group away, and accounts differ on whose they were. Haiti cancelled a lease on Tortuga after officials read the group's newsletter, and a hurricane destroyed an oil rig bound for the Misteriosa Bank. Abalonia, planned in 1966 for Cortes Bank about 111 miles off San Diego, lost its anchor ship when waves broke it up on Bishop Rock. A later plan there, Taluga, was stopped when the US declared the bank part of its continental shelf. Leicester Hemingway's raft New Atlantis, 8 by 30 feet off Jamaica, relied on the US Guano Islands Act of 1856, was refused by the Universal Postal Union when it tried to sell stamps, and was destroyed by storms before any court tested it. Autopia, on the Saya de Malha Bank in the Indian Ocean, stalled for lack of money after a steel frame was built in 2002. Its founders called the site high seas. Most of the bank does lie in international waters, but part lies in the exclusive economic zone of Mauritius, which treats the bank as under its administration, so the position depends on the exact spot.

Money brings its own legal risk. New Utopia, planned for the Misteriosa Bank, was never built and existed as an offer of bonds at 9.5 percent. On 8 April 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued, a judge froze the money, and in January 2000 Lazarus Long, the promoter, accepted a final judgment. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised. Investors, insurers and banks all live in real countries, so their rules reach the project wherever its reef is.

Then come the physical problems. A low-tide reef has no fresh water and no soil, and storms have destroyed rafts, ships and rigs in the cases above. A reef also carries environmental duties. The South China Sea panel held that building land at seven reefs breached a country's duties on the marine environment. Serious medical care means a boat to someone else's port, and people there remain under their home countries' law, including US tax on worldwide income.

Two misunderstandings recur. One is that "international waters" means no one can stop a project. The shelf rules defeated this idea at Grand Capri and Cortes Bank. Another is that a reef beyond every country's zone would be free for the taking. The seabed there belongs to the deep ocean floor regime under UNCLOS, and no country or person may take any part of it as their own (Article 137). A declaration of independence also does not supply the "defined territory" that the Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty defining a state, requires.

The lawful version is modest. A coastal country can license a research or reef restoration station on a reef in its zone, and the station then operates under that country's law. Another version is to give up the reef altogether. A participant in Operation Atlantis says the group later bought Hatchet Caye, an ordinary island in Belize, and lived there until 2005. A reef can offer a physical base for a while. It offers little legal protection, and nearby states have repeatedly acted within months.

exile-and-landless-authority.essay:
A government in exile is a body that claims the right to govern a place while operating from another country. Someone else holds the land. The exile body holds a claim, a community of supporters and whatever standing other governments choose to give it. It helps to picture an office, a set of elected officials and a list of members, all located in a foreign city and all concerned with a homeland they cannot enter or do not control.

This arrangement is different from a micronation, a self-declared small country. A government in exile normally grows out of a real political event at home, such as a flight from an invasion or a declaration of independence that was overrun. The claim therefore rests on a history that many people recognise, and it has a population that cares about it. A person starting from nothing has none of that, and an office abroad with a flag would have the legal standing of a private club.

The law here begins with a question that is not fully settled, which is what makes a state. One view, called the constitutive theory, says a state exists only when others recognise it. The other, the declarative theory, says recognition is not required if the tests in the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty defining a state, are met. Those tests are a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries. Article 3 of that convention takes the second side, saying a state's political existence does not depend on recognition, and what governments actually do typically falls somewhere between the two. A body in exile has trouble under both. Under the first, it depends on others agreeing. Under the second, it does not control the territory it names. The country in control simply keeps the territory, and neither theory gives the exile body any way to remove it.

The longest-running examples show what can be done anyway. The Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic declared independence in Minsk on 25 March 1918, during the German occupation in the First World War, and Germany did not officially recognise it, though it had diplomatic contacts with neighbours such as Finland and the Baltic states. It left Minsk as Bolshevik armies advanced at the end of 1918 and has been in exile since 1919, and as of 2026 it is described as the oldest existing government in exile. A Red Army advance in 1945 forced it to move again, to western Germany. Today it works as an advocacy group among Belarusians in North America, Britain and elsewhere. It says it holds a symbolic mandate that it wants to hand to a democratically elected Belarusian parliament.

The Tibetan case is the fullest working model. In March 1959, as he fled to India, the 14th Dalai Lama, then Tibet's head of government, rejected the 1951 Seventeen Point Agreement with China, and on 29 April he re-established his cabinet in exile. The Central Tibetan Administration, based in Dharamshala in northern India, now has courts, a parliament and an executive under the Charter of the Tibetans in Exile, adopted in 1991 and amended in 2011. That year the Dalai Lama gave up his political duties and executive power passed to an elected leader called the Sikyong. Penpa Tsering was sworn in for a second five-year term in May 2026.

Suppose a community wants to run something like this. The first problem is the host. The body must sit in some country, and that country decides how much activity it allows. It can allow offices, meetings and elections, and it can stop them, since the host's law applies on its soil. Many hosts have reasons to be careful, because the government at home may object. The Tibetan administration operates by India's tolerance.

The second problem is money. An exile body has no territory to tax, and it cannot compel payment. Tibetans abroad make yearly contributions recorded in the Green Book, a document sometimes called a passport, and funding comes mainly from these contributions, private donations and aid from governments such as India and the United States. That aid is given for welfare work, and receiving it does not amount to recognition. No country recognises the administration as a sovereign government, meaning one with the legal right to rule Tibet.

The third problem is keeping people. Voters are scattered, children grow up as citizens of other countries, and each generation must choose to stay involved. Members stay under the law of wherever they live for tax, marriage, inheritance, police and courts. The exile body's papers may have value inside the community, but they do not replace a national passport. The Green Book is sometimes called a passport, and that name does not make it one.

The fourth is pressure from home. Members with relatives or interests in the homeland are exposed there. In June 2023 the Belarusian KGB declared the Rada an extremist group.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic shows how far standing can go when territory and diplomacy are added. The Polisario Front proclaimed it on 27 February 1976 after Spain left Western Sahara. It claims 266,000 square kilometres and controls about 90,000 east of a 2,700-kilometre sand wall built by Morocco, a share given as anywhere from a fifth to 30%. Daily government runs from the Rabuni camp in Tindouf, Algeria, and the camps there held about 173,600 people by a 2023 estimate. It is a full member of the African Union, and counts of recognition range from 33 to 46 UN members. Recognition can also be taken back. Many countries have withdrawn or suspended it, the United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty in December 2020, and in 2026 Mali said it was withdrawing recognition. A referendum promised in 1991 never took place because the two sides dispute who may vote, and on 31 October 2025 the Security Council voted, with 11 in favour, for talks based on Morocco's autonomy plan.

Exile can end in a return, when the government at home changes. Poland's government left the country in September 1939 and sat in London from 1940. France withdrew recognition on 29 June 1945, the United States and Britain on 5 July, and the Holy See last, in 1972. On 22 December 1990 the last exile president, Ryszard Kaczorowski, handed the state symbols to Lech Wałęsa in Warsaw.

Some common ideas do not survive these cases. An exile government does not become a state through age, since the Rada has more than a century behind it and holds no territory. A good internal record does not bring recognition either, as the Tibetan elections show. It is also a mistake to assume that having no land removes all risk. A state has little to seize once a host allows the body to operate, so such bodies tend to last, but the host can change its mind and the home state can act against members.

The form that lasts is a modest one. A real community abroad runs elections, keeps a membership roll, collects voluntary contributions and speaks for its homeland to foreign governments, in a host country that tolerates it. The Tibetan and Belarusian cases show this can last for decades. Its limits are clear in the same cases. It gains no territory by its own efforts, it depends on a host, and whether other governments deal with it is their decision.

unrecognised-state.essay:
Some places run themselves like countries without being accepted as countries. They have a president, a parliament, police, sometimes a currency and an army. A recognised country still holds legal title to the land, while a local government actually runs it. The ownership is therefore disputed. Somaliland, Transnistria, Northern Cyprus and Taiwan are the best known examples, and each is far from what a private founder could create, since all the current cases came out of collapse, war or foreign protection.

To follow how these places work, it helps to separate two questions. One is whether a place meets the practical tests of being a state. The usual checklist is Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty, which asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other states. Article 3 adds that a state's political existence does not depend on recognition by others. The other question is whether other countries accept it, which is called recognition. Recognition is a political decision made government by government, and no court or agency hands it out. A place can pass the first test and fail the second for decades.

Somaliland is the example most often given. It was a British protectorate that united with Somalia in 1960. A war against the government of Siad Barre ended in a declaration of independence in 1991, as Somalia fell into civil war. Since then it has held its own elections and issued its own currency, and it governs most of the land it claims in relative peace, with about 6.2 million people on 176,120 square kilometres. Somalia still claims it. No country recognised it for 34 years, partly because, according to The New York Times, other governments fear recognition could encourage secession elsewhere. On 26 December 2025 Israel became the first UN member to recognise it, and as of October 2026 it remained the only one. That shows how slowly the second question moves, even where the first is well answered.

The UN Security Council can actively keep a place out. When the northern third of Cyprus declared independence in 1983, nine years after Turkey invaded following a Greek-backed coup, Resolution 541 called the declaration legally invalid and asked UN members not to recognise it. Only Turkey does. Other countries treat the area as Republic of Cyprus territory under Turkish occupation. The International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, explained in its 2010 Kosovo opinion that declarations such as this one were condemned because of their link to unlawful force or to other grave breaches of basic international rules, and not because they were one-sided. Courts abroad have applied this. In Loizidou v. Turkey in 1996, the European Court of Human Rights refused to give legal effect to a Northern Cyprus constitutional clause taking over abandoned property, because the international community does not regard the north as a state. The owner kept her title, and Turkey was held responsible because its army had effective control of the area. So a local government's laws may bind people on the ground and still mean nothing to a foreign court. So the north relies on Turkey for economic, political and military support, and its trade goes through Turkey. Trade shows what this means day to day. In the Anastasiou case in 1994, the European Court of Justice held that British authorities need not accept plant health certificates issued by Northern Cyprus, because the system relies on cooperation between recognised authorities. Exporters then shipped through a Turkish port to get Turkish papers, with delays that can spoil perishable goods. This dependence is the usual price. Other governments' refusal of recognition cuts a place off from treaties, banks and UN bodies, and it then needs one patron for what ordinary countries get from many sources.

Consider what daily life looks like. Transnistria, legally part of Moldova, has run its own government, parliament, army, police and post office since a 1992 war, in which Russian troops already stationed there took the separatists' side and about 1,000 people died. Its central bank issues a ruble that can be exchanged only inside the territory. Its citizenship papers are not accepted abroad, so many residents hold Moldovan citizenship, and many also hold Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian passports. Its population fell from 555,347 in 2004 to 475,373 in 2015. Even Russia, which keeps soldiers there, does not recognise it as a state. The money, travel and treaty problems fall on ordinary people, who work around them by keeping a second nationality from a real country.

Rights can be a further problem. A Transnistrian resident told Deutsche Welle he was arrested four times for disrespecting state order. In September 2024 its parliament made public use of the name Transnistria punishable by a fine or up to 15 days in jail.

Force remains the biggest risk, because the recognised country never gave up its claim. Artsakh, the ethnic Armenian government in Nagorno-Karabakh, won a war in 1994 and ran its own president, parliament and elections for about 30 years, relying on Armenia, which never formally recognised it. No UN member did. Azerbaijan retook most of the land in 2020, blocked the only road in December 2022 and attacked in September 2023. Almost the entire population left for Armenia within days, in what is widely described as an effective expulsion, and the president signed a decree dissolving all state institutions by 1 January 2024. On 22 December 2023 he said no official document required the dissolution, and his office called it empty paper. A government in exile was set up in Yerevan, and it holds no land. Since other states had not recognised Artsakh, Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, the ban on force against a state, gave it no obvious protection, and Azerbaijan was acting on land the world accepted as its own. The UN General Assembly's Friendly Relations Declaration of 1970 adds a duty not to use force to violate international lines of demarcation such as armistice lines, without prejudice to anyone's position on the land's status. Whether that wording reached Azerbaijan's 2023 attack is not settled. Rojava in north-eastern Syria, a Kurdish-led administration from 2012, lost most of its land to a Syrian offensive in January 2026 and merged into the Syrian state that August.

A different arrangement can give stability without a claim to be a separate country. Wa State in Myanmar signed a ceasefire in 1989 and has run its own army and administration since then, with the Chinese yuan as money and electricity from Chinese companies. It accepts Myanmar's sovereignty on paper, and Myanmar's 2008 constitution recognises the northern part as a self-administered area. Part of its early income came from opium and heroin, and thousands are reported to have died when 80,000 former opium farmers were forcibly moved between 1999 and 2002. Taiwan sits at the other extreme. It has about 23.3 million people, and its government was a founding member of the UN until the 1971 vote gave China's seat to Beijing. The People's Republic of China refuses relations with any country that recognises Taiwan, so states have to choose, and 11 UN members and the Holy See recognise it. Honduras switched to Beijing in 2023, and its president Nasry Asfura, who took office in January 2026, campaigned on reversing that, while as of February 2026 his government was still weighing the consequences. A population of that size has not been enough to change this.

A person might think that any group could copy these cases by holding land long enough. The cases do not support that. Each began with an existing people in a territory, with fighters or a foreign army, at a moment when a state was collapsing. Somaliland came from a civil war, Transnistria from the end of the Soviet Union, Northern Cyprus from an invasion. A private group that buys land inside a country and declares independence would meet police and tax officers. If it took up arms, it would be charged under ordinary criminal law. None of this can be bought. For that reason the chance of building one from nothing is put at about 3 percent.

The other figures reflect those places that already exist. They hold their land fairly well, with the chance of holding off outside states near even, and their law is firm in their own courts. For a private group, the chance of getting its own territory under its own laws this way is much lower. Recognition as a state stays rare, with the chance put at about 15 percent, with Israel's move on Somaliland as the single recent gain after 34 years of self-rule, and Artsakh as the reminder that a government can run for decades and end within days. For someone already living in one of these places, the realistic approach has been to keep a recognised passport, to rely on foreign currency and patrons, and to expect that the status question may outlast a lifetime. For an outsider, these places teach mainly what full statehood costs, and show that recognition by even one UN member can take a generation.

taking-over-a-state-or-town.essay:
This route starts from something that already exists. Instead of looking for empty water or unclaimed rock, a group tries to take over a government that is already running, either a country's or a town's. The land stays where it is, owned and governed by the same existing country or local government. There are two very different ways to try this. One is to move people in and vote. The other is armed force, usually by mercenaries, meaning soldiers for hire.

A town is a unit of local government. It gets its powers from the state or country around it, and those powers cover local matters such as the town budget, local services and, in many places, the use of land. Moving to a town and voting there is ordinary legal behaviour. Suppose a few hundred people move into a town of about a thousand and elect a majority of its council. They can then cut the budget and change local rules. The next morning, state law, national law, the courts and the tax office apply as they did before. Voters and courts in a town can only change what local government controls, and a council has no power over criminal law, passports or the country's borders.

The first bump is getting enough people to come. The Free State Project, a plan for libertarians (people who favour very limited government) to move to New Hampshire, began in 2001 with an article by Jason Sorens that proposed an independent libertarian nation or, failing that, concessions from the US government. Sorens calculated that 20,000 people moving to one small state could change it. Pledges reached 20,000 on 3 February 2016, and by May 2022 about 6,232 people had moved. In the 2017 to 2018 term, Free Staters held 17 of the 400 seats in the state House of Representatives. A movement called NH Exit Now, formed in 2026, calls for secession, and New Hampshire remains a US state. In Texas v. White in 1869 the US Supreme Court held that a state cannot secede on its own, with no way out "except through revolution or through consent of the States".

The second bump is daily life and cost. A smaller attempt, the Free Town Project, began in 2004 when a splinter group chose Grafton, New Hampshire, for its lack of zoning laws (rules on how land may be used) and its very low property tax. No records were kept of how many came. The population rose from 1,138 in 2000 to 1,340 in 2010, with nearly all the newcomers men, many living in yurts, trailers, tents and shipping containers. They voted through a 30% cut in the small town budget and removed funding for the county's senior citizens' council. Lawsuits they filed to set legal precedents raised the town's costs.

The third bump is the neighbours, and then the higher authorities. The largest case is Rajneeshpuram in Oregon. In 1981 followers of the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh bought the 64,281-acre Big Muddy Ranch for $5.75 million and within three years had built a city of up to about 7,000 people. The nearest town, Antelope, had under 60 people. Its residents voted in April 1982 on dissolving the town to avoid a takeover, and the followers had enough votes to defeat the plan. In May 1982 the ranch voted to become a city. Oregon's attorney general argued that the new city merged church and state, and a land-use group argued that it broke land-use law. Federal Judge Helen Frye ruled against the city in the church-and-state suit in late 1985, too late to matter, and that ruling was not contested. The Oregon Court of Appeals ruled in 1986 that the incorporation had not broken the state's agricultural land goals, and the Oregon Supreme Court closed the litigation in 1987, which left the city vacant and bankrupt but legal under Oregon law.

Criminal cases brought the project down before those lawsuits were settled. In 1984 some leaders deliberately spread disease to lower turnout in county elections, sickening 751 people and sending 45 to hospital, and a plot to kill the US attorney for Oregon followed. Rajneesh, accused of immigration violations, entered a plea without admitting guilt and agreed to leave the country. The commune broke up in 1985.

Armed takeover is a crime in the places involved, and foreign governments, police and informers have usually stopped it early. The first obstacle is money. For the 1981 attempt in Seychelles, an island country in the Indian Ocean, the mercenary Mike Hoare advised raising $5 million, and $300,000 was found. The second is secrecy, because people must be hired and weapons moved. In Operation Red Dog, a 1981 plot by white supremacists against Dominica in the Caribbean, about $70,000 was collected, and the replacement boat captain, Michael Howell, went to the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. On 27 April 1981 nine men were arrested at a New Orleans marina as they prepared to board, with three undercover agents in the group.
