US law punishes preparing, from within the United States, a military expedition against a country at peace with it, with up to three years in prison (18 USC 960). In Seychelles, a security officer at the airport found an AK-47 in the bag of one of the 53 men.

The third is the law of every country along the way. After the Seychelles gunfight, most of the mercenaries hijacked an Air India airliner to Durban. South Africa, which had encouraged the plot, charged them under its aviation law over the hijacking and not over the coup attempt, and 34 served about four months. Hoare himself got ten years and was released in May 1985 under an amnesty, after about three. Seychelles sentenced four captured men to death, and all six prisoners were pardoned after talks and a $3 million payment. In the Wonga Coup of 2004 against Equatorial Guinea, police at Harare airport in Zimbabwe impounded a Boeing 727 with 64 former soldiers and arrested Simon Mann, who served three years in Zimbabwe and was then sentenced in Equatorial Guinea to more than 34 years, until a pardon in 2009.

Bob Denard is often taken as proof that this works. He landed in the Comoros in 1978 with 43 men, overthrew Ali Soilih and for 11 years ran a 500-strong presidential guard under President Abdallah. He held power through a recognised president and founded nothing new, and witnesses at his later trial said French intelligence had supported him. After Abdallah was shot in 1989 Denard left, and when he landed again in 1995 the French army ended the attempt within about a week. A French court later convicted him. He is the one long-lasting case, and his control ended as well.

South Africa's apartheid government declared four homelands, or Bantustans, independent between 1976 and 1981, after the Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 made every Black South African a citizen of one, while saying they stayed South African citizens for purposes of international law. Apart from South Africa and the four themselves, which recognised one another, no government recognised them, so a government's own declaration settled nothing abroad, and they were absorbed back in 1994. Slab City in California, a camp of about 4,000 people in winter and 150 in summer on a former Marine base, has no local government, but California and US law still apply, though they are largely not enforced there.

The open form is winning local office under the existing state's law, and Marinaleda in Spain is its longest example. Landless farm workers there formed the Workers' Unity Collective, won 9 of 11 council seats in 1979 and kept the same mayor until 2023. After a hunger strike in 1980 and a 30-day occupation in 1984, 1,200 hectares of a duke's farm were handed over for local use in 1991. Critics say almost 66% of its income comes from higher levels of government. It remains an ordinary Spanish municipality under Spanish law. The voting route can win local offices and change how a place lives, for as long as the voters stay and the laws above allow it, and final authority stays where it was. Recognition as a new country by this route is close to nil.

combo-always-moving-habitat.essay:
This idea avoids building anything fixed. A community lives on a ship that never stays long in one place, sailing across open ocean, passing through countries' coastal waters and calling at one port after another. It combines a flagged ship with the rule that lets ships pass through a country's waters, called innocent passage. The hope is that a home in constant motion never settles under any coastal government for long enough to be governed by it.

Much of this is settled and in the founder's favour. A ship under a real flag is lawful, and Article 90 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives every state the right to sail ships on the high seas. There, under Article 92, the ship answers only to its flag state. No treaty limits how long a ship may keep sailing. A moving ship also avoids the main rule that stops platforms. Article 60 gives a coastal state control over artificial islands and structures in its 200-mile resource zone, and a ship passing through is not one of these. Article 58 keeps the freedom of navigation in that zone for all countries. MS The World has worked this way since 2002, with residents who own their apartments and elect an advisory board, under the Bahamian flag.

The rules become tighter near a coast. The territorial sea is the belt up to 12 nautical miles from shore, where a country has full authority apart from the right of innocent passage (Article 17). Passage has a specific meaning. Article 18 says it means sailing through without entering port, or going to or from a port, and that it "shall be continuous and expeditious". Stopping and anchoring count only when they are a normal part of navigation or forced by distress. Article 19 lists what makes passage not innocent, including loading or unloading any person or goods contrary to customs or immigration laws, research, launching aircraft, and "any other activity not having a direct bearing on passage". So innocent passage is a right to cross. It is no basis for lingering, and it gives no right to live offshore in one spot within 12 miles.

Ports are the part most often misunderstood. A flag gives no right to enter a port. Ports lie in internal waters, and Article 25(2) recognises that a coastal state may set conditions on admission and act to prevent any breach of them. Women on Waves, whose Dutch-flagged ship carries a clinic, found this in 2004 when Portuguese warships blocked it. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression, but that ruling rested on human rights law. In Guatemala the army blocked the pier within 24 hours of the ship docking. Once in port, residents and the ship fall under that country's law as well.

Some points are open. Women on Waves also raises the unresolved question of whether a ship that docks, boards a country's citizens and takes them out for an act banned at home is passing innocently. Whether a ship used as a permanent home, returning to the same waters again and again, stays within the words "continuous and expeditious" has not been tested in any known ruling. Reading the text, it seems that the passage rules look at what the ship is doing on each trip through the belt, and that a home on a real route would be treated like any passenger ship. A ship that repeatedly drifted just offshore for residents' convenience would look more like the stopping that Article 18 does not allow. A practical point follows from this. A ship registered as seagoing has to keep the certificates and crew that go with that, and a resident community may struggle to pay for them.

Follow one year of such a life. The flag state's law applies on board. Crew and safety rules follow the flag, under Article 94. Every landing is an immigration event. A resident has to hold a passport and any visa that each port demands, so a person without valid papers stays on board or is refused. Food, fuel and spare parts come from ports, and repairs from shipyards. The move-along approach gives no escape from tax, because a citizen's home country may tax regardless of where the person sleeps, as the United States does under Cook v. Tait. Banks ask for a home address and a tax residence. Medical care beyond the ship's clinic means going ashore. A child born on board usually takes nationality from the parents, and the 1961 statelessness treaty treats the birth as occurring in the flag country only to prevent statelessness.

The cases show that the money usually fails before the law does. Villa Vie Odyssey sold cabins from $99,999, and on 26 October 2026 in Sihanoukville residents were told to leave because the company could not secure fuel. Life at Sea Cruises cancelled its three-year voyage in 2023 without ever having a ship. MS Satoshi failed for a different reason, because it was meant to stay at anchor, and liability insurers would not cover a ship used that way. That suggests that continual sailing can be easier to insure than sitting still, though the cost of fuel and crew is far higher.

As a way to live at sea, this route has more practical potential than nearly any other, and it gives no territory and no law of the residents' own. The strongest version is a solid company or residents' association owning a well-maintained ship under a respected flag, on a real itinerary, with a private contract setting the internal rules. Such a community can last for decades and choose where it goes. Its members stay citizens of their own countries, its flag state can remove it from the register, and any port can refuse it. Having no territory also leaves it without a basis for statehood under the usual tests.

combo-safety-zone-possession.essay:
Nobody may own the Moon, yet a base with a large safety area around it might keep other people away in practice. A group could try to build this up over decades, with one announced work zone after another, until it held a stretch of ground in all but name. This combines the settlement of a body with a set of principles written for avoiding collisions. It is one of the most discussed grey zones in space law.

The texts first. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, bars appropriation of the Moon and other bodies by claim, use, occupation or any other means. Article I keeps them free for use by all states, with free access to all areas. Article IX tells states to have due regard for the interests of others and to consult before activities that would cause harmful interference. Article XII says stations on the Moon are open to representatives of other parties, with reasonable advance notice and on a reciprocal basis. Those articles bind parties. The Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles with 78 signatories as of 28 October 2026, add safety zones in Section 11. A zone is the area where operations or an unusual event could reasonably cause harmful interference. Its size should reflect the operation and be set by commonly accepted scientific and engineering principles. It is to be temporary, ending when the relevant operation ceases, and signatories should notify each other and the UN Secretary-General. They commit to respect reasonable zones and to coordinate before operating inside them. Section 11 also says they will respect free access to all areas under Article I. The Accords describe this as a way of implementing the treaty.

What is open is how far this can go. No zone has been tested, and no court has been asked. The Accords depend on the word "reasonable" and on self-assessment by the operating state. Critics fear that a zone others must keep clear of could work in practice as a claim, since a site such as a sunlit peak near an ice deposit on the lunar south pole may be the only one of its kind. Supporters, including NASA, say that it respects the treaty, since it only requires notice and coordination. Only signatories have made that commitment. China and Russia lead a separate plan, the International Lunar Research Station, and have not signed. Reading the text, it seems that a non-signatory has no duty to respect a zone under the Accords, and that it does owe due regard under Article IX if it is a party to the treaty. Those two standards may not give the same answer on a real site.

International law on territory adds a further open point. A writer in Völkerrechtsblog notes that courts in territorial disputes have looked for what are called effectivités, acts of real administration such as making rules and running local government, and they have sometimes treated these as strong evidence of title when no one else has a claim. Under the treaty, such acts cannot produce title on the Moon. That writer was discussing SpaceX's terms of service for Mars, and his concern is that such acts of control may be used later, if the rule itself weakens. So safety zones matter as much for what they could be used to say later as for what they say today.

Here is how the process could run. A company under a state's licence builds a base near an ice deposit. Its state announces a zone of a few kilometres while vehicles land and dig. The zone is real and reasonable, because rocket landings throw dust at speed. As the operation grows, the zone grows, and because the base is permanent, the operation does not end. Other missions consult, and coordination takes time and data. A rival's request to work inside is delayed for safety reasons. The rule never says "no", and a late arrival moves elsewhere. Over decades, the base's neighbourhood looks much like private land. Residents make rules for the area, a security office directs visitors, and a registry records who has what. That would be a real practice, even if no one calls it property.

The limits are also real. A state makes the announcement, and a private group cannot make one alone. Licensing and supervision continue under Article VI. The state can change its policy, and other states can demand consultations. Article XII gives representatives of other parties a right to visit stations on a reciprocal basis, which is hard to square with a closed area. If an operator physically blocks another party's lawful mission, that party has a claim of breach against the licensing state, and it has no court with automatic jurisdiction. Harm would be handled by diplomacy, or under the Liability Convention's claims process. A small group could also find a bigger neighbour simply ignoring it. Moon Express's 2016 payload approval shows how US officials handled supervision case by case, with letters that do not bind a future agency.

The real potential for practical control of a site is considerable compared with most space routes, and it would come under a state, with a much lower chance of getting a territory under the group's own laws. A safety zone is the strongest available legal argument for controlling access to a stretch of the Moon for a long period, and whether it would hold up for that purpose is untested. The strongest version is a state-backed base with continuous activity, an honest engineering case for its zone, public notices and a record of allowing visits. That provides a working settlement with practical control over its neighbourhood. It gives no title and no independence, and critics would say it comes close to the line that Article II draws.

combo-observer-status.essay:
Most people assume a body is either a country at the United Nations or nothing. There is a middle ground. Some bodies that are not ordinary states have won a seat near the table, with standing in diplomatic rooms and immunity from some national laws. A project with no land could try to combine real international work with such a status, and so gain much of what recognition gives without being a state. To see whether it could, it helps to look at who has it and how.

The UN's own list is short. Two non-members hold a standing invitation as observers and keep permanent missions, the Holy See and the State of Palestine. The General Assembly gave Palestine non-member observer state status by resolution 67/19 on 29 November 2012. Other entities with a standing invitation include the International Committee of the Red Cross, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, the International Olympic Committee, the Inter-Parliamentary Union and the Sovereign Order of Malta. These lists are decided by the General Assembly, so member states control entry. That much is settled. A body cannot apply itself into observer status against the wishes of the majority, and observer status is not membership or a vote in the Assembly. Whether such a resolution makes something a state is a separate matter. No general rule says that it does, and governments continue to differ on Palestine.

Each of those bodies got there through its own history. The Holy See has the Catholic Church behind it and Vatican City under the 1929 Lateran Treaty with Italy. The Order of Malta ruled Rhodes and Malta for centuries, lost its last land in 1798, and kept diplomatic ties with more than 100 states because they chose to continue them. It became a UN observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. The Order issues passports, coins and stamps and signs treaties, and it counts only three senior officers as citizens.

The Red Cross is a different and more useful case. The International Committee of the Red Cross is a private Swiss association and it is not sovereign. Its status comes from a job states gave it. The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 name it in their text, so it is written into treaties. On 19 March 1993 it signed a formal agreement with Switzerland that protects its property and archives, gives staff legal immunity, exempts it from taxes and gives it secure communications at the level of embassies. Switzerland does not recognise passports issued by it. It has similar agreements with other governments. A private body has therefore gained many of the practical protections of a state, by being useful to all sides in war.

The International Olympic Committee shows a further use of status, which is giving standing to others. Taiwan's team competes as Chinese Taipei under a formula worked out after the IOC recognised the People's Republic's committee in 1979. Taiwan uses the same name at APEC, the Pacific trade forum, and takes part in the World Trade Organization as a Separate Customs Territory. Those memberships exist because the bodies' rules allow non-state economies or sports teams to take part. That gives a template for a place with no recognition, and Taiwan's size and trade are what bring the others to the table.

For a new community, the first thing to separate is ordinary accreditation from special status. Non-governmental organisations can seek accreditation at the UN's Economic and Social Council, which is a route to attend meetings and gives no diplomatic standing. The Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization, founded in 1991, works as an advocacy body for peoples without seats. Suppose a new group spends twenty years running a hospital ship or disaster relief. Governments may sign agreements letting it work in their waters, with duty-free passage and some protection for staff. Reading the Red Cross and Order of Malta examples, it seems that immunity agreements can be won one state at a time, on the strength of a service states want, and that a host government must agree first. No self-declared nation is known to have gained anything like this from scratch.

The open questions are these. It is not settled whether a body with a standing invitation has any right to keep it, since the Assembly could in principle change its mind. It is also not settled how far the Order of Malta's standing rests on sovereignty at all, as against a long habit among states. Nobody can say in advance how many agreements would be enough for others to treat a new body as an international person, because the question has no threshold in any treaty.

Money and paper follow the status. A body with a host agreement can usually bank and move goods with less friction. Its staff keep their own nationalities and tax homes. Its immunity covers what the agreement says and no more, and residents of a community would not be covered unless they are staff on official business. Passports issued by such a body work only with states that have agreed, as the Order's do.

The potential for gaining standing is low for a new body and real over long periods. The strongest version is a neutral service organisation that does something states need and cannot easily do themselves, wins a headquarters agreement, then gains named roles in treaties. It would have to give up any claim to rule people or land, because the immunity is granted for the work. Such a body might last a very long time and would remain something other than a state. A founder seeking a place to live under their own laws would not get that from this route.

combo-company-run-flag.essay:
Many people are surprised to learn that some national ship registers are run by private companies, sometimes on another continent. A ship flying the flag of Liberia is registered through a company based in Virginia. That raises an obvious thought for a founder. If a flag is a service sold by a company, perhaps a founder could negotiate with that company, or set up one like it for a small country, and obtain a flag on special terms. The idea combines an ordinary flag, a deal with a host government and a business arrangement.

The history explains how this came about. Liberia's register began in 1948 under President William Tubman with the help of Edward Stettinius, a former US Secretary of State, and the first ship, the World Peace, was registered in March 1949. The International Trust Company ran it until 1999, when Liberia's government appointed the Liberian International Ship and Corporate Registry (LISCR), a Delaware company based in Virginia, to manage the register and collect the fees owed to the state. That appointment rests on an Act of the Liberian Legislature. The register brings in roughly $24 million a year, and in the 2007-08 budget it was about six percent of government revenue, while during the civil war maritime money was about 70 percent. International Registries, Inc. of Reston, Virginia, descends from the original Stettinius company. According to one account it moved its business to the Marshall Islands after Charles Taylor demanded too much money. The timing of that move is not clear, since the Marshall Islands government started its register in 1988 and Taylor's government gave the Liberian contract to LISCR in 1999. International Registries provides its administrative and technical support, including vessel registration, inspections, seafarer documents and radio licences.

The law on who holds the power is clear. Article 91 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says "every State" fixes the conditions for its nationality and that ships have the nationality of the state whose flag they may fly. A company can process the paperwork and collect fees, but the nationality comes from the state. Article 94 places the duties of supervision on the state as well. Open registers are generally accepted as lawful, and the writer Eduardo Cavalcanti de Mello Filho treats that as settled, while noting that a small state can be a responsible flag. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea held in the M/V Saiga (No. 2) case that the genuine link requirement in Article 91 gives other countries no criteria for challenging a ship's registration.

Some things are open. Whether a third state may refuse to respect a flag whose government knowingly lets ships evade supervision is unsettled. Mello Filho calls these "flags of deceit", and he argues that the Saiga reasoning is thin and that non-recognition may be available. The Tribunal's approach suggests the only remedy is to report the problem to the flag state under Article 94(6). So a registry that exists mainly to sell cover may stay valid on paper while other governments test how far they can ignore it.

Recent events show how far a state can hand this work over and what can then go wrong. Gabon authorised a UAE-based firm, Intershipping Services, to run its register in 2018. By 2024 it was the fastest-growing by tonnage, and the EU and Britain sanctioned the firm in July 2025. Comoros withdrew authority from private operators and brought certificate issuance back in house. Cameroon expelled the tanker Smyrtos from its register in May 2026, and Britain boarded it the next month. Earlier, Sweden pressed Nicaragua to withdraw the registration of the Radio Nord ship, and the owners moved it to Panama's register. In each case the state's decision was the one that counted.

Follow a founder through this. The ordinary route is available. A company formed for the purpose applies, the ship passes vetting on age, condition and owner, the owners are screened against sanctions lists, and the fee is paid. The result is a normal flag with that country's law on board and no special status. Reading the text, it seems nothing in Article 91 would prevent a small state from writing a statute that offers a special class of register for residential platforms, or appointing a founder's company as its registrar, as Liberia and Gabon appointed theirs. That would need a government and a legislature willing to act, and the registry company itself could not offer it. It would also bring the founder's company under the law of wherever it is based. Companies in Virginia answer to American courts and sanctions rules, and Liberia's statute limits LISCR's investors to US nationals.

The deal would be weak in the ways that matter most to a founder. A government that grants a registry contract can end it, as Liberia did in 1999, and a change of president could change the terms. Pressure from a powerful state tends to arrive at a small government's door. MS Satoshi's owners asked Panama to class their ship as non-seagoing, which would have lifted most treaty duties, and Panama refused. The flag would also carry its treaty obligations on safety and crew, since a state cannot contract those away by private agreement. A special class that left a ship with no real supervision would risk being treated as a flag of deceit.

The strongest version is a small state that passes a real law, supervises real safety standards, and contracts a founder's company to do the administration in return for fees that matter to its budget. No founder is known to have done this. Liberia shows that the money can matter a great deal to a state's budget, which gives a government a reason to agree, and it also shows that governments sometimes squeeze a registry for revenue. It would give stability and a say over the paperwork. Sovereignty would remain with the state that owns the flag.

antarctica-claimed.essay:
Antarctica covers 14,200,000 square kilometres, and seven countries say parts of it belong to them. Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom hold eight separate claims, drawn mostly as wedges running to the South Pole. France dates its claim to 1840, and Britain's dates to 1908, when it said it needed to regulate and tax whaling. The claims of Argentina, Chile and Britain overlap. Most other countries do not recognise any of them, and the United States and Russia keep the right to make claims of their own. For a person wondering about setting up on the ice, the first thing to understand is that this argument was deliberately frozen.

The freeze comes from the Antarctic Treaty, signed by twelve countries in Washington on 1 December 1959 and in force since 23 June 1961. It governs everything south of 60 degrees South, including ice shelves, and rights on the high seas in the area remain. It now has 58 members, of which 29 are Consultative, meaning they take part in decisions, and 29 are Non-Consultative. Article I allows peaceful purposes only, with no military bases or exercises. Article IV is the heart of it. Under IV(1), no member gives up or loses its claim or its position on anyone else's claim. Under IV(2), acts or activities while the treaty is in force cannot support or deny a claim or "create any rights of sovereignty", and no new claim may be asserted. Sovereignty means the legal right to rule a place. The effect resembles two neighbours who agree to stop arguing over a boundary and agree that nothing either does in the meantime will count in the argument.

This means that the usual way of winning land by living on it does not work here. Chile and Argentina have tried harder than anyone. In February 1984 Chile moved families to Villa Las Estrellas on King George Island, beside an air base, with a school, civil registry, post office and bank. Juan Pablo Camacho, born there that November, received life insurance and study funding from Augusto Pinochet at a ceremony in the presidential palace, and the local radio station is named Radio Soberanía, meaning sovereignty. Argentina flew Silvia Morella de Palma to Esperanza Base when she was seven months pregnant, and her son Emilio Palma was born there on 7 January 1978. Some sources count 11 births on the continent. Article IV says none of this can build a legal claim. Two governments placing families, schools and registers on the ice have gained nothing in treaty law from doing it, and a private group would have much less standing than either of them.

Practical access runs through governments as well. Article VII(5) requires each member to give advance notice of all expeditions organised by its nationals or from its territory, and of its ships. Members of the Madrid Protocol, a treaty added to the Antarctic Treaty to protect the environment, must also assess the environmental impact of such activities beforehand under Article 8. Article 7 bans any activity relating to mineral resources other than science. So the country of your passport or your departure port is the practical limit. In practice, treaty countries issue the permits. Australians need an environmental assessment approved by the Australian Antarctic Division, and New Zealand requires government approval to visit the Ross Dependency. Britain requires a permit for anyone on an expedition organised in the UK or leaving from it, and for British-flagged ships, and it asks for applications at least four months ahead for a new or unusual trip. Organisers must be self-sufficient and able to handle emergencies such as oil spills. About 124,000 cruise visitors came in 2025, and around 30 yachts visit the Peninsula each year, all of which is visiting and gives no one a claim. These rules are enforced. Jarle Andhøy, a Norwegian skipper, sailed to Antarctica in 2012 on the yacht Nilaya without authorisation, after the Norwegian Polar Institute had held up an earlier trip because he had not supplied information on his activities and insurance. A Norwegian district court convicted him in June 2014 and fined him 45,000 kroner, about $7,000, rejecting his argument that the rules did not apply because he never landed. The Treaty does not address private ownership of land, and nothing in it gives a private person a way to hold ground. Claimant countries may treat a sector as theirs, while other members are free not to recognise that under Article IV(1)(c). A settler could therefore face the law of a home country, a departure country and a claimant all at once.

Then there are the physical facts. At Villa Las Estrellas about 150 people live in summer and 80 in winter, with a nearest major hospital over 1,000 kilometres away, and BBC Future reported in 2018 that residents on long stays have their appendix removed before coming. All of this rests on a Chilean military air base. A private settlement would have to bring in its own fuel, food and transport, and no one is obliged to supply them. Any rescue would come from a government station or a ship, on that government's terms.

The closest thing to a private base is Greenpeace's World Park Base at Cape Evans on Ross Island, in the sector New Zealand claims. It ran year-round from 1987 to 1992 and remains the only non-government year-round base. Greenpeace wanted a voice at treaty meetings and wanted to stop mining. Treaty governments officially ignored it and gave it no help, though New Zealand would have helped in an emergency. The countries were negotiating a treaty to allow regulated mining at the time. Australia and France withdrew from it, it failed to gain enough support by its deadline of 25 November 1989, and the Madrid Protocol was agreed in 1991 and came into force in 1998. Having met its aim, Greenpeace removed the base in 1991 and 1992. A study in Polar Record estimated total fuel spills at under 200 litres, with contamination in one spot reaching 70 centimetres into frozen ground. So a well funded organisation with ships and public support held a camp for five years, as a campaign. It claimed no land and it took the base away.

Some misunderstandings are common. Many people believe the mining ban expires on a set date. The Madrid Protocol's Article 25(2) lets any Consultative Party call a review conference once 50 years have passed since the protocol took effect, which by simple arithmetic falls in January 2048, and that is a right to call a conference, which is not an expiry date. Article 25(5) adds that the mining ban continues unless a binding legal regime on mining is in force, including an agreed way of deciding whether any mining would be acceptable. A change adopted at such a conference would need a majority of the parties including three quarters of the states that were Consultative when the protocol was adopted, and to take effect it would need ratification by three quarters of the Consultative parties, including all of those original ones. If an adopted change has not taken effect within three years, any party may give notice to leave the protocol, with withdrawal taking effect two years later. Another is that a country outside the treaty, or a citizen of one, is free to act as they like. The treaty binds its members. An individual from outside it is still a national of some country, and most routes pass through a member's territory. Article X also commits each member to make appropriate efforts, consistent with the UN Charter, so that "no one" engages in activity in Antarctica contrary to the treaty's principles or purposes. Reading Article IV(2), it seems that member countries would apply its wording on "any rights of sovereignty" to any new claim, although no court has been asked to rule on a claim by an outsider. A third is that Marie Byrd Land, the unclaimed sector, escapes all this. It does not, since new claims are barred there too.

A person who wanted to do something real here could join a national research programme or a permitted expedition, or work with a group trying to shape treaty meetings, as Greenpeace did. Someone leaving from a treaty member's territory would be notified to other members by that country, with an impact assessment if it has joined the Madrid Protocol. Those paths give access and sometimes influence. They do not give any right over the land. The odds reflect this, with the chance of building at about 5 percent and of holding at about the same, recognition close to nothing, and the chance of getting a territory under its own laws much lower than the first two. Access is hard to arrange independently, and the treaty has closed the legal route for as long as it stays in force.

combo-igo-register.essay:
The Registration Convention lets someone other than a single country keep a register. An international intergovernmental organisation, a body set up by treaty among governments, can take on the rights and duties of a launching state if it conducts space activities, declares that it accepts them, and has a majority of member states that have joined both that Convention and the Outer Space Treaty (Article VII). The Liability Convention has a similar clause (Article XXII). A project could try to use this route. A group of small states would create an organisation by treaty, and that organisation, rather than any one state, would register and supervise a shared station. This combines places run by international agreement with orbit.

The route exists in practice. The UN's table of 2016 shows objects registered by the European Space Agency (65) and EUMETSAT, the European weather satellite organisation (7), and the office notes declarations by others, including Intersputnik in 2018. So an organisation can register without being a state. It is also settled that the Outer Space Treaty applies to activities carried on through such organisations, and that practical questions are to be sorted out by its parties with the organisation (Article XIII). Liability does not vanish. Under Article XXII of the Liability Convention the organisation and its members that are parties are liable jointly and severally, with claims going first to the organisation and to the members if it has not paid within six months.

This is the most formally solid way of avoiding a single state's register, and it has limits that can be read from the text. The condition about a majority of member states means that most of the founders must have joined both treaties. UN figures of January 2026 give 77 members of the Registration Convention. Many small states have joined neither. UN officials have themselves listed organisations that fail this test among the reasons objects go unregistered. Reading the text, it seems that two or three states with the right memberships could form such a body, and that its status would rest on their real commitment. A treaty body made up of one small state and a private company would not qualify, since a company is not a state.

What is open is how slight such a body can be and still count. The Convention says the organisation must "conduct space activities", and it does not say how much. It also does not settle whether an organisation can be a launching state when it only pays for a launch from a member's territory, though the words "launches or procures" read naturally to include that. Nothing rules out a body set up for one project, and nothing has tested one. It is also unknown how a private company could sit inside such an organisation, since membership of a treaty body is for states, and how far the organisation could delegate its supervision to the company that runs the station. No such body is known to have been proposed, and no government is known to have addressed the idea.

Follow it step by step. Say three small countries sign a treaty creating an Orbital Authority, and it declares acceptance to the UN Secretary-General. The treaty can give the Authority legal personality under the law of its members, although other states need not treat it as anything more than their dealings with it require. It must then obtain a launch. The launch provider's state stays a launching state, keeps its own licence conditions, and will want assurance about supervision. Radio remains with the members, since filings with the International Telecommunication Union go through member countries. A US citizen or US company that launches still needs a licence under 51 USC 50904, because the statute looks at citizenship, and a treaty among other states does not change that. Rocket and station parts remain under export controls, and export regulators will examine a new buyer of that kind.

Residents of the station would be governed by whatever the treaty says. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty speaks of a "State Party", and how this applies to an organisation is covered by Article XIII only in general terms. A treaty among states could make rules for criminal law, as the partners on the International Space Station did under their 1998 agreement, in which each partner keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens (Article 5), with special rules on crime (Article 22). A settlers' assembly might be given real powers by that treaty, and those powers would rest on the treaty, which the member states could change.

The route has some potential as a form of registration. It offers a station with several sponsoring governments, so that no single state's politics can end the project, along with a real legal personality and a right to register. It offers less dependence on any one state than a private registration does, although the member states keep control and the station has no law of its own. It also needs several governments to bear unlimited liability for damage on Earth, and most small governments would be slow to accept that for a private group's benefit. The strongest version adds a substantial state or a group of them with real space agencies. The nearest cases are the European Space Agency and the International Space Station, both built by states for state purposes.

combo-bankrupt-village.essay:
News stories regularly announce that a whole town has been sold. The idea built on this is to buy a failing village, or a government in financial trouble, and thereby acquire the place and the power that runs it. It combines a purchase, a takeover of a town, and a claim inside a state.

What can be bought and what cannot is settled. A town consists of private land parcels, plus a municipal government where one exists. A person can buy all the parcels. A public government has no owner, so no one can buy it. Buford, Wyoming, is the best-known sale. On 5 April 2012 Don Sammons sold it at auction for $900,000 to two Vietnamese men, one later named as Pham Dinh Nguyen. What they bought was about 10 acres of private land with a trading post and gas station, and Buford was an unincorporated community within Albany County, which continued to govern it. The buyer rebranded it PhinDeli Town in 2013, the store was boarded up in 2017, and by 2021 the fuel station was back in business.

Bankruptcy gives no further opening in the United States. Chapter 9 of the federal bankruptcy code is the process for a municipality that cannot pay its debts. Section 109(c) says that an entity may use it only if it is a municipality, is specifically authorised by state law to do so, is insolvent and meets further conditions. In other words the state keeps control over who may enter bankruptcy. A court then helps the municipality adjust its debts, and there is no auction of the government. Other countries respond to failing towns by merging them. Italy's austerity plan of 2011 called for towns under 1,000 people to merge with neighbours, which is what led Filettino's mayor to declare a principality in protest, and how towns are organised was still decided by the Italian parliament.

What is open is less about law and more about what a very small population lets an owner do in practice. Owning all the homes in a real municipality, as Vernon's city government did with its housing, gives great influence over who lives and votes there. Whether a new private owner could use this to direct a local government depends on state law on evictions, voting and fair housing. In one Vernon election the city cut off the power of challengers and a judge stepped in. Reading the record, it seems that the combination of very few voters and one landlord is effective, and that it draws state attention once it is noticed.

History does contain true sales of a ruler's rights after money trouble, and they show why the modern version does not work. Before 1699 an imperial commission decided that Schellenberg and Vaduz, whose counts were in debt, should be sold to clear their debts, and the Liechtenstein family bought them. Those were personal lordships, which could be sold under the imperial law of that time. The fief of Sark has also changed hands by sale, and still has a very old structure, yet it answers to the British Crown. In 2010 German politicians suggested that Greece, in its debt crisis, sell islands, and Greece did not. A government in debt might sell land and state companies, while keeping the right to rule.

Follow the steps. A buyer finds an empty village on a listing. It pays for the land, and the sale is entered in the public land register. Any old buildings come with liabilities, and the buyer pays local property tax. The local council, or the county, has planning control. Bringing in residents needs water, sewers and permits, which is why many such villages are empty. A buyer who declares independence, as Seborga's claimant has done since 1963 and Romkerhall's innkeepers have done for tourists, gets publicity and possibly visitors, while the state carries on running the place. A small place that declares it and then refuses taxes faces the same collection system as anyone else.

The potential as a home and a local power base is modest and real. The strongest version is a group that buys an entire near-empty place in a country with few rules on such purchases, brings in residents, and forms or takes over the local government in a lawful way, using the voters-and-charter route. That gives a physical home, control of planning and a lot of practical freedom. It gives no more legal separation from the country than that route gives.

indigenous-prior-sovereignty.essay:
Many countries were formed on land where other peoples already lived and governed themselves. Those peoples, called Indigenous peoples, often say that their authority is older than the country and that they never gave it up. The country usually treats the matter as a domestic one, to be settled under its own law. Each side begins from a different starting point, and the courts that decide most disputes belong to the country.

This route is open only to a people with an existing claim, one that comes from a long history on the land. A new founder cannot acquire it by moving somewhere, joining a group or buying property. The real gains have come through negotiated land claims, court rulings and long use of a document, and each result stays within the existing country. That explains why self-rule here can grow a good deal while recognition as a separate state stays close to nil.

To see how the law came to this point, it helps to go back to the rule that European powers brought with them. In Johnson v. M'Intosh in 1823, the United States Supreme Court considered a land purchase from the Piankeshaw people. Chief Justice John Marshall set out the doctrine of discovery, under which a European power gained sovereignty (the right to rule) over land it discovered, along with the sole right to buy out the Indigenous occupants, who kept only a right to occupy it. The case is still taught and is the basis of the American law of aboriginal title, the rights Indigenous peoples keep over their land. In 1831, in Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, he described Indian tribes as "domestic dependent nations", and in Worcester v. Georgia in 1832 he held a Georgia law on Cherokee land void. So in US courts the country holds final authority, and the argument is over how much it left in place.

Courts can still give large results within that frame. McGirt v. Oklahoma, decided in 2020, is the leading example. In the 19th century Congress set aside land for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation as a reservation. The question was whether the reservation ended when Oklahoma became a state. By 5 to 4, in an opinion by Justice Neil Gorsuch, the court held that Congress had never ended it, so the land is still Indian country, the legal term for land under tribal and federal authority. Under the Major Crimes Act, a federal law on serious crimes, Oklahoma could not prosecute Native Americans for the listed crimes there. A state appeals court applied the same reasoning to nine other nations, so almost all of eastern Oklahoma counts as Indian country.

In 2021 the state appeals court ruled that McGirt did not apply to old convictions, and the US Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to that ruling. In 2022, in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, the Supreme Court held that the state shares with the federal government the power to prosecute crimes by non-Native people against Native victims there. A later case can narrow an earlier win. McGirt also concerned who may prosecute crimes on the land and did not make the nations independent states.

International law offers a statement of principle. The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted by the General Assembly on 13 September 2007, says in Article 3 that these peoples have the right to self-determination and in Article 4 the right to autonomy or self-government in internal and local affairs. Article 46 says nothing in it authorises action that would dismember or impair the territorial integrity of sovereign states. It is a resolution and does not bind countries as a treaty does. Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States voted against, and each later endorsed it in some form.

Negotiation has produced the largest result on the ground. Nunavut, in the Canadian Arctic, covers 2,093,190 square kilometres and had 36,858 people in 2021, of whom 84 percent were Inuit. Inuit organisations and the federal government began discussing a split of the Northwest Territories in 1976. Residents backed division in a vote in 1982, and the land-claims agreement was completed in September 1992 and ratified by nearly 85 percent of voters. Parliament passed the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act and the Nunavut Act in 1993, and the territory began on 1 April 1999. A 2024 agreement gives its government control over its land and resources. From the first talks to the first day of the territory took 23 years, and Nunavut is a territory of Canada that makes no claim to be a state.

Elected bodies inside a country are another form. The Sámi, an Indigenous people of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, elect parliaments in three of those countries, opened in 1989, 1993 and 1996, and Sweden's must follow decisions of the national parliament. In Russia, as of 2017, the authorities did not recognise the Kola Sámi Assembly as a lawmaking body. None of these bodies claims independence.

Documents show what happens at a border. The Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, have issued their own passport since at least 1923, when one went to the Cayuga statesman Deskaheh for a trip to the League of Nations. Other countries decide case by case. In July 2010 Britain refused it for the Haudenosaunee lacrosse team, which turned down an American offer of US passports. Israel accepted the team's passports in 2018, subject to Canadian assurances that they could return, and Ireland accepted them in 2022. The European Union lists it as a fantasy passport, and it is not accepted for entry into Canada. Countries decide whether to accept the passport, recognise the government or pass the law.

Conflict with a country can last far longer than one government. The Kīngitanga, the Māori King Movement in New Zealand, began in 1858 as a rival authority. Troops crossed into the Waikato region in July 1863 and the government confiscated 486,500 hectares. The movement continues, and its monarch is not recognised in New Zealand law or by many tribes. In 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal, which hears Māori claims against the Crown, concluded that the chiefs who signed the Māori text of the 1840 treaty did not give up sovereignty, which leaves open how and when the Crown gained it.

Unity among the people concerned is often the hardest bump. The Hawaiian sovereignty movement traces its case to the overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893, and in 1993 Congress passed an Apology Resolution acknowledging that the overthrow was illegal. In Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs in 2009, a unanimous US Supreme Court held that the resolution's "whereas" clauses did not change the state's rights and obligations over the ceded lands of the former kingdom. The groups differ on what should follow. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi reported 21,000 members in 1997, the Nation of Hawaiʻi wants a republic, and many groups opposed the Akaka Bill, which would have begun federal recognition. Justice Anthony Kennedy halted a 2015 vote count for a planned convention. In 2007 the Republic of Lakotah, led by Russell Means, announced withdrawal from old treaties. Recognised Lakota tribal governments had not backed it, and a federal official said the withdrawal did not mean anything.

A silent government has not agreed to anything, and in Australia the courts have closed the question from the other side. In Coe v. Commonwealth in 1993, Chief Justice Mason of the High Court struck out a claim of Aboriginal sovereignty, writing that the Mabo decision of 1992 is entirely at odds with the idea that sovereignty adverse to the Crown lies with the Aboriginal people, and that the Crown's sovereignty cannot be challenged in Australian courts. The Murrawarri people in Australia declared independence in 2013 and asked the Crown to produce a treaty, a deed of cession or a declaration of war by a deadline. The Crown did not reply, and the council took silence as confirmation, but the government has not acknowledged the republic, and it uses Australian money.

The path that has brought gains is a recognised people negotiating with the country, backed by a court case or a strong historical record, for land, money and powers written into law. It takes decades, it depends on the people concerned acting together, and it delivers self-rule inside the existing state. Nothing in these cases has yet produced a new country that others recognise, and a person with no such claim has no way to use this route.

eez-shelf.essay:
The sea next to a coast is divided in law into belts, measured outward from a line called the baseline, usually the low-tide edge of the land. A nautical mile, the unit used at sea, is about 1.85 km. The first belt, out to 12 nautical miles, is the territorial sea, where the coastal country has nearly the same authority as on land. The next, reaching 200 nautical miles (about 370 km), is the exclusive economic zone, or EEZ. Under the water lies the continental shelf, the seabed extending out from the coast. In law the shelf reaches at least 200 nautical miles, and in some places it runs further.

These belts come from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Coastal countries wanted the fish, oil and minerals off their shores, and every country wanted ships and aircraft to keep moving. So the coastal country does not own the water outright. It holds rights to the resources (Articles 56 and 57), while others stay free to sail, fly and lay cables, paying due attention to its rights (Article 58). A public road across a farm works in a similar way. Anyone may travel the road, and only the farmer may plant crops or put up a barn. Shelf rights do not depend on occupying the seabed, so a country that has never sent anyone there still holds them (Article 77). The United States has not joined UNCLOS, and it claimed its own 200-mile zone by presidential proclamation in 1983.

A Flanders Marine Institute poster using 2019 data counts 230 EEZs covering 136,850,878 km², leaving out joint arrangements and overlapping claims. It counts each separate zone, so a country with overseas territories appears several times. Russia's single zone is the largest on that count at 7,734,809 km², followed by Australia's at 6,871,622 km². The United States, whose zone is split on the poster among its mainland, Alaska, Hawaii and other areas, has more than 3.4 million square nautical miles in all according to the US agency NOAA, which is about 11.7 million km².

The rule that decides nearly everything is Article 60, which Article 80 extends to the shelf. Only the coastal country may build or authorize three things in its zone. These are artificial islands, installations that have an economic purpose, and any structure that could interfere with its rights. It also has sole legal power over them, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law. Artificial islands are not islands in law, so they have no territorial sea of their own and change no sea boundary (Article 60(8)). The country may set safety zones around them, normally of 500 metres at most. It may also board and arrest to enforce its fishing rules (Article 73) and may chase a ship out to sea for violations in the zone, known as hot pursuit (Article 111).

Suppose a group anchors a platform 100 miles off Florida and declares it independent. The spot is inside the US EEZ, so the first question is whether the structure had US permission. If the group asks and gets it, the platform comes under US tax and immigration law, and the independence it wanted is gone. If it does not ask, the record offers comparisons. In the 1960s promoters began building on Triumph and Long Reefs, about four and a half miles off Florida and outside the narrow belt the US then claimed. In 1970, in United States v. Ray, a US appeals court ordered a permanent ban, holding that the country's exclusive rights over its shelf were enough even though it did not own the reefs. When a company proposed a nation called Taluga on Cortes Bank, about 111 miles off San Diego, the US government reportedly declared the bank US territory as part of its shelf. That wording goes further than shelf law, which gives rights over the seabed and its resources and does not make the seabed part of the country.

One part of the law is unclear. UNCLOS does not define "artificial island", and it does not say whether a small floating home on a mooring is an island, an installation or a ship. The answer matters. An artificial island falls under the coastal country whatever it is used for. An installation falls under it only if it has an economic purpose or could interfere with the country's rights. A boat passing through is plainly using the freedom to sail. A structure that stays put and houses people for the long term looks more like what Article 60 covers, which appears to rule out an independent project unless the coastal country agrees. The coastal country has the boats on site, so its reading takes effect first and any court comes later.

The clearest real case is XLII, a six-metre-wide cabin on a weighted column in the Andaman Sea, built by a company called Ocean Builders. Its owners said it sat just over 12 nautical miles off Phuket, and other accounts say about 14. The American bitcoin trader Chad Elwartowski and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019, and he said 20 more would be sold. The Thai navy said they had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April. Thailand revoked his visa and charged them under a law carrying life in prison or death, saying they had endangered national sovereignty, and navy boats towed the cabin toward shore as evidence. Ocean Builders argued that the site was in the contiguous zone, the band 12 to 24 miles out where a country has limited powers, and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its EEZ. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged. How the case ended is not known, so no court is known to have decided whether Thailand's criminal law reached that far.

A real country gets no special treatment under these rules. In 2011 President Anote Tong of Kiribati, whose low-lying islands are threatened by rising seas, said his government was considering floating islands, at about $2 billion to come from other countries. He named no site, three years later his government bought land in Fiji, and no platform was built. A platform would not by itself carry the sea rights that natural land generates.

If the structure counts as a ship, it needs a real country's flag, which brings that country's law on board (Articles 91 and 94). Ocean Builders' later cruise ship plan, the MS Satoshi, collapsed in 2020 because no insurer would provide the liability cover a ship's owners need. Payments between countries travel through banks that hold accounts with each other, and those banks need a supervisor they can rely on, which a platform lacks. One law journal puts a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million, and selling stakes to raise such money can count as selling investments. The US regulator sued the promoter of New Utopia over a $350 million bond offering that raised $24,000.

Tax follows the person. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, as the Supreme Court held in Cook v. Tait in 1924. Food, fuel and parts come through a port, and that port's country sets the terms. Ship captains are required to help people in danger at sea when they safely can (Article 98), and a rescued person lands in some other country under its law, so serious medical care means going ashore. A birth, marriage or will on a platform would need a registry others accept, and without one a child's papers and an inheritance would appear to depend on the parents' home countries.

The commonest misunderstanding is that everything past 12 nautical miles is international waters. That is correct for passing ships and aircraft and wrong for resources and fixed structures. A second is that a declaration changes the zone. The usual test for a state, in the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries, and a structure that is no island in law provides no territory.

The lawful way to build here is an agreement with the coastal country, which alone can authorize the structure and could write special rules for it into its own law. Such grants have proved fragile, on land and at sea. Honduras changed its constitution in 2013 to allow private zones such as Próspera, on an island, and its Supreme Court struck those laws down in 2024. French Polynesia signed a memorandum with the Seasteading Institute in 2017 and said in 2018 that it was void. Whatever freedom exists is a grant from one government that a later government can review.

abandoned-platforms.essay:
Steel and concrete structures stand in open water off many coasts, and some are no longer in use. A disused platform already has a deck and legs and needs no dredging, so people have tried since the 1960s to use wartime sea forts and purpose-built platforms as bases for independent projects.

The first thing to understand is that an empty structure is not an ownerless one. Two separate kinds of right apply. One is ownership, which belongs to whichever company or government built or bought it, and entering without permission can be trespass. The other is legal power over the place, which belongs to a country. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, an installation in a country's exclusive economic zone, the belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles from its coast where it controls resources, stays under that country's sole legal power. The same applies on its continental shelf, the seabed extending out from the coast (Articles 60 and 80). Oil platforms stand on a shelf, so they normally fall under that power. Buying a platform from its owner would appear to transfer ownership only, because the country's legal power does not come with the sale.

The treaty also expects old structures to disappear. Abandoned or disused installations must be removed to keep shipping safe, and any part left standing must be made public so that ships can avoid it (Article 60(3)). In practice that duty usually reaches the operator through the coastal country's own rules. Sinking one is no easy way out, since the London Protocol, a treaty on dumping, treats all dumping at sea as prohibited unless explicitly permitted. A platform has no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has, so it cannot be the base of a claim to the water around it (Article 60(8)). Nor is it part of the coast when boundaries are drawn (Article 11).

Suppose a group boards a disused oil platform 50 miles off a coast and raises a flag. Boarding is physically possible. The owner, who may still be responsible for removing the platform, now has unauthorized people on its property. The coastal country has legal power over the structure, so its police or navy can come out. If anyone is hurt, or the structure fails, the questions of who pays would go to that country's courts.

Sealand is the case everyone cites. Roughs Tower was built by Britain in 1943 and sunk in place on a sandbar, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk and 7 off Essex. That was then outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea. Roy Bates, a former army major, had just lost a court case over Radio Essex on Knock John, another fort, because the court found that fort lay on the landward side of the legal line measuring the limit. He moved to Roughs Tower, took it from Radio Caroline staff, and declared the Principality of Sealand on 2 September 1967. In May 1968 his son Michael fired a pistol near a boat servicing a buoy. A judge at Chelmsford ruled that October that the firearms law did not apply, because Parliament had never extended it beyond three miles. That ruling decided only how far a statute reached. In 1978 a Cologne court held that Sealand was no state, in a case brought by Alexander Achenbach, a German who had drafted its constitution. That August Achenbach's associates seized the fort while the elder Bateses were away, and the family retook it by helicopter. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which now covers the tower, and it has left the place alone since. The Bates family says Britain and Germany have recognized it in practice, and neither government accepts this. Roy Bates died in 2012. Michael lives in England, the family sells titles and an online citizenship at about $10 a month, and one caretaker lives on the fort. Sealand's fort stood outside the limit when the claim began, and a new project would not have that history.

Other governments did not leave their forts alone. Sunk Head, about 18 km off Essex, stood clearly outside British waters too. When the law banning offshore broadcasting took effect in August 1967, Royal Engineers placed 3,200 pounds of explosives and blew it up on 21 August, leaving only stumps. Red Sands, home of Radio 390, lost in the High Court in 1966 on a measurement from a sandbank that shows only at low water, and it went off the air on 14 August 1967 under the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. In June 1966 men boarded Radio City's fort in a dispute over a transmitter, its owner Reginald Calvert was shot dead at the home of a rival, Oliver Smedley, and Smedley was cleared on grounds of self-defence. The killing turned public feeling against the stations, and enforcement rose.

REM Island was built for commercial radio and television about 10 km off Noordwijk and fixed to the seabed in cement, beyond Dutch territorial waters as then measured. Broadcasts began in August 1964. The Dutch Senate passed a law on 1 December 1964, and the government put it into effect on 12 December. Accounts differ on whether it declared the seabed below the platform Dutch territory or applied Dutch law to installations on the Dutch part of the continental shelf. Boats and police helicopters arrived five days later, and accounts differ on whether marines or police officers boarded. Rose Island, a 400-square-metre platform nearly 12 km off Rimini, declared independence on 1 May 1968. Italian police and tax officers took control on 26 June, about eight weeks later, and blockaded it. The navy set explosive charges twice in February 1969, the second time on 13 February, and a storm sank what remained on 26 February. The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, held the independence claims unfounded and said Italian citizens stay subject to Italian law abroad.

Holding a fort leaves the other problems open. HavenCo was set up on Sealand in 2000 to keep customers' data beyond the reach of courts. Law professor James Grimmelmann found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's internet links more than any government did. Co-founder Ryan Lackey left in 2002 after disputes with the Bates family and could not sue, because Sealand's monarch headed its courts and going to a foreign court would have undercut the claim of independence. Operations stopped in 2008. Banks need a supervisor they can rely on, and a fort has none. Sealand's passports were revoked in 1997 after a Madrid-based ring sold fakes, and using such a document at a border may bring charges. Unauthorized broadcasting from the high seas can be prosecuted by several countries, including any country that receives the signal, and their ships may arrest those involved (Article 109). Old steel and concrete need upkeep, and a 2006 fire on Sealand sent one person to hospital, with damage estimates ranging from £100,000 to half a million pounds. People on board keep their home countries' tax duties, and a rescue lands them in another country. Locking someone up on the platform could also be treated as unlawful detention by another country's courts, since no one else accepts the platform's own courts.

Common misunderstandings follow from Sealand's fame. The 1968 British ruling said a statute stopped at three miles and did not recognize Sealand. Occupying a structure gives no title to it, and buying one gives no country. The usual test for a state, in the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with others. Sealand has had one or two residents in recent years, and its territory is a deck that UNCLOS treats as no island.

The lawful path is an ordinary lease or purchase from the owner, with the coastal country's approval, for a business such as research or tourism, under that country's law and with a plan for eventual removal. REM Island's later life points the same way. The Dutch government used it to measure sea temperature and salt levels, and it has been a restaurant in Amsterdam's harbour since 2011. A new occupation claiming independence would have little legal basis on a shelf or in an exclusive economic zone, and most of its chance of lasting would depend on a government choosing not to act.

undersea-water-column.essay:
A habitat under the sea is hard to see, and some people expect it to be hard for the law to reach. In law, depth changes very little. The water and the sea floor follow the zone at the surface above them, and being underwater does not create a separate legal space.

The ocean has layers of law, under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. In the territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles from a coast, the coastal country has full authority over water and seabed, and submarines must travel on the surface and show a flag (Article 20). Further out, the seabed is usually a country's continental shelf, the shallow sea floor extending from its coast. Article 77 gives that country exclusive rights to the shelf's resources, and Article 80 applies Article 60, so artificial islands, and installations with an economic purpose or that could interfere with its rights, need its permission. Further out still, the water above is high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, while the bottom is "the Area", the deep seabed run by the International Seabed Authority (ISA). Article 137 bars anyone from taking any part of it. Article 147 applies ISA rules to installations used for mining, so it does not appear to clearly reach a habitat with no mining.

So a person must first ask whether the habitat moves. A moving craft would likely count as a vessel. High-seas freedoms apply to the water (Articles 86 and 87), so a submerged vessel under a flag appears to be treated as a ship, although UNCLOS does not define "ship". A flag means a real country's registration, and that country's law comes aboard. Without one, the rule in Article 110 on boarding a vessel with no flag still applies to a submarine, though a warship has to find it first. Hiding is a practical advantage only, and it ends at every port call. It can also be a crime in itself. A US law, 18 USC 2285, makes it an offence, with up to 15 years in prison, to operate or embark in a submersible vessel without nationality that travels beyond a single country's territorial sea with the intent to evade detection.

A fixed habitat is the harder question. On a continental shelf it needs the coastal country's permission where Article 60 applies, and any anchor appears to give that country a physical point of contact. Research installations follow the rules of the zone where they sit, have no island status, and get safety zones of 500 metres at most (Articles 258 to 260). On the deep seabed, taking any part as your own is barred, and the ISA's rules on installations are written for mining. The treaty gives no clear answer on whether a stationary habitat tethered to the seabed counts as a ship or an installation, and the question appears open. Article 87 lists among high seas freedoms the building of artificial islands and other installations "permitted under international law", which leaves what is permitted to be worked out elsewhere. Since 17 January 2026 a further treaty applies among its members, the BBNJ Agreement on marine life outside national waters. Its Article 28 requires each member to assess the likely effects on the marine environment of planned activities under its jurisdiction or control in those areas before authorising them. Reading that text, it seems a habitat run under a member's flag or by its companies would be caught if it met the treaty's thresholds. The seafloor reaches more than 8 km deep in the Mariana Trench, according to the ISA, while the deepest habitat described below went to 610 feet off a coast.

To see why it stays shallow, it helps to understand saturation diving. Water pressure forces breathing gases into the body, and after long enough at depth the body reaches a steady state. Divers in that state can work outside for hours, and they need to decompress, returning slowly to surface pressure, only once at the end of the mission. They cannot simply swim up in an emergency. A sick person in a habitat therefore has a slow trip to any hospital.

The history starts with governments. Jacques Cousteau's Conshelf experiments put two divers, Albert Falco and Claude Wesly, on the sea floor off Marseille in 1962, with accounts differing between 10 metres for seven days and 12 metres for two weeks, and in 1963 placed six people 10 metres down in the Red Sea off Sudan for 30 days. Air, water, food and power all came from a large team on the surface. Part of the money came from French petrochemical firms, and later work showed that robots and divers from the surface could do industrial jobs more efficiently, so companies lost the reason to pay for people on the bottom. The US Navy's SEALAB I went to 192 feet off Bermuda in 1964. SEALAB II followed in 1965 off California, where Scott Carpenter stayed a record 30 days. SEALAB III went to 610 feet in February 1969, 18 months late and $3 million over budget, and the aquanaut Berry Cannon died during a repair. A Navy inquiry found his breathing equipment lacked the chemical that removes carbon dioxide, and a 2024 study by an ocean engineer pointed to electrocution. The programme was halted.

What has lasted operates under a coastal country. Aquarius sits 62 feet down, 5.4 miles off Key Largo in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a protected area run by the US government. Built in 1986 and placed there in 1993, it was owned by the US ocean agency NOAA, and Florida International University took over operations in 2013. Jules' Undersea Lodge, a former research laboratory, is in a lagoon at Key Largo with a dock and a gift shop, and it is a building under water to which state and federal law apply. DEEP, a private UK-based company, installed its prototype Vanguard at Tennessee Reef in the same sanctuary in June 2026, designed for up to four people on missions of five days or more, and it was working toward classification by DNV, a body that certifies marine equipment. Its planned Sentinel modules would hold six people each at 200 metres for 28 days. Because they can be moved, a different country's permission would apply at each site.

The plans further out have not been built. Proteus, proposed by Fabien Cousteau for a marine park off Curaçao with government backing, was reported to need US$60 million to build and US$75 million to run for three years, and in October 2024 it was still in planning. Ocean Spiral, a 2014 design by Shimizu Corporation, described 5,000 people in linked spheres at ¥3 trillion, about US$25 billion, and expected Japan's government and private investors to help pay. Aquatica, proposed by Dennis Chamberland, a former NASA bioengineer, spoke of children born under water with schools and hospitals. Its first step, a four-person house called Leviathan, is not known to have been placed, and the plan named no site or legal basis. Any seabed divers can reach from a shore base would most likely lie on some country's shelf.

Suppose a family wanted to live on such a habitat beyond any permit. Surface boats would have to bring food, gas and spare parts from a port, and that port's country sets the terms. Children would need birth records and schooling from somewhere. A law journal puts even a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million. Crime on board would come under the law of the flag country or of the people's own countries, since US law, for one, reaches any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation for offenses by or against US nationals.

The main misunderstanding is that depth brings legal shelter. Nothing in UNCLOS gives it. A second is that living on the bottom earns a claim to it. SEALAB, Conshelf and Aquarius all kept people on the sea floor for long periods and gained no rights to the seabed. A third is that a habitat is a territory for the purposes of statehood. Research installations have no island status, and the Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist for a state, asks for a defined territory and a permanent population. Staying long term also depends on supply from the surface.

What is possible is the form that exists, a licensed habitat for research, training or tourism in a coastal country's waters, staffed in rotation and supplied from shore. Going deeper or further out adds cost and risk and brings no new legal shelter, and the habitat's position remains that of a licensed structure under the country above it.

leases-and-extraterritorial-spots.essay:
People often imagine that an embassy, a foreign military base or an airport transit lounge is a little piece of another country, or of no country at all. The legal picture is different, and understanding it shows why these places offer so little to someone who wants a territory of their own. In almost every case the host country keeps final authority. Another country or body runs the place under a lease, a treaty or a diplomatic rule, and what that occupant can do depends on the words of the agreement.

A lease between countries works much like a lease on a flat. The owner stays the owner, the tenant gets the use of the place, and the document says how long and on what terms. Guantánamo Bay, a US naval base of 117 square kilometres in Cuba, has been held under a lease since 1903. Article III of that lease shows the idea exactly. The United States recognises "the continuance of the ultimate sovereignty of the Republic of Cuba", the final legal right to rule, while it exercises "complete jurisdiction and control" as long as it occupies the land. It began at $2,000 a year in gold and has been $4,085 a year since 1974. A 1934 treaty, in Article III, says the lease can end only if both sides agree or the United States leaves. The Cuban government that took power in 1959 says the base was imposed by force and is illegal, and it has cashed one rent cheque since then, which Fidel Castro said was deposited by mistake. The base still operates, and Cuba still objects. In Boumediene v. Bush in 2008, the US Supreme Court ruled that detainees held there have a constitutional right to challenge their detention in court, so even that base is not a place without law.

Leases can also be forced on a weaker country, and they can run out. In 1898, after China's defeat by Japan, Britain leased the New Territories of Hong Kong, including 235 islands, for 99 years with no rent. The treaty is often described as an unequal one, meaning it was forced on a weaker state.
