Because the lease would end on 30 June 1997, Britain and China negotiated in advance, and under their 1984 Joint Declaration all of Hong Kong passed to China. The Panama Canal Zone, 1,432 square kilometres, was granted to the United States in perpetuity, which means with no end date. It had its own governor, courts and police. Riots in 1958, 1959 and 1964 led to negotiations, and the zone was abolished in 1979. So a grant with no end date came to an end after about 76 years, by a new treaty.

In all these known cases, the party receiving a lease was a country or a country-like body. The nearest thing to a private group is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries and no land of its own. A treaty signed in 1998 gives it the upper part of Fort St Angelo in Malta for 99 years, with listed privileges and legal protections. Either side may give notice in the 50th or 75th year, with the end taking effect five years later. Malta keeps ownership, its flag flies beside the Order's, Maltese courts generally have jurisdiction, and the Order may not grant asylum there. The Order had nine centuries of history behind it and worldwide humanitarian work, and it still got a use arrangement in a fort. No new founder has come close to such a deal.

Embassies work on a different principle. Article 22 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations says embassy premises are inviolable and that the host country's officers may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission. That rule protects the work of diplomats, and it does not turn the building into foreign soil. Article 41 says people with diplomatic privileges must respect the host country's laws and that the premises must not be used in ways incompatible with the mission's functions. Julian Assange showed what the rule gives and what it leaves out. He entered Ecuador's embassy in London, a suite of rooms on the ground floor of a block of flats, on 19 June 2012, and Ecuador granted him asylum. Britain did not accept the asylum. International law gives the embassy's government less here than people suppose. In the Asylum case of 1950 between Colombia and Peru, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, said that sheltering someone in an embassy derogates from the sovereignty of the host country, found that Colombia could not settle the nature of the offence by its own decision, and found no proven regional custom that would let it do so. Britain and Ecuador were not parties to that case, and reading it, it seems to support Britain's refusal without deciding it. It suggested that it could use a 1987 British law to enter, then withdrew the suggestion, and police guarded the building at a reported cost of £6.5 million in the first two years. He could not leave without being arrested, and he stayed nearly seven years. In April 2019 Ecuador's president ended the asylum and invited police in, and they arrested him. He was held in Belmarsh prison until June 2024, when he pleaded guilty in the Northern Mariana Islands to one US count of conspiring to obtain and publish national defence information and his sentence of five years and two months was counted as served, so he was freed that day. His safety depended entirely on the wishes of the government that ran the building. A private person can be there only as that government's guest, and a change of president ended it.

Airports are the place of the greatest misunderstanding. Films and news stories talk of an international zone, as if travellers past passport control had left the country. These zones are fully under the legal power of the country where they sit, and local law applies inside them. A court has said so in plain words. In Amuur v. France in 1996, about asylum seekers held at Paris-Orly airport, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that "despite its name, the international zone does not have extraterritorial status", that French law applied to them, and that holding them there was a deprivation of liberty that breached the European Convention on Human Rights. Mehran Karimi Nasseri lived in Terminal 1 of Charles de Gaulle Airport near Paris from 1988 to 2006, about 18 years, and French law applied to him throughout. Belgium and France both offered him residency, and he refused to sign because the papers did not use his chosen name. He gained no status from staying, and he died at the same airport on 12 November 2022. Edward Snowden spent 39 days in the transit area of Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow in 2013 after the United States revoked his passport, and he left when Russia granted him asylum. A transit area is a place people get stuck when no country will take them, and being stuck there gives them no rights over it.

Some other arrangements look similar. The UN headquarters in New York and its offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi are areas where the UN has been given some authority by agreement, and most local and national law still applies in them. The United States has a special visa, the C-2, so that delegates can attend meetings. The Tomb of Suleyman Shah in northern Syria was made a Turkish concession by the Treaty of Ankara in 1921, and Turkey moved it in 1973 and again in 2015, the second time on its own and over Syria's objection.

Suppose a group tried to use this route. They would first have to find a government willing to sign a lease with them on terms that give more than an ordinary tenant has. If a government offered only a normal lease, the group would be a tenant under that country's law, paying rent and tax. If it offered privileges, those would come through that country's own law or a treaty, and private groups cannot sign treaties in the sense governments use. Any term could end by notice, by a court or by the next government. Banks, insurers and suppliers would look at who holds final authority and would deal with that country's rules. Staff and residents would keep their existing citizenship and tax duties, and children born there would take their nationality from the rules of real countries.

What a private group can actually get is a plain commercial lease of land, or a service role under a body that already has status. Either one can run for a long time. Herm, in the Channel Islands, has had tenants since 1737, and its lease was extended in 2023 to 2069. Neither gives any authority. The odds here reflect that. A lease can hold fairly well in law and in practice, and Guantánamo has lasted since 1903, but the agreement that does so is between states. Embassies and airports have sheltered people for years, and no territory passed to any of them.

combo-floating-host-zone.essay:
Most people picture a floating settlement far out at sea. A different plan is to float one near shore, inside a country's waters, with that country's agreement and a special legal framework. This combines the territorial sea or the exclusive economic zone with the host's carve-out. It gives up the attempt to escape the coastal state, in exchange for calm water, a nearby port and a government partner.

The law of the sea is clear on the framework. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, gives a coastal state sovereignty in its territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles, or about 22 kilometres, from its coast. Beyond it, out to 200 nautical miles, lies the exclusive economic zone, where Article 60 gives the coastal state the exclusive right to build and to authorise artificial islands and certain installations, and exclusive legal power over them, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law. So a host can permit a floating zone and set its rules. Without permission, a long-term structure is at risk. Thailand's navy raided the XLII seastead 14 nautical miles off Phuket in 2019, and Thai officials raised the possibility of the death penalty, on a charge of violating sovereignty.

One gap remains in UNCLOS. It does not define artificial island, and it does not say whether a small floating home on a mooring is an island, an installation or a ship. A structure that stays in place and houses people looks more like what Article 60 covers, but no international court has decided this, and no court outcome in the XLII case is known. The couple living there were not caught. With a host agreement the gap matters less, because the host has already said yes. It matters when a host's successor later changes its mind or when a third country's ship wants to pass.

The real attempts all turned on politics and money. On 13 January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the Seasteading Institute for studies toward seazones with a special governing framework. A memorandum records intentions and usually binds no one. Local people objected, the opposition demanded withdrawal, and in February 2018 the government's position was reported that the deal had no legal force and had expired at the end of 2017. In the Maldives, the government signed with the Dutch developer Dutch Docklands in 2010, and signed again in 2019 and 2022 after a change of government, for a housing project on a 200-hectare lagoon near Malé. Reports differ on how much has been built. At Busan in South Korea, the city, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX signed in November 2021 to build a prototype, with about $200 million anticipated and with South Korean law applying to property, police and courts. A local report in October 2023 said no concrete financing had been presented. Kiribati's president spoke in 2011 of floating islands costing about $2 billion, to come from other countries.

What is open, and what has not been tested, is how far a host can go. A country that has authority over its waters could in principle pass a statute giving a floating zone its own commercial law, in the same way as a zone on land. Whether a French territory, for example, could have done so without Paris is something no court has had to decide for this project. Reading UNCLOS, it seems that a coastal state may delegate management inside its waters, and that it cannot pass on its international position, since other states' rights of passage and navigation, and the coastal state's duties, run to the state itself.

Follow the steps. The first is a site study and a set of letters. Next comes a law, which means a public debate, with fishermen and neighbours among those heard. Marine engineers and insurers then want storm data and a classification society's approval, and lenders want the land-law equivalent of a title, which water cannot provide unless the host's law creates one. Boats, ports, medical care and supplies come from the host. A birth or a will on the platform runs under host law, as the host has authority. Environmental review of a lagoon may be the point at which the plan stops. Each change of government reopens the deal, as the Maldives shows.

The form that fits this law is close to what Busan proposed, which is new floating housing under the ordinary law of a willing host, perhaps with a modest economic zone added. It can answer real needs, particularly for low islands with rising seas, and it can be built with existing engineering at high cost. It gives no separation. A floating city under such an agreement is a neighbourhood of that country, and its residents remain under its law.

underground-subseabed.essay:
Some people expect that a place deep enough underground, or under the sea floor, must be out of reach of governments. Digging is one of the easier ways to build a large private space, and the law runs downward from the surface, so going down does not change which country a person is in.

The rule on land comes from an old saying. The Latin phrase cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos means "whoever owns the soil, it is theirs all the way to the sky and to the depths". It has been traced to the 13th-century Italian lawyer Accursius, and William Blackstone gave it its broad form in his Commentaries on the Laws of England in 1766. Modern law keeps a limited version. Below the ground, an owner holds rights to what is underneath, although in many places minerals beyond a set depth belong to the government, which often leases them out. The saying settles who owns a chamber under a plot of land. That owner still holds it under the law of the country it lies in, as the owner of a basement holds it under the same town's rules as the house above.

A country's authority also runs down. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a coastal country's authority reaches the seabed and the rock beneath it in its territorial sea, the belt of sea next to its coast (Article 2). Past that belt, the continental shelf is the seabed and the rock beneath it, out to the edge of the continental margin, where the continent's underwater slope ends, or to 200 nautical miles (Article 76(1)). The coastal country alone may explore the shelf and take its resources, and nobody else may do so without its express consent, even if it never uses them (Article 77). Article 85 adds that the shelf rules do not limit a coastal country's right to exploit the rock below by tunnelling, however deep the water above. So the water over a shelf may be open to every ship while the rock beneath stays under the coastal country's control. A private mining shaft or tunnel there would need its consent. The deep ocean floor beyond the shelves is not part of this system and has its own rules against private claims.

Suppose someone buys a disused missile silo in Kansas and announces a sovereign republic in it. The silo part has been done. In 2008 Larry Hall bought an Atlas missile silo at Raven Ridge near Concordia for $300,000. It goes down 197 feet. He built Survival Condo, a bunker of 15 floors and 12 condominium units for up to 75 people, with a pool, gardens, three years of stored food, armouries and a jail cell, at about $20 million by 2012. All of it remained ordinary property. Peter Ziegler, who bought a unit in 2013 and lent the company $3 million, died in 2017, and his estate sued in January 2019, saying assets had been moved to other companies. The two sides settled that August. Debts, lawsuits and courts reached the bunker as they reach any other property in Kansas, and a declaration of independence would not change which courts have power there.

The buyer's first bumps are the same as for any building. A bunker has an address, so officials can simply enter it. Ordinary police, fire and licensing law apply. Geology comes next. Vivos, a California shelter company, planned a site for 5,000 people in a former mine of 2,700,000 square feet at Atchison, Kansas, and cancelled it in June 2014 after Army geologists raised concerns about collapses. Its plan for a Soviet-built complex at Rothenstein in Germany was expected to need sprinklers throughout under fire rules. It lists 575 bunkers of about 2,150 square feet each at the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot in South Dakota. Its membership figures, about 100,000 members and over 1,000 buyers in 2022, come from the company. Then there is daily use. Survival Condo had no owners living there in 2020, and a bunker's owner still needs electricity, water, food deliveries, schools and hospitals from above.

CyberBunker is the case of someone who did call it a republic. In 1995 Herman-Johan Xennt bought a former NATO bunker of 20,000 square feet at Kloetinge in the Netherlands, built in 1955 to survive a nuclear attack. His web-hosting business took any website except those with child abuse material or terrorism. Its spokesman, Sven Olaf Kamphuis, called it the Republic of CyberBunker and styled himself a minister. In 2002 a fire exposed a laboratory making the drug MDMA, three men were jailed, and the town refused a business licence. The servers moved above ground while the firm kept advertising the bunker. A Hamburg court barred it from hosting The Pirate Bay in 2010, and Kamphuis was arrested in Spain in 2013 over an attack on the anti-spam group Spamhaus. That year the firm bought a second bunker at Traben-Trarbach in Germany. Investigators tapped its traffic under a warrant from 2015 and sent in undercover officers posing as a gardener and a cleaner. In September 2019, 600 police raided it. In late 2021 the court in Trier convicted all eight defendants of belonging to a criminal organisation, though not of aiding their customers' crimes, with sentences of up to five years and nine months. Germany's Federal Court of Justice largely upheld the verdict in 2023. Warrants, wiretaps and undercover work all operated as they would against any business.

Pionen, a data centre in central Stockholm, makes no such claim. It occupies a 1943 wartime shelter of 1,100 square metres under 30 metres of granite, behind a door 40 centimetres thick, and the internet provider Bahnhof opened it on 11 September 2008. WikiLeaks kept servers there in 2010. It has a street address, and Swedish law applies as to any other business. A hardened site protects servers from physical harm, and its legal protection comes entirely from the law of the country it stands in. HavenCo on the sea fort Sealand sold a similar home for data and relied on a claim of independence, and that business stopped in 2008.

The remaining pitfalls follow from staying in one's own country. Taxes stay. The US taxes its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, a rule the Supreme Court upheld in Cook v. Tait in 1924. Internet addresses come from regional registries through a real legal entity. Passports issued by a bunker republic are not recognized, and using one at a border may bring charges. Children attend ordinary schools and inherit under the ordinary law, and a will or a mortgage works as usual.

The main misunderstanding is that depth is distance from the country. Rock under a shelf already has a holder by treaty, so tunnelling under the sea floor does not reach a free zone. Owning land also does not include the right to set its law.

Such a site stays within the law as what these businesses already are, a private bunker, data centre or shelter under local law with its permits in order. Buying the land is the easy part. Such a place can give physical security and some privacy. It does not change which country a person is in or protect against a lawful order.

geo.essay:
Geostationary orbit is a single ring around Earth, directly above the equator and 35,786 kilometres up, according to the European Space Agency. A satellite in this ring travels at about 3 kilometres per second and goes around once every 23 hours and 56 minutes, which is the time Earth takes to turn. Seen from the ground, it appears to hang over one spot. Dish antennas can therefore stay pointed in one direction, and weather satellites can watch one region continuously. Three evenly spaced satellites can cover most of the planet. Only one such ring exists, which makes positions in it valuable. No person has ever lived in it.

Reaching it takes two stages. A craft first follows a long oval path that climbs to 35,786 kilometres, then fires its engine again at the top to round the path into a circle. Operating there then requires a filing by a country and a launch licence, and those two requirements are the heart of the matter.

The general law is the same as in low Earth orbit. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, bars any country from taking over outer space (Article II). A treaty country must permit and oversee private activity (Article VI), and the country that registers a craft has legal power over it (Article VIII). The treaty does not name this orbit, and it does not define where outer space begins. That gap produced the one serious attempt to claim the ring.

On 3 December 1976, eight countries on the equator, Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Congo, Zaire, Uganda, Kenya and Indonesia, signed the Bogotá Declaration. They called the orbit a scarce natural resource and said the part above each signer's territory fell under that country's sovereignty, meaning its full legal control. Parts above open ocean were to be shared by all nations. Their argument was that the treaty never defined outer space, so it did not cover the orbit over their land. Many of them were newly independent and objected to a system that favoured countries that already had satellites. Other countries did not accept the claim, and it won little support. The usual view is that the orbit is part of outer space and so falls under the treaty's ban, although no court has ruled on the point. Two signers kept it in their law. Colombia's constitution lists its segment of the orbit as part of the country (Article 101), and its Constitutional Court said in 2004 that the country had not given up sovereignty over it. Ecuador's 2008 constitution also asserts rights over the orbit (Article 4). How a court would treat a private station parked above either country has not been tested.

In daily practice the ring is run through radio. Every satellite needs radio frequencies to work, and two transmitters on the same frequency in the same direction spoil each other. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio and satellite coordination, keeps order. It has 194 member countries. Its founding treaty, the ITU Constitution, says radio frequencies and orbits, including the geostationary orbit, are limited natural resources, that countries should have fair access to them, and that no station may cause harmful interference (Articles 44 and 45).

Under the ITU's Radio Regulations, a country's national authority submits notices for a planned satellite. The country then works out any conflict with other countries' satellites, and those that filed earlier generally have the stronger position. Approved frequency assignments are entered in the Master International Frequency Register, the official global list. Filings carry fees to recover the ITU's costs. People often call the result an orbital slot, which is a recorded right to use certain frequencies from a certain position. It is an entry on a list, and it is not land.

This is the obstacle that matters most. A frequency filing can only come from the national authority of a member country. A station without one would have no recorded protection from interference, and other operators would appear to have no duty to coordinate with it. A country outside the UN can join the ITU only with the agreement of two-thirds of the members, and a self-declared state would first have to persuade them that it is a country at all.

Tongasat shows both how open and how closed this system is. Matt Nilson, a businessman who had moved to Tonga, a small kingdom in the South Pacific, persuaded its king in 1987 that even a tiny country could apply. The government authorised the venture in April 1988, and in March 1990 he applied for 16 of the 180 slots then available. Intelsat, a satellite operator, and the United States objected. The ITU agreed in March 1991 after he cut the request to six, and Tonga eventually held nine. The plan was to rent each one for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government. Lawyers have described this as in effect a flag of convenience for space, meaning a country that lends its registration to outside operators, and later filings came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. Tonga could do this because it is a country. China later wanted one position and Tonga gave way in exchange for aid, and on 17 August 2018 Tonga's Lord Chief Justice ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. In 2019 the court made an appeal depend on a security payment of about $15,000, and how the appeal finally ended is not known.

Suppose a private group wants a small habitat in this ring. It would need a friendly member country to file for frequencies, or to rent a position that a country already holds. It would need a launch licence, which in the United States comes from the Federal Aviation Administration with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. It would need an entry on a register, and the Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to do that themselves. That country then holds legal power over the habitat and everyone aboard, so the filing, the licence and the register all lead back to a government. Costs follow. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, and this ring is far higher. The habitat would sit in a crowded band and would be expected to leave at the end of its life. In 2023 the US Federal Communications Commission issued its first debris fine, to Dish Network, because its satellite EchoStar-7 ran low on fuel and stopped short of the higher "graveyard" orbit it had agreed to reach.

Everyday problems are the same as on any space station. Food at 2.77 kilograms per person per day must come from Earth, and medical care beyond first aid means a return trip. Crime falls under the registering country and under each person's home country. Americans still owe US tax returns.

Misunderstandings tend to centre on the word "slot". Holding one gives no sovereignty, no right to exclude anyone physically, and no standing as a state. The Bogotá claim is also misread as a live rule, when only two constitutions keep it and other countries have not accepted it. Standing directly over an equatorial country does not place a station under that country's law, except in the eyes of that country.

The lawful form is an ordinary licensed station, registered by a cooperating country, using frequencies that country has filed or rented. Tonga's experience suggests a small country may be willing to act as the filing partner for a fee. A private group would still need that country to apply for it, and would stay under its law and its power to withdraw. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, put building here at about 3 percent and holding out against outside control at about 15 percent, because the station depends on its filing country for radio protection and on its licence to operate. The chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower.

run-by-international-agreement.essay:
Most land on Earth belongs to one country, and that country's government makes the rules there. A small number of places have been handled differently. After a war or a long quarrel, several governments signed a treaty that took a city or a region away from any single country and placed it under an international body, a committee of foreign powers, or two countries acting together. The owner of such a place is whoever the treaty names. In the past that has been the League of Nations (the international body that came before the United Nations), the UN Security Council, a committee of foreign consuls, or a pair of neighbouring states.

The reason these places exist is usually that two or more strong countries each wanted the same spot and none could take it without a fight. Handing it to a neutral arrangement let everyone avoid losing. Danzig is the clearest example. After the First World War, Poland had been promised secure access to the sea, and the obvious port was Danzig, but about 90 percent of its people were German. So Article 100 of the Treaty of Versailles, the peace treaty with Germany, took the city from Germany, and Article 102 made it a Free City under League of Nations protection. It covered 1,952 square kilometres and held 366,730 people in 1923. It had its own parliament and its own currency, while a League High Commissioner watched over it and Poland handled its foreign relations and defence and ran its railways and post.

Tangier followed the same logic. France and Spain both wanted this Moroccan port on the Strait of Gibraltar, and Britain wanted it neutral, so the three signed a convention in Paris in December 1923. The zone covered 373 square kilometres and began operating in June 1925. An appointed assembly made laws, a committee of foreign consuls supervised it, and a Mixed Court with judges named by five European countries replaced the separate courts each foreign power had run. The zone had no tariffs, exchange controls or income taxes, and it held 85 banks by 1950. People who dream of a low-tax free territory sometimes point to it. Those low taxes were possible because several governments had agreed to allow them and kept foreign consuls in charge.

Other treaties used the same tool for a set period. The Saar Basin, a coal-mining area between Germany and France, was taken out of German government for 15 years by Article 49 of the Treaty of Versailles and held in trust by the League. A five-member commission alone made the law there, and a regional council could only advise. At the end of the 15 years, on 13 January 1935, residents voted, and 90.8 percent chose Germany. The Memel Territory on the Baltic was handed by Article 99 to the victorious Allies, who ran it through French officials until Lithuanian militias seized it in January 1923. A convention in 1924 accepted the seizure, and a German ultimatum took the territory away in March 1939.

The UN later took on similar jobs. The Free Territory of Trieste was created by the 1947 peace treaty with Italy and accepted by the Security Council in Resolution 16, as a neutral state under the Council's direct responsibility. The Council had to appoint a governor, and it never did. The Soviet Union rejected 12 nominees between October 1947 and March 1948, and the post stayed empty. The territory stayed split between Allied and Yugoslav military rule for seven years, and in 1954 a memorandum signed in London divided it between Italy and Yugoslavia. The border was settled only by the Treaty of Osimo between those two countries, signed in 1975 and ratified in 1977. A plan for Jerusalem, called the corpus separatum (Latin for separated body), went further on paper. The General Assembly adopted it in 1947, with a UN-appointed governor and a referendum after ten years. It was never carried out, because the 1948 war left the city divided between Israel and Transjordan. Resolution 1244 placed Kosovo under UN administration from 1999, and a UN authority ran Eastern Slavonia, a region of Croatia, from January 1996 to January 1998 with about 4,800 soldiers, so that it could return to Croatia without more fighting.

A related form is the condominium, a territory governed jointly by two or more powers. New Hebrides, now Vanuatu, was shared by Britain and France from 1906 to 1980. Brčko District in Bosnia and Herzegovina, created on 8 March 2000, has 493 square kilometres and 83,516 people, and it is held jointly by the country's two internal entities because its population is mixed. Andorra, in the Pyrenees, is a sovereign state whose head of state is shared by two foreigners by virtue of their offices, the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell.

The record shows how these places end. They last as long as the powers that signed keep agreeing. Germany annexed Danzig on 1 September 1939, the day it attacked Poland. Tangier returned to Morocco by a protocol signed in October 1956, once France and Spain had ended their rule over the country. The Saar and Eastern Slavonia ended as designed, by a vote and by a handover. Trieste never began to work as intended. Brčko and the Andorran arrangement continue today in the forms described here. The UN mission in Kosovo also still exists under Resolution 1244, with minor day-to-day functions since Kosovo declared independence in 2008.

Suppose a group of private people wanted to set up a territory this way. They would need a treaty, or a decision of the UN Security Council, and they have no standing to obtain either. A treaty in the legal sense is an agreement between countries, and an agreement signed by a private group would look to governments like a private contract. A Security Council decision needs nine of 15 votes and no veto from any of the five permanent members. Nothing in the history shows any of those bodies acting at the request of founders. They acted because governments had a dispute to settle, usually at the end of a war. A person cannot start this process, and the people living in these places did not choose the arrangement either. The residents of Danzig and Trieste were placed under it by others.

A common misunderstanding is that an international territory is free of national law and open to anyone with a good plan. These places had a great deal of law, written by foreign governments, with foreign officials enforcing it. Residents did not get a say in the basic structure. In the Saar, an elected council could offer only advice for 15 years. Another misunderstanding is that a treaty guarantees survival. It gives strong legal standing while the signatories honour it, which is why a place like this gets middling estimates for law and for holding on to land once it exists. Those estimates stay middling, since each case ended or was altered when the powers behind it changed course, and the chance of a private group getting its own territory under its own laws is much lower.

What an ordinary person can do is take part in such a place as a resident or to work for a government or citizens' group pressing for one as a settlement to a dispute. Local people can have influence at the moments when a treaty offers a vote, as Saar residents did in 1935. A new territory created in this way is very unlikely to be started by a private founder, and it would become recognised as a separate state only rarely. Its existence would depend on outside powers from its first day to its last.

secession-and-decolonisation.essay:
Almost every country that has joined the world map in the past hundred years got there in one of two ways. A colony or an administered territory came out from under its ruler, or part of an existing country broke away from the rest. These are the routes that have actually produced new states, for peoples already on the land, so they deserve careful study. They also need something a private founder does not have, an existing people living on a territory who want to govern themselves. The land belongs to the existing country unless it agrees to let go or loses control.

The idea behind these routes is that a people can decide its own political future. International law has treated colonies and similar territories as a special case. The UN keeps a list of non-self-governing territories, places whose people have not yet governed themselves, and Western Sahara is still on it. In its Chagos opinion of 25 February 2019, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, called General Assembly Resolution 1514 a defining moment in state practice on decolonisation. It found that Britain's separation of the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius before independence made that decolonisation unlawful, because a people's right covers its territory as a whole. Britain and Mauritius signed a treaty on 22 May 2025 to hand over the islands while keeping the Diego Garcia base for an initial 99 years. In April 2026 Britain shelved the legislation after the United States withdrew its support, because the treaty cannot take effect without US consent under a 1966 agreement between the two countries. Three small Pacific countries show how a territory can leave such status on negotiated terms. The Marshall Islands, Micronesia and Palau were part of a UN trust territory run by the United States, and each chose to become a sovereign state, a self-governing country in law, while signing a compact giving the United States authority over its defence in exchange for guaranteed money. Those compacts took effect in 1986 and 1994 and have no end date, though the economic terms are renewed.

Part of an ordinary country stands in a harder position. The leading explanation is the Supreme Court of Canada's 1998 Reference re Secession of Quebec. The court held that Quebec cannot leave on its own under Canada's constitution, since secession would need a constitutional amendment. It held that international law gives no general right to break away, and it limited any such right to colonial rule and foreign occupation. It mentioned a further possibility, a right as a last resort for a people blocked from the meaningful exercise of self-determination inside its state, and it did not need to settle that point, since it found that Quebec's people have such meaningful exercise. A state that governs all its people without discrimination keeps its territorial integrity. The court added that a clear majority on a clear question would oblige the rest of Canada to negotiate, while a majority alone has no legal effect and cannot dictate the terms. Canada's Parliament then passed the Clarity Act. An independence referendum is a public vote in which residents decide whether their territory should become a separate country. A Yes does not always bring independence. A count of Wikipedia's table as it stood in November 2026 gives about 123 votes since 1817. Of these, 59 ended in a No, 31 in a Yes followed by a recognised state, 12 in a Yes with control on the ground and no or partial recognition, and 16 in a Yes with no independence. Western Australia voted Yes in 1933 and stayed in Australia. Nevis voted Yes in 1998 and fell short of the two-thirds it needed.

What separates success from failure is mostly whether the parent country has agreed, or has lost the power to refuse. South Sudan's vote came from the 2005 peace agreement that ended a long war, which fixed the terms and date in advance. Turnout had to reach 60 percent. In January 2011, 98.83 percent chose separation, and South Sudan joined the UN that July. Montenegro used a right written into the constitution of its union with Serbia. A disputed rule required 55 percent, and Yes got 55.5 percent in 2006, by 230,711 votes to 184,954. All five permanent Security Council members accepted the result within two days. Eritrea had already defeated Ethiopian forces when it voted under UN observers in 1993, and 99.83 percent chose independence. Timor-Leste voted in 1999 under a UN mission after Indonesia's president agreed to the vote, 78.5 percent rejecting autonomy. Militias then carried out mass violence, and an Australian-led force restored order before independence in 2002.

Scotland shows the agreed route ending in a No. The Scottish and UK governments signed the Edinburgh Agreement in 2012, which temporarily gave the Scottish Parliament power to hold the vote, and 55.3 percent voted No in 2014. On 23 November 2022 the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament cannot hold another one on its own, and the UK government has refused to transfer the power again. Bougainville shows that even a huge majority can be left waiting. It voted 98.31 percent for independence in 2019, under a peace agreement that made the result non-binding, and Papua New Guinea's parliament has the final decision. In July 2021 the two governments agreed on independence by 2027, subject to that parliament's approval, and in July 2026 a forum of Bougainville leaders recommended 1 September 2030 as the target date. The result was tabled in parliament on 27 August 2026, and the prime minister said the two governments would meet in October to set a date for the vote. By November 2026 no date had been reported, and the parties dispute the majority required. New Caledonia had three agreed votes. Independence lost by 57 percent and 53 percent, and in 2021 No took 96.5 percent under a boycott by Kanak leaders, who had asked for a delay after a COVID-19 outbreak. Riots in May 2024 killed 14 people. The Bougival accord of July 2025 and the Élysée-Oudinot accord of January 2026 proposed a new status, and the main pro-independence alliance, the FLNKS, withdrew from Bougival and boycotted the talks. On 2 April 2026 France's National Assembly rejected the constitutional bill, 190 to 107, so the status remains unresolved.

Without consent, the parent country has many tools, and they come in a rough order. The courts come first. Catalonia's parliament approved a referendum law on 6 September 2017, and Spain's Constitutional Court suspended it the next day and declared it void that October. Police come next. National officers used force at polling stations on 1 October, when Yes took 90.18 percent on a turnout of 43.03 percent. Then the government takes over. On 27 October the Catalan parliament declared independence, and the same day Spain's Senate approved direct control under Article 155 of the constitution. No state recognised the declaration. Criminal cases followed, and an amnesty for crimes linked to the referendum passed in 2024.

Beyond that lies war. Biafra declared independence from Nigeria in 1967, five states recognised it, and around two million civilians are estimated to have died before it surrendered in 1970. Katanga broke away from Congo in 1960, funded by a mining company with exclusive copper rights, and UN forces ended it by January 1963. In the United States, the Republic of New Afrika claimed five southern states in 1968, and it declined in the early 1970s after raids and mass arrests that jailed its leaders.

A common misunderstanding concerns the International Court of Justice's 2010 opinion on Kosovo. Serbia asked whether Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence broke international law, and the court found by 10 votes to 4 that it did not. That means that international law contains no ban on writing and issuing such a declaration. It does not mean that the declaration creates a state, or that other countries must accept it. The court said the rule of territorial integrity, the rule that protects a state's borders, operates between states, which is why it does not bind the authors of a declaration. It also explained that the Security Council's past condemnations of declarations, such as the one for Northern Cyprus, came from their link to unlawful force or similar grave breaches. Asked by participants whether a part of a people has a right to separate outside colonial or foreign rule, or a right of "remedial secession" after severe abuse, the court recorded radically different views and declined to answer. That question remains open. Judges Simma, Sepúlveda-Amor and Yusuf said the court should have addressed it, Judge Cançado Trindade affirmed Kosovo's right to supervised independence, and Judge Koroma wrote that self-determination does not allow the dismemberment of a state without its consent. Russia, Spain and Cyprus, which have or fear separatist movements of their own, opposed Kosovo's declaration in written statements. Kosovo is recognised by 110 UN members, and 8 others have withdrawn recognition. It belongs to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and it is not a UN member, because admission needs Security Council approval with no veto. Kosovo also came out from a NATO-backed UN administration, under Security Council Resolution 1244, which few other territories have behind them. Abkhazia and South Ossetia show the limits of having a strong backer. Russia recognised both in 2008 after a war with Georgia, and only a handful of others followed. Abkhazia depends on Russia for about half its budget, and most residents use Russian passports. The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is a full member of the African Union and is recognised by somewhere between 33 and 46 UN members, and Morocco holds most of its land, with the promised referendum never held. On 31 October 2025 the Security Council voted, with 11 in favour, for talks based on Morocco's autonomy plan.

Suppose a real region with a real movement wanted to try this. The stages are a long political campaign, a popular mandate shown in elections, talks with the parent country for a binding vote, then negotiation over debts, borders, currency and citizens after a Yes. Abyei in South Sudan shows how a border question can remain open for years. Puntland in Somalia shows another path, self-government since 1998 without any claim to be a separate country. A private founder cannot do this. No one can buy a population's consent, and this is why the chance of a founder even starting a state this way is only about 3 percent, and the chance of a founder getting a territory under its own laws is much lower, even though the same route gives a real population a much better chance of that. The title that results, once it is agreed, is about as strong as title gets, and the existing odds for law and for holding the land reflect that.

antarctica-unclaimed.essay:
Almost all of Antarctica is claimed by one country or another, but one large wedge has no claimant. It runs from 90 degrees West to 150 degrees West and is mostly called Marie Byrd Land, about 1,610,000 square kilometres including the Eights Coast. It is the largest unclaimed land on Earth. Norway's tiny Peter I Island, at about 90 degrees 35 minutes West, lies inside that band and is the one exception. This wedge attracts people looking for empty ground, and a number of them have announced countries there from their homes. To see why those announcements have no legal effect, it helps to start with how land used to be claimed and what changed.

Countries used to gain land by finding and occupying a place that belonged to no one. Lawyers call such a place terra nullius, Latin for nobody's land. Seven countries staked out parts of Antarctica, most of them between 1908 and the 1940s. Nobody claimed this sector, which Wikipedia calls remote even by Antarctic standards. The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 and took effect in 1961, and it governs everything south of 60 degrees South. Article IV(2) says that "no new claim, or enlargement of an existing claim" may be asserted while the treaty is in force. It also says acts during the treaty cannot create rights of authority over the land. So the old method was shut off just as this wedge was left over.

Someone usually objects at this point that the treaty binds only countries that joined it, and that it does not stop an individual. That is right as far as it goes. The treaty binds its 58 members, and under Article 34 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, the treaty about treaties, an agreement does not create obligations for a state that has not consented to it. Whether the Antarctic freeze nevertheless binds outsiders is an old argument that no court has decided. Malaysia brought the continent's future before the UN General Assembly in 1983, and treaty members opposed UN involvement. Marie Jacobsson, in a 1998 Lund University thesis on exactly this question, concluded that the treaty itself does not create a regime valid against everyone, while certain of its provisions express customary law or have gained that status, meaning unwritten rules that bind states generally.

A private claim fails without having to settle that argument, because the older rules of international law already shut it out. In its Western Sahara opinion in 1975, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, described occupation as a means of "acquiring sovereignty" and looked to state practice to judge it. In the Ligitan and Sipadan case in 2002, about two small islands claimed by Indonesia and Malaysia, the same court said that "activities by private persons cannot be seen as effectivités", meaning acts showing a state actually governing a place, unless they rest on official regulations or governmental authority. So a settler acting alone builds no title for anyone, and a settler acting under a government's authority would run into Article IV(2). Reading these rules together, a private claim has no route under the older law or the treaty. Members also carry a duty that reaches past their own governments. Under Article X of the treaty, each member undertakes to make appropriate efforts, consistent with the UN Charter, so that "no one" engages in activity in Antarctica contrary to the treaty's principles or purposes. If a citizen of a treaty member went to this sector, that country's own permit rules would apply. Under Britain's rules, for example, anyone on an expedition organised in the UK or leaving from it needs a permit. Norway's rules caught the skipper Jarle Andhøy, whom a Norwegian court fined 45,000 kroner in 2014 for sailing to Antarctica without authorisation in 2012, even though he said he never landed. An individual from a country outside the treaty would still most likely travel through a treaty member's territory.

Getting there is where the legal rules become practical. Article VII(5) requires members to give notice of expeditions organised by their nationals or from their territory. The Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the treaty that protects the environment, applies here as in the claimed sectors. Article 3 sets environmental principles, Article 7 bans mining, and Article 8 requires an impact assessment beforehand. Most routes pass through the territory of a treaty member, whose government would have to notify the others. So the same limits apply as in the claimed sectors, and the absence of a claimant does not create an open door. The United States and Russia, as successor to the Soviet Union, maintain that they have reserved the right to make claims later, and Article IV(1)(b) of the treaty preserves any basis of claim a member may already have, including from the activities of its nationals. Reading those texts, it seems likely that either government would object to a settler in a sector it could one day claim, although no such case has arisen.

The physical challenge is at least as large. A settlement would need fuel, food and shelter for a continent where even Chile's Villa Las Estrellas, a government settlement on an island near the mainland beside an air base, has a major hospital over 1,000 kilometres away and asks long-stay residents to have their appendix removed before they come. Marie Byrd Land is far more remote. Food, water and power would all have to be flown or shipped in, and the mining ban rules out paying for it from the ground. If something went wrong, the people who came would be the nearest government station's rescue problem, and that government would then be involved. Medical care, schooling and inheritance would all stay under the law of a person's own country.

The real cases show how these claims work in practice. The Grand Duchy of Westarctica was declared in 2001 by Travis McHenry, a US Navy intelligence specialist who read in the CIA World Factbook that no state had claimed the land. He wrote to many countries, and only other micronations, meaning tiny self-declared countries, responded. By 2006 his Navy superiors knew he was writing to foreign governments and told him to choose, and he kept his job and handed the title to a friend. He began issuing fantasy passports as souvenirs in 2004 and stopped after learning that a scammer in Kenya was selling them to refugees as real travel documents. In July 2025 Indian police arrested Harsh Vardhan Jain for running a fake Westarctica embassy from a rented house in Ghaziabad. In 2014 Westarctica registered as a non-profit, and it now campaigns on climate. It has no one on the land.

The Grand Duchy of Flandrensis, started by Niels Vermeersch of Belgium in 2008 as a two-week hobby, claims five islands off this coast, Siple, Cherry, Maher, Pranke and Carney. It registered in Belgium as a non-profit in 2021 and counted 741 citizens of 71 nationalities. It says it does not seek diplomatic recognition and does not intend to visit. Its founder spoke at a climate summit in Paris in 2022. The Kingdom of Talossa, begun by a 14-year-old in Milwaukee in 1979, includes part of Marie Byrd Land in its claim along with the east side of Milwaukee. It counted 157 active citizens in 2023, and none live on the Antarctic land. None of the three has built anything or been tested in any court, and the claims have stayed untested because nobody has gone there.

These cases show what can actually be accomplished. Such a project can be a website, a non-profit, a climate campaign or a hobby community registered under the law of the founder's own country. Those are real activities with real members, and they can draw attention to melting ice. They bring no land rights. The risks that have actually appeared are the ones found in any self-declared country. Passports get misused by others, officials or employers take an interest, and someone may use the name for fraud.

A project that could actually go ahead keeps these limits in view. A person could register a non-profit at home, publish a clear statement that its papers are not travel documents, and take part in climate or polar education. A person who wanted to stand on the land would have to join an expedition that follows notice and impact rules from a treaty member. The odds reflect the position, with about a 5 percent chance of building anything, about 10 percent for holding it, and a fraction of one percent for recognition, and the chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower than the first two. Marie Byrd Land being unclaimed has not made it available, since the same treaty that froze the existing claims closed this sector to new ones.

mars-and-beyond.essay:
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, about half the size of Earth, with a day of 24.6 hours and a year of 687 Earth days. It is a cold, dusty desert with a very thin atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide. Temperatures range from about 20 C down to about -153 C. It has no global magnetic field, and its atmosphere offers little protection from falling rocks. Water exists mainly as ice just under the surface in the polar regions. Only robots have ever been there. Its distance is the main thing to examine in law and in practice. A radio message takes several minutes each way, and at times more than 20, so no one on Mars can hold a live conversation with Earth.

The legal starting point is the same as for the Moon. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, covers natural bodies in space generally, and nothing in it stops at the Moon's orbit. No country may take over a planet by claiming authority, by use or occupation, or by any other means (Article II). A country must authorise and keep overseeing private activity (Article VI). The country that registered a craft has legal power over it and its people, with no mention of any distance where this ends (Article VIII). Countries must also avoid contaminating other worlds (Article IX). For the countries that have joined it, the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with few members, extends to all bodies in the solar system other than Earth (Article 1).

There is also a scientific rulebook. COSPAR, an international committee of space scientists, keeps a Policy on Planetary Protection, an international standard on keeping other worlds free of contamination from Earth, last revised in January 2026. It works through national space agencies and has no treaty force of its own. A licensing country could still apply it to a private mission as a way of meeting its duty under the Outer Space Treaty.

The machines already on Mars show how property works there. The Soviet probe Mars 3 made the first soft landing in December 1971 and failed 110 seconds later. It remains Russian property today. NASA's Viking 1 lander of 1976, Phoenix of 2008 and InSight of 2018 sit silent, and they still belong to the United States. So do the rovers Curiosity and Perseverance, including the sealed sample tubes Perseverance left on the ground for a later mission. China's Tianwen-1 lander and Zhurong rover remain China's after dust covered Zhurong's solar panels and it failed to wake in December 2022. In each case the country owns the machine and gains no title to the ground.

The best-known attempt to write a different rule came from a private company. In October 2020 the test-phase customer terms for Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service, said that for services on Mars or in transit there "the parties recognize Mars as a free planet and that no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities", with disputes settled "through self-governing principles". A term in a private contract binds only the people who signed it. It cannot release SpaceX from the United States, which under the treaty must authorise and supervise it. An article in Völkerrechtsblog, an international law blog, argued that SpaceX's conduct in space counts as that of the United States, and that such a claim risks breaching the ban on taking over a planet. A note at the University of Richmond said the clause tried to sidestep international law. No court has tested the clause, and it is not known whether later versions of the terms keep it.

Suppose a private group plans a settlement. Before departure it needs a launching country, an entry on a register and a licence. That country is responsible for the group and in legal control of what it registers. Next comes timing. Earth and Mars come nearest about every 26 months, so ships leave in batches. China's Tianwen-1 took from 23 July 2020 to 10 February 2021 to reach Mars orbit, a little over six months. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries.

Money is where the real attempts have failed. Mars One, a small Dutch venture announced in 2012 by Bas Lansdorp, planned a one-way colony paid for partly by a reality television show, at an estimated $6 billion for the first mission. It said 202,586 people applied, while Joseph Roche, a physicist among the finalists, said only 2,761 had completed the process, and the company later confirmed his figure. On 15 January 2019 the Civil Court of Basel in Switzerland declared Mars One Ventures bankrupt with debts of about 1 million euros. No hardware was built. The Mars Society, founded by the engineer Robert Zubrin in 1998, is a volunteer nonprofit whose physical work has all been on Earth, at simulated Mars bases on Devon Island in Canada and in the desert. It held contests on designing a colony of 1,000 and a city state of one million, with a $10,000 prize for the second, and it has adopted no known constitution for Mars. Elon Musk's stated hope, as reported by Universe Today, is 1,000 Starship rockets carrying 100 people per trip every 26 months, toward a million people. Such a transport system does not yet exist.

A 2020 model by the researcher Salotti in the journal Scientific Reports estimates about 110 as the minimum for a self-sustaining colony, by comparing the work required for survival with the time people have available. It holds only under the model's assumptions. No project has produced its own food at scale. Each person needs about 0.84 kilograms of oxygen a day, and space station crews used food at 2.77 kilograms per person per day, so a failed harvest would be a serious emergency when the next ship might be two years away.

Daily life brings its own bumps. No hospital would be near. Astronauts of member countries must assist each other (Article V), which helps only if another crew happens to be there. A crime would fall under the registering country and under home countries, and US law reaches offences by or against US nationals outside any nation. American settlers would still owe US tax returns every year. Children born there would take whatever nationality their parents' countries give, since the treaty does not mention birth, and whether its words about "personnel" cover a child born on Mars is not settled.

Paper claims appear here too, and they fail for the same reasons as elsewhere. In 1997 three men in Yemen complained to their Prosecutor General that NASA had invaded Mars, which they said they inherited from ancestors 3,000 years earlier. A popular history newsletter says the complaint was rejected, and no court record is known. Deed sellers also offer plots on Mars. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, has warned that such deeds can mislead buyers.

The most common misunderstanding is that distance removes the law. Distance slows enforcement, since no navy could arrive in less than months. In law, the registering country's power continues, and a settlement relying on ships from Earth would also depend on whoever licenses those ships. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, reflect this by putting the chance of holding off outside control once there at about 35 percent, and recognition as a state at about 0.2 percent. The usual test in the Montevideo Convention of 1933 asks for a defined territory, and the Outer Space Treaty denies one.

A settlement could lawfully go ahead if it were licensed and registered by a supportive country, with local rules agreed among residents by contract, and growing self-reliance that gives it more practical freedom over time. The same odds put building even that within 25 years at about 2 percent, and the chance of getting a territory under its own laws is lower still. Its legal status would remain that of a registered outpost.

combo-cbi-private-community.essay:
Citizenship by investment is a programme in which a country grants its nationality in return for a payment or investment. A private community is a town, estate or zone run by a company or association under contract with its residents. Stacking the two means that a group of like-minded people each buy the same small country's passport, or arrange a deal with that country, and then live together on private land there. The appeal is that they would hold a real nationality, with a real seat at the United Nations behind it, and live by their own contract rules, with the state at a distance because it was paid to stay friendly. No new state is founded, and the group lives under one that already exists.

The first thing that is settled is that a country may grant its nationality on its own terms, as a matter of its own law. A passport bought this way is a real passport. The second settled point comes from the International Court of Justice in Nottebohm, a 1955 case. Friedrich Nottebohm, a German who had lived in Guatemala since 1905, obtained Liechtenstein nationality during a short visit to Europe in 1939. Liechtenstein later sued Guatemala on his behalf, and the Court held the claim inadmissible. Nationality granted without a genuine connection did not entitle Liechtenstein to protect him against Guatemala, the country where he actually lived. The Court did not say the nationality was void inside Liechtenstein. So a bought passport works for travel where states accept it, and it may not give the person a government able to press a claim against their long-time country of residence.

The third settled point is new and applies within Europe. On 29 April 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in Commission v Malta, case C-181/23, that Malta had broken EU law by running a scheme that gave nationality through a transactional procedure in exchange for set payments. The Court called this the commercialisation of nationality and, through it, of EU citizenship. It relied on Article 20 of the EU's founding treaty on citizenship, on the duty of cooperation among member states and on the relationship of solidarity and good faith between a state and its nationals. Malta had argued that EU law requires no prior genuine link and that Nottebohm could not supply such a rule. The Court did not make a genuine link the test. It found the breach in the scheme's transactional nature. So the ruling closes this route for EU member states. It does not bind Caribbean or Pacific programmes.

Those programmes depend on outsiders in another way. Much of a passport's value is its visa-free access. The European Commission proposed suspending the visa waiver for Vanuatu over its scheme, which charged about $130,000. The Commission pointed to a very low rejection rate and to citizenship granted to people listed in Interpol's databases, and in March 2022 the EU Council suspended the waiver for holders of ordinary Vanuatu passports issued since 25 May 2015. The partner state can hold firm and its passport can still lose value overnight. The OECD monitors high-risk schemes because they can be used to get around bank reporting. A bank may therefore ask a holder for proof of real ties.

The Comoros shows a third way this can fail. Around a decade before 2018 the Comoros Islands agreed with the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait to sell citizenship to stateless people in those countries, known as Bidoon, in return for development money. In 2018 its parliament reported that nearly 48,000 foreigners had received passports, that thousands were sold outside official channels by what it called mafia networks, and that up to $100 million had gone missing. When a small state sells nationality in bulk, the buyers depend on that state's own honesty and politics.

Now suppose the community stage. A group of 2,000 people buys the passports of an island country and buys private land there. They write a contract covering rules of the estate, private arbitration and shared services. On the estate, ordinary property and contract law gives them a good deal of freedom, as in a large condominium or gated town. But criminal law, immigration, tax, building rules and the courts all remain the state's. Being citizens gives them something foreigners lack, which is the right to stay and a right to vote, so a group of that size in a very small country could become politically important. Reading the rules of ordinary democracy, it seems such a group could lawfully try to elect representatives and seek a special law. The Free State Project and the takeover of Antelope, Oregon, by followers of Rajneesh show how moving voters can work and how it can provoke a response. Whether local voters would tolerate a bought-in bloc is a political question nobody can answer in advance.

The state's position is the open part. Nothing in international law stops a small state from giving such a community a special zone, and a later government can reverse it. Honduras's Supreme Court struck down its zone laws in 2024 with retroactive effect. Whether a state that sells its nationality to a group has any wider duty to the group is untested. Nobody has tested the full stack of mass citizenship plus a governing contract in one place.

The potential is real but limited to the level of a very favourable host deal. The strongest version is a stable small state that passes a special zone law after a real public debate, a community whose members actually move there and live there, so that Nottebohm's genuine connection grows over time, and an investment treaty behind the zone. The support of the country's own voters would decide how long it lasts. The group would get only the autonomy the host's law allows, under a real flag, and a later law could end it.

combo-lease-on-station.essay:
Under this model a private group does not try to escape the state that registered a space station. It leases space or operating rights on the station and runs its own community there by contract. Residents sign a long agreement that sets the rules, the fees and how disputes are settled. This combines the idea of a lease with low Earth orbit. It is the form most likely to be built, because it asks no government to give anything up.

Two sources explain the idea. One is the ORBIS lease, a model contract drawn up by Spencer MacCallum, a scholar of privately run communities, and discussed by Alexander Salter of Texas Tech University in a 2019 article in the Journal of Air Law and Commerce. Salter starts from Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, which bars any country from taking space as territory, and argues that since states cannot extend territory there, rules for conduct must come from elsewhere, with a proprietary community as the best candidate. The other is MirCorp, which in 2000 obtained commercial rights to the Russian station Mir, with the Russian company RSC Energia as a major shareholder. It paid for the last crew to live on Mir, and it signed up a paying passenger before the money ran out and Russia brought the station down in March 2001. No settlement has used an ORBIS lease.

The settled law sits under any such contract. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty gives the state on whose registry an object is carried jurisdiction and control over the object and its personnel. Article VI makes states answer for national activities and requires authorisation and continuing supervision of private ones. A contract binds the people who sign it. It does not release any government from a treaty, and it does not take away any government's power. The International Space Station shows how registry law works in a shared habitat. Under the partners' 1998 agreement, each keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens (Article 5). The European Space Agency describes modules as treated like the partner's territory, so European law applies in the Columbus laboratory. Article 22 has special rules for crime, under which a country may prosecute its own citizens for what they do in any module.

What is open is how much room a state of registry may leave. Salter reads the ban on national territory as opening a space for private rule-making, and others reply that Article VI keeps private settlers under a country's supervision. Nobody has tested how much supervision counts as "continuing". A US licence requires insurance and permits the government to block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds, but US rules on occupant safety are largely on hold in a learning period set to end on 1 January 2028. It is also unanswered whether residents can validly sign away rights under the home law, or whether a private lease can have its own penalties. Reading the text, it seems that a contract can decide ordinary matters such as rent and house rules, and that serious crime and safety stay with a state. How a court on Earth would treat a contract clause that removes rights its own law protects has not been tested for a station.

Here is how it would go. A company registered in some state signs an agreement with the owner of a station, or builds its own under that state's licence. Vast's Haven-1 and the planned Axiom Station and Starlab are in this family, although none has flown or seeks self-government, and all depend on government customers or licences. The company writes a lease that sets a common code. A resident signs before launch. The resident's home state still reaches them as a citizen, including through tax in countries that tax citizens abroad. A resident who commits a crime on board comes under whichever state's law applies, and the company has no power to sentence anyone. When the resident leaves or falls ill, the return flight lands in some country, under its law. Children and inheritances would be handled by home countries, since the treaty does not mention them.

The practical pressure is on price. Launch alone, at about $3,246 per kilogram on a Falcon 9, comes to about $3.3 million per person each year for about 1,000 kilograms of food. Aurora Station offered 12-day stays at $9.5 million and closed. By 2013 Bigelow Aerospace had put $250 million of its founder's money into inflatable modules, and it laid off its 88 staff in March 2020. A lease does nothing to reduce that cost, and a lessee depends on the station owner for air and power, with limited ability to walk away. Export rules slowed MirCorp's tether, and the same rules would reach parts bought for a leased module.

The potential here is the largest of the orbital routes if the goal is a community with private contract rules, under the law of the state of registry, and not a state. A friendly state of registry could leave most internal matters to the lease, in the way many countries let private housing associations or company towns run their own rules, and that could produce a real society with its own daily order. The strongest version adds a clause on arbitration with awards enforceable through courts on Earth, and an agreement with the state of registry about what it will and will not supervise. The limits are that the state remains free to change its mind, and that a resident can always appeal to it.

combo-charter-ship.essay:
A ship at sea already works a bit like a small town. The next step would be a community where every resident signs one governing contract, a charter, that sets the rules for life on board, the services, the dues and how disputes are decided. It combines an ordinary flag registration with a private constitution and private arbitration. Nobody claims a new state. The community's rules would sit on top of the flag state's law, much as the rules of an apartment block sit on top of a city's.

Start with what is settled. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), every ship on the high seas sails under a flag, and Article 92 says only the flag state has legal power over it there, with narrow exceptions. Article 94 makes the flag state responsible for safety, crew and seaworthiness. A ship with no flag, or with a micronation's flag, can be boarded by any warship on suspicion of having no nationality under Article 110. So a charter operates under the flag and cannot replace it.

The working model is MS The World, built by shipping professionals. It has 165 residences owned by the people on board, is registered at Nassau in the Bahamas, and is managed from Florida by a company that hires the crew, with an elected residents' board that advises on route and finances. That is a one-contract community in substance, since owners bought into shared rules. It has run since 2002 and claims nothing. Bahamian law applies at sea, and each port's law applies in port. It carries 150 to 200 people and a crew of about 280, so it is small and expensive.

A cheaper version failed on money. Villa Vie's Odyssey ended in October 2026 when its company could not secure fuel. Life at Sea sold 111 cabins and never had a ship, and 78 customers asked US prosecutors to investigate about $16 million in deposits. If the ship or the company goes, buyers of a home at sea have only contract claims against a company.

Insurance can stop it before any government acts. MS Satoshi was bought in 2020 for a floating community in the Gulf of Panama, to sit anchored full-time. Its owner told investors that no protection and indemnity insurer would cover a stationary residential ship. Without that insurance there could be no crew, the ship would lose its class rating and then its flag. No navy was involved. It seems from that case that the insurance market is treating a residential ship as something different from a working vessel, although a moving ship with a professional manager has not met that barrier.

The contract's reach is the interesting part. Under the New York Convention, residents can agree to private arbitration for civil disputes, with a land seat that makes the award enforceable. The contract can set dues and rules and can provide for expulsion at the next port. It can choose a governing law for those matters, subject to what the flag state and courts accept. It cannot reach crime, since the flag state's criminal law applies, and home states often apply their own as well. US law covers offences by or against US nationals in any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation. A private security officer who locks a resident in a cabin risks a charge of unlawful detention unless the flag state's law gives a captain's authority for that case. A captain has traditional powers to keep order on a voyage, and those belong to the captain under the flag's law. The charter could not give them to the community's council.

Reading UNCLOS, it seems that nothing stops a flag state from allowing such a charter, and that a flag state could also pass a special law for a residential ship, as Honduras did for zones on land. No flag state is known to have done so. How far a contract may displace flag state rules on employment or consumer rights is a question for that state's own courts, and no court is known to have considered a charter of this kind. Whether a ship staying at sea for decades, with children born on board, would be treated as a ship or as something else is also unsettled. UNCLOS does not define "ship" at all, so it sets no test based on movement. A long-term anchored ship in an exclusive economic zone would invite the argument that it is an installation under the coastal state's control under Article 60. The Thai navy raided a small floating home off Phuket in 2019, and no court outcome in that case is known.

Then come the indirect routes. Founders and crew remain nationals of their own states, with duties to report income. A US citizen on board still files tax returns every year, and banks report the account. Ports decide who may land and can inspect the vessel. Fuel, food and repairs all come from ports, and supplies can be refused to a ship with legal troubles. A radio licence comes from the flag state. A flag state can strike a ship from its register, and Women on Waves shows that a ship's protection depends on staying in its flag state's good graces, since Dutch law and a Dutch permit gave it legal ground.

Birth and death need thought too. A child born on board takes nationality from parents and from whatever the flag state's law gives. Article 1 of the 1961 statelessness treaty addresses birth on a state's territory, and Article 3 of that treaty treats birth on a ship as birth in the flag state's territory for its purposes. A burial, a will or a divorce goes to a real court.

The potential for a residents' community is solid at the size of a village, and a state is out of reach. The strongest version is a professionally managed ship under a reputable flag, owned by its residents through a company or cooperative, moving regularly, fully insured, with an arbitration clause seated in a respected land jurisdiction. That gives people a floating community of their own rules on most daily matters, able to move away from any single coastal state. It remains under a flag state that it does not control.

host-state-carve-outs.essay:
A country can, if it chooses, set aside part of its own land and give it different rules. It might have separate business courts, lower taxes, its own regulators or even a form of self-government. This is the one route to separate rules that starts with the consent of the government in charge, and that is why it has actually produced separate commercial courts and tax rules, with the host keeping the final word. The host country keeps full authority unless it gives the land away by treaty, and the grant usually comes through its ordinary laws. What one legislature grants, a later court or legislature may take back. A person who follows this route is making an arrangement with a government and accepting that government's final word.

The best working example of separate commercial rules is the Dubai International Financial Centre, a business district of 110 hectares in the United Arab Emirates. In 2004 a federal law allowed each emirate to set up legal structures for financial centres, and Dubai then passed one law creating the centre and another creating its courts, which began working in 2006. Inside the zone, civil and commercial cases follow common law, the English system built on past court rulings, and they are heard in English, apart from the rest of the country's legal system.
