The centre has its own financial regulator and offers companies a 50-year guarantee of zero tax on corporate income. Other laws, such as criminal law and immigration rules, still apply. It is a place to do business under different commercial rules, and it remains part of Dubai.

Honduras shows the other end of the range. In 2013 the country changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development, known as ZEDEs, areas with their own laws, courts and taxes. An earlier plan had already been struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself. Próspera, on the island of Roatán, applied in 2017. It was built with American venture capital through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council, and it offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land. Then politics changed. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, and on 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect, according to Reuters.

Próspera's response shows what a company can do when a host reverses itself. It turned to treaty arbitration, in which a panel of arbitrators decides a dispute between an investor and a country. Its owners relied on a promise of stable rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries, and brought a claim at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body. The claim began at about $10.775 billion. Honduras's Attorney General says it has dropped to $1.63 billion, a cut of about 85 percent. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024 and rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. The case was still pending in October 2026, and the zone continues to operate during the dispute. An arbitration panel can award money. It cannot give a company back the power to make law on Honduran soil.

At the far end of the range sit two old cases that did produce something close to a state. Vatican City, 44 hectares inside Rome, came from the Lateran Treaty of 1929 between Italy and the Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church. The treaty recognised the Holy See's full sovereignty over the new state and settled a dispute that had lasted about 60 years, since Italian forces took Rome in 1870. The Holy See is a non-member observer state at the UN, alongside the State of Palestine. This depended on a global church and on a government that wanted to settle with it. The Sovereign Order of Malta, a Catholic order, describes itself as sovereign and reported relations with 111 countries in 2021, and it has no land except what others let it use. A new founder has neither background.

Other carve-outs are based on long custom. Mount Athos in Greece, 335 square kilometres with 20 Orthodox monasteries, governs itself under Greek law, with the monks controlling entry through a permit system. Sark, in the Channel Islands, held on to a feudal government granted in 1565 until the billionaire Barclay brothers challenged it under the European Convention on Human Rights, and a new constitution replaced it in 2008. Cherán in Mexico threw out loggers, police and politicians in 2011, and a federal Electoral Tribunal ruling that November backed its request to choose leaders by custom.

Freetown Christiania in Copenhagen shows how such room can be won from below. Squatters moved into old barracks in 1971, and the Supreme Court ruled in 1978 that the site should be cleared, an order that was never carried out. Parliament legalised the community in 1989. A 2004 Act reaffirmed the state's control, and the Supreme Court confirmed the state's full right of disposal in February 2011. So the community lost in court and then bargained. It agreed that June to set up a fund, and in July 2012 residents became legal owners of about 19 of the 84 acres. In 2013 Parliament repealed the special Christiania law, leaving the same laws as the rest of Denmark. Residents and authorities dug up the main dealing lane, Pusher Street, in 2024 after repeated shootings, which unlocked state money, and in February 2026 residents reluctantly accepted a public housing plan. About 900 people live there, half a million people visit each year, and Danish law applies.

Many announced zones have never been built, which is the common pitfall for people who invest in them. Akon City in Senegal, which its promoter said had 2,000 acres from the president, carried a $6 billion price tag, and in 2025 the state agency that controlled the land said the project no longer exists. Bitcoin City in El Salvador relied on a $1 billion bond, and a later deal with the International Monetary Fund undercut the bitcoin policy behind it. It is not known to have been built. Forest City in Malaysia received a Special Financial Zone in 2024 after its Chinese developer ran into debts, with just over 1 percent of the development thought to be inhabited by one 2024 report. The Maldives Floating City was signed in 2010 and signed again in 2019, and finished homes have not been confirmed.

The same approach, separate rules granted by a host, seems able to work at sea. Article 60(1) of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea says a coastal country may authorise artificial islands and installations in its exclusive economic zone, the belt of ocean where it controls resources. A floating city could therefore have a host's permission, on that host's terms. The Seasteading Institute and the government of French Polynesia signed a memorandum on 13 January 2017 for a floating prototype with legal semi-autonomy in the territory's waters. After a local presidential election changed the politics, the territory cut ties on 14 March 2018.

Suppose a group wants to do this today. It would need a government with a reason to agree, usually jobs or investment, and a law that its courts will uphold. It would ask for the grant to be written into the constitution, for a long promise of stable rules, and for a treaty that allows arbitration if the promise is broken, and Honduras shows that even a constitutional change can be undone. It would need to deal early with neighbours, because local land fears fed the opposition in Honduras. Its residents would keep their nationalities, and their home countries would go on taxing them where their laws do so. Banks would rely on the host's regulators, which is why a real regulator matters. This is the most workable route to separate courts and tax rules, with roughly even odds of building and funding it and somewhat under even odds of holding it through later elections. The chance of getting a territory under the group's own laws, with criminal law and the final word included, is much lower. The zone stays part of the host country, so it does not produce recognition as a separate state.

the-sun.essay:
The Sun is a star, a ball of extremely hot gas at the centre of the solar system. It lies about 149.6 million kilometres from Earth and measures about 1.4 million kilometres across. It has no solid ground, and no one can go there. A territory on the Sun therefore cannot be a physical place. Every attempt to create one has been a matter of paper, and all of it has happened on Earth. The limits come from people and offices here, such as the notary who records a statement, the rules of the website used to sell plots, and a local court.

To see why a paper claim achieves so little, it helps to start with what ownership is. When a person owns a house, a government keeps a record of that ownership, its courts will settle a dispute over it, and its police will remove a trespasser. Ownership depends on a government standing behind it. Space has a special rule that removes that support. The Outer Space Treaty, which took effect in 1967, is the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article II says that outer space, including the Moon and other natural bodies in space, is not subject to "national appropriation", meaning a country taking it as its own, whether by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. If no country may claim the Sun, no country has authority to hand out title to pieces of it.

The argument on the other side is about the treaty's wording. Article II mentions nations and says nothing directly about private people. María Ángeles Durán of Vigo in Spain argues that this stops countries from owning a star and leaves individuals free to do so. Dennis Hope, a Nevada entrepreneur who sells deeds to the Moon, reads the treaty the same way. Most space lawyers disagree, according to a review of the writing on the point in the law blog Völkerrechtsblog. They point to Article VI, which makes each country answer for the space activity of its private companies and citizens, and says such activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty member. A private person is therefore still acting under a country's responsibility. Spain has joined the Outer Space Treaty. It has not joined the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with 17 members, whose Article 11 says plainly that no natural person may own the surface of the Moon, and whose Article 1 extends its Moon rules to other natural bodies in the solar system apart from Earth. Neither treaty defines "celestial body", the term in the original text, though the Sun is ordinarily described as one. No court is confirmed to have ruled on any of this for the Sun, so the wording argument remains open in that narrow sense.

Durán's case shows what happens at each step. In 2010 she went to a notary, an official who certifies legal documents. The notary recorded her statement that she was "owner of the Sun, type G2 star". The Spanish news site Genbeta says the notary did not take it seriously, asked the notaries' professional body, and was told to record what she said. That is the limit of what such a document does. It proves a person made a statement on a certain day. It does not prove the statement is true, and it gives no sovereignty, meaning a government's full authority over a place. Genbeta adds that the Spanish property registry has no power over the solar system, so her claim could not be entered there.

She gave a second legal reason, usucapion, an old rule inherited from Roman law under which long use of a thing can turn into ownership of it. Her point was that she had benefited from sunlight for decades. Everyone else on Earth has done the same.

Next came the money. She threatened to charge people for using solar power, later saying she had meant electricity companies. No payment is known to have been made. She then sold plots on eBay, the online auction site, at 1 euro per square metre, with a certificate for each. About two years after she opened the account, eBay removed the listings under its policy on intangible goods, meaning things that cannot be physically delivered, and blocked her account. A private website needs no treaty to do this, because its own rules decide what may be sold on it.

She sued eBay in court number 5 of Alcobendas, near Madrid. The amount is reported as 10,000 euros by The Register and about 7,500 pounds by Scottish Financial News. Accounts of the result differ. A report from June 2015 said a Spanish court recognised her claim and let her pursue the dispute, with a first hearing set for 17 June 2015. The Mexican newspaper Excelsior said in 2022 that the court declared itself competent and let her sue, and it dated recognition of her ownership to 2012 without citing documents. Genbeta later wrote that the court dismissed the case and that a Spanish court said in 2016 that a person cannot legally own the Sun. It names no court document and credits Excelsior, whose article does not say this. How the case finally ended is not confirmed. A court that admits a case for hearing has agreed only to listen to it. Letting someone sue is a different thing from finding that she owns what she claims, and no confirmed ruling says she owns the Sun.

Suppose a claimant now sends an invoice to a solar power company. The company can simply refuse, and the claimant must then go to court and prove ownership with a document that only records her own words. Gregory Nemitz, an American, claimed the asteroid Eros and sent NASA a bill for $20 when its probe landed there. NASA refused, the State Department said Article II rules out private ownership of an asteroid, and his federal court case was dismissed.

The claims also collide with each other. Virgiliu Pop, a Romanian space lawyer, claimed the Sun himself to show that such claims are bogus. James Mangan registered a claim to all of outer space in Cook County, Illinois, in 1949. With no official register for such things, there is no office that could decide between them.

A notary's stamp is often taken for government approval, and it is not. A court accepting a case is often reported as a court accepting the claim. Silence from a government or the United Nations is taken as permission, as Hope has done, when it only means no one replied. A person who buys a plot receives a certificate and nothing a court is known to enforce. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, warned in 2023 that deeds to property on natural bodies in space raise the chance that individuals will be misled.

Statehood offers no way around this. The usual test, from the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other countries. A star where nobody can live fails the first test before the others arise. Estimates of every kind of success here are zero.

What can actually be sold is a souvenir, offered honestly as a souvenir. It carries no rights over the Sun or over anyone who uses its light, and it depends on the rules of whichever website and court the seller happens to use. Sunlight itself remains free to collect, since no one needs title to the Sun to put up a solar panel. Nothing can be built at the Sun, and the only activity on record is paperwork and online sales.

combo-digital-continuity.essay:
Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 10,000 people on low islands that may become uninhabitable within decades. Its answer combines two things. One is a digital copy of the country, with all 124 islands and islets mapped and its culture, language and elders' stories recorded, so that people abroad and future generations can keep them. The other is a legal promise from other states that Tuvalu stays a state whatever happens to its land. The second half is the one that matters in law. People who want a landless nation ask whether this could be a model for them. To answer that, it helps to see exactly what has been decided.

The test for a state, in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, lists a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and capacity to deal with others. On a strict reading, a state with no land fails. The Pacific Islands Forum, the regional body, declared in 2023 that the presumption of continuity applies in the context of climate-related sea-level rise. Australia's Falepili Union treaty with Tuvalu, signed on 9 November 2023 and in force on 28 August 2024, commits Australia to recognise Tuvalu's future statehood and sovereignty despite sea-level rise, and offers residency to up to 280 Tuvaluans a year. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that 26 countries had legally recognised Tuvalu's digital statehood by December 2023, with a goal of 50. These are promises by particular states, and they bind those who gave them.

In its climate advisory opinion of 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice said, at paragraph 363, that "once a State is established, the disappearance of one of its constituent elements would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". An advisory opinion does not bind states, though it carries weight. Two readings exist, and commentators Syla and Kent set them out. On one view the Court only restated an old rule, that states stay states through occupation or collapse. On the other it accepted that statehood can survive without territory or population in the climate setting. The sentence does not mention sea level or climate, and Judge Tomka questioned whether customary law supports a wider reading, while Vice-President Sebutinde and Judge Aurescu wanted the Court to go further. Readers differ on the International Law Commission's study group on sea-level rise. Jean-Baptiste Dudant, a law professor who assisted one of its co-chairs and writes in a personal capacity, says its final report of 2025 treated continuity as the answer, while Syla and Kent say its reports do not argue that state practice has yet extended the presumption to climate change. In May 2026 the General Assembly, by resolution 80/263, with 141 states voting in favour, said it "affirms the continuity of statehood in the face of sea level rise". General Assembly resolutions do not bind by themselves, and Britain said the resolution reflects the opinion and does not develop it. Dudant saw growing belief among states that continuity is legally required in these exceptional circumstances alone. On 24 September 2026 all 193 UN members agreed by consensus a political declaration affirming a presumption in favour of continued statehood despite sea-level rise, along with UN membership. Harry Aitken, an Australian legal adviser who led talks on its legal elements and writes in a personal capacity, says that whether these positions become law depends on how other states respond. So this is moving quickly and is not finished. The legal conditions and consequences of continuity are still unsettled, and no state has yet lost all its land, so the question has never been tested.

For a new project the most important words are "once a State is established". Reading those words, and the General Assembly's context, it seems that continuity protects an existing state and creates nothing. A self-declared online nation has no prior statehood to continue. The digital record gives a real people a means of keeping culture, and Tuvalu's rests on UN membership. That difference rules out the common hope that a digital twin can make a country from scratch. No court has accepted such an argument, and the Montevideo territory test remains in place for new claimants. Estonia's data embassy in Luxembourg is the related state practice, in which a recognised country keeps copies of its records in a protected server abroad under agreement. It also depends on an existing state.

There is also a price, in Tuvalu's case. Under Falepili, Tuvalu agreed to engage with Australia before any security partnership with another state, and former Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga said the treaty would undermine its sovereignty. Prime Minister Feleti Teo sought reassurance without revising it. A promise of protection came with a limit on freedom of action, which a small state often accepts for security.

A private group could copy the technique of asking states one at a time for a written promise, and a promise is valuable even if it binds only those who gave it. It could also copy the record keeping, which costs little. A diaspora community with an actual homeland at risk, such as a people on a sinking coast within a larger state, might use the record for cultural survival and argue for rights in law, and it would lack a state's voice in the UN. Suppose a group asks a government to sign a paper promising future recognition. That government would need a reason. Tuvalu's reason is sympathy and a shared interest in Pacific stability. A group with no existing people or place offers neither. Reading what those promises say, a promise to a group that does not yet meet the tests would be a political statement at most, unless other states also act on it.

The potential for keeping statehood is high for existing threatened states and very low for new ones. The strongest private version is a partnership with such a state, helping to build its records and services, with the state making the claims. That gives the private group a contract and useful work, and the state holds the sovereignty.

asteroids.essay:
An asteroid is a lump of rock, metal or ice that orbits the Sun on its own. Asteroids range from boulders to small worlds, and most have very weak gravity. People are interested in them for two reasons. They might be mined for materials such as water ice, and in theory someone might one day hollow one out or build on one. No one has lived on an asteroid, and no funded plan to settle one is known. The nearest published proposal is a 2020 paper by the Finnish physicist Pekka Janhunen on a settlement in orbit around Ceres, the dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, and it remains on paper.

The law treats an asteroid the same way it treats the Moon. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, covers all natural bodies in space. Article II says no country may take one over by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Under Article VI, a private group needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and that country answers for it. Under Article VIII, a craft stays under the law of the country that registered it, even after it lands. The Moon Agreement, a separate treaty that few countries have joined, applies its Moon rules to other bodies in the solar system except Earth. Those rules include a ban on private ownership of the surface. Its Article 1(3) says they do not apply to meteorites that reach Earth naturally, so a rock that falls in your field is a separate matter.

The best-known claim shows how this works in practice. Gregory Nemitz, an aerospace consultant from Nevada, claimed the asteroid Eros in March 2000 because he wanted to establish that private people can own property in space. On 12 February 2001, NASA landed its NEAR Shoemaker probe on Eros and left it there. Nemitz sent NASA an invoice for $20, the parking and storage fee for the next century. NASA refused, saying his claim had no basis in law. He wrote to the State Department, which replied that in its view Article II rules out private ownership of an asteroid. In November 2003 he asked a federal court in Reno to decide the matter. The judge ordered the case dismissed in April 2004, and the claim was dismissed on appeal in 2005. No court gave him title, and the lasting product of the case is an official American position against private ownership of an asteroid.

Paper claims continue anyway. A statement by the International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, says deed claims have been extended to other natural bodies in space, and one deed seller told Discover magazine that he owns about 95 planetary bodies. Fraud has appeared here too. In 1999, officials at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the regulator of investment markets, listed share offerings for exploring a near-Earth asteroid among fraudulent internet schemes.

The real legal development concerns what is dug out of an asteroid, as opposed to the asteroid itself. A useful comparison is fishing on the open sea. No one owns the ocean, yet a boat owns the fish it catches. The United States adopted this reasoning in 2015. Title IV of the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, now 51 USC 51303, says an American citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid resource may own, transport, use and sell it, subject to American law and the international obligations of the US. The law also disclaims any national ownership of a body in space. Luxembourg passed a similar law on 20 July 2017, and its own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows this. The United Arab Emirates followed with Federal Law No. 12 of 2019, and Japan with Act No. 83 of 2021. Section 10 of the Artemis Accords, a set of principles that countries sign as a political commitment, says extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body. Whether one country can grant rights that others must respect is still debated, and no court has tested any of these laws. The debate has moved to the UN's space committee, COPUOS, whose working group on space resources published a consolidated draft of principles in September 2026, with non-binding status and negotiations still running towards an April 2027 session. Its Principle 2 says extraction that complies with the Outer Space Treaty "does not inherently constitute national appropriation". The draft does not say who holds title to extracted material or what effect national laws have abroad. Russia pressed for treating resources "in place" as part of outer space and had earlier suggested a moratorium on their use, which is not in that draft. The United States, Canada and the United Kingdom objected to the word "shall" in non-binding principles. None of them gives anyone ownership of the asteroid.

Suppose a company in one of those countries sets out to mine an asteroid and house workers there. It first needs a launch licence. In the United States that comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. The craft must go on a country's register under the Registration Convention, a treaty on listing objects launched into space, and private people have no way to register themselves. That country then keeps legal power over the craft and the people aboard. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. If the craft damages something, the Liability Convention makes the launching country pay, so that country has good reason to demand insurance and supervision.

The next problem is money. Planetary Resources announced itself in 2012, and Deep Space Industries nine months later. Both built small spacecraft and both stood to gain from the new laws. Neither mined anything. A later start-up, AstroForge, launched the small test satellite Brokkr-1 in April 2023, and that mission failed because of communication problems. Its probe Odin, launched on 27 February 2025 to fly past the asteroid 2022 OB5, was declared lost on 6 March 2025. A further craft, DeepSpace-2, was planned for launch in the second half of 2026. A funding round for Planetary Resources with a major mining company fell through in 2017, which led to large layoffs, and in October 2018 the blockchain firm ConsenSys bought it on undisclosed terms. Bradford Space announced on 1 January 2019 that it had bought Deep Space Industries, by then working on small-satellite engines. The writer Jeff Foust concluded that the boom had been a bubble. Japan's Hayabusa 2 brought back a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020. Transport costs make the difficulty clear. A Falcon 9 rocket delivers cargo to low Earth orbit at about $3,246 per kilogram, and that is only the first and cheapest part of a trip to an asteroid. Supplying one person with food alone, about 1,000 kilograms a year, would cost about $3.3 million at that low-orbit rate, by simple arithmetic.

People who did reach an asteroid would meet further bumps. A claimed asteroid gives no right to exclude others. Article I of the treaty keeps all of space open to every country, and Article XII opens stations on natural bodies to visits by other members' representatives, on a basis of reciprocity and with advance notice. Help in an emergency could be months or years away, depending on the asteroid's path. Crime would remain under the law of the registering country and of people's home countries. Americans would still owe US tax returns, because the duty follows citizenship. A person who signs up to a self-declared asteroid nation changes none of this.

Common misunderstandings come from mixing up these layers. Owning ore is often reported as owning the asteroid. A national mining law is often taken to mean that the country has claimed territory, when these laws go out of their way to deny that. A deed from a website is taken for a title, and an invoice like Nemitz's is taken for a legal claim. The Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist for statehood, asks for a defined territory, and Article II denies that to anyone on an asteroid.

The lawful path open today is a licensed robotic mining company based in a country with one of these laws, which owns what it extracts and sells it under that country's law. A crewed base would follow the same pattern, with staff living aboard a registered craft under the registering country's authority. Distance would make outside control slow, which is why holding on once there is estimated at about 30 percent, while the chance of building at all is estimated at about 1 percent, and the chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower. Under such a law a company could own its machines and its ore, and nobody would own the asteroid.

high-seas.essay:
The high seas are the part of the ocean beyond every country's coastal zones. The ocean covers more than 70% of Earth's surface. About 58.6% of the sea surface is high seas, by the calculation of MarineRegions, a marine geography database, which works out at roughly 40% of the whole planet. Parliamentarians for Global Action, an advocacy group, gives 43% of Earth's surface in one place and about half in another, because the figure depends on how the area is defined. Either way, this is the largest part of the planet that no government owns, which is why people who want to start a new society keep looking at it.

The rules come from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. It has been in effect since 16 November 1994 and has 172 members. The United States has not joined it. The high-seas rules cover all sea outside a country's exclusive economic zone (its coastal resource zone, up to 200 nautical miles or about 370 km), its territorial sea (the belt next to its coast), its internal waters and the waters between the islands of an island nation (Article 86).

These waters are open to all countries, which may sail, fly over, fish, lay cables, do research and build artificial islands (Article 87). Each must pay due regard to the others. Building comes with two conditions in the treaty's wording, that the structure be "permitted under international law" and that it respect the continental shelf rules.

Two points in this are often missed. The freedoms are worded as belonging to countries and are not granted to private people, so a person uses them through a country. And no country may validly claim any part of the high seas as its own (Article 89). A new state could not gain a piece of this sea by occupying it, because the rule against claims applies to every state.

The high seas are governed through ships, and each ship carries one country's law with it. A country decides for itself which ships may fly its flag, there must be a genuine link between the country and the ship, and the country must then supervise it (Articles 91 and 94). A ship sails under one flag only and answers to that country on the high seas (Article 92). A warship may not normally board another country's ship. The exceptions are reasonable suspicion of piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting, having no nationality, or secretly being of the warship's own nationality (Article 110). Having no flag is the main obstacle for a founder, because it lets a warship of any country come aboard to check. The article speaks of ships, so applying it to a fixed structure is an inference and has not been settled.

Suppose a group tows a barge out 300 nautical miles and declares a republic. The first decision is whether to register. Registering with a willing country means accepting that country's law on board. Declaring its own flag means other countries will see no flag at all. Supplies come from a port, which puts the group's boats under that port's law on each visit. The people on board also remain nationals of their home countries, and a country such as the US claims power over certain federal crimes committed by or against its nationals in "any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation" (18 USC 7(7)). Americans still file tax returns under Cook v. Tait, the 1924 Supreme Court case on worldwide income. Giving up US citizenship without holding another nationality leaves a person stateless.

The next question is the seabed, because the water and the sea floor have separate rules. Most of the open ocean is too deep to anchor in cheaply, so a founder would look for a shallow bank. Beyond 200 nautical miles, the sea floor may still be part of a country's extended continental shelf, seabed where that country holds the resource rights (Article 76). The water above stays high seas (Article 78), but artificial islands and fixed structures on that shelf come under the coastal country's control (Articles 60 and 80). Beyond every shelf lies the deep seabed, where no country may claim sovereignty and no person may take any part as their own (Article 137). The International Seabed Authority controls mining there. The treaty does not say plainly whether a long-term mooring on the deep seabed needs anyone's permission, and it gives the owner of the mooring no title to the ground.

A newer treaty adds paperwork for countries that have joined it. The BBNJ Agreement, on marine life in areas outside any country's control, was adopted on 19 June 2023 and took effect on 17 January 2026. In November 2026 it had 145 signing countries and 105 members, and its first members' meeting is set for 11 to 22 January 2027. Members must assess the environmental impact of planned activities under their control there before allowing them (Article 28). The treaty also adds rules on genetic resources from sea life, over which no country may claim authority (Article 11), on marine protected areas, and on helping countries build their capacity.

Then comes money. Published estimates start at about $50 million for a small deep-sea platform and reach billions for a city. Residents would need a bank, and international payments move between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks. A place with no banking law and no supervisor gives those banks no one to rely on, so a bank on the platform would have no route to the outside system, and residents would in practice keep accounts in real countries. Selling shares in a future country can count as selling securities, as Lazarus Long found in 1999 when US regulators sued him over $350 million in bonds for a Caribbean nation called New Utopia. He had raised $24,000. Medical care means going ashore. Flag countries must require their captains to help people in danger at sea when they can do so safely (Article 98), and a rescued person is then landed in some other country under its law.

The real cases show where projects stop. Among projects that aimed at the high seas, Aisland is the one where people lived aboard for a long period, and its anchorage in the Persian Gulf was not itself on the high seas. Samuele Landi, an Italian businessman sentenced in his absence to 14 years for fraud, lived on an 800-ton barge about 30 miles off Dubai with shipping containers for quarters. He planned to move to the Saya de Malha Bank, a huge underwater plateau in the Indian Ocean, and hoped for about twenty barges by 2028. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke the barge in two. Landi and two employees died. No government is known to have moved against the barge before that.

The Seasteading Institute, founded in 2008 by Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman with $500,000 from Peter Thiel, hoped for a seastead by 2014 and missed the date. It then turned to working inside a country's waters and signed a non-binding memorandum with French Polynesia in 2017. That government pulled out in 2018. Eric Klien's Atlantis Project of 1993, or Oceania, published a full constitution before building anything, needed about $1 billion, and collapsed in April 1994 for lack of interest. Its site, 50 miles off Panama, was in fact inside a coastal resource zone. Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman, failed to buy land from Kiribati and the Gambia and announced Arca Noë in 2020 for what he called neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice. No structure is known to exist.

The commonest misunderstanding is that no owner means no law. In fact every ship, every person aboard and every port call stays attached to some country's law. Another is that a declaration is enough. The tests of statehood in the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty, ask for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries, and open water gives no territory to define.

The simplest lawful form is a registered vessel under a real flag, with residents agreeing private rules by contract. It would stay under that flag country's law, and it could move if conditions changed. No coastal country holds title here, so the legal position is better than in most places at sea, although no one can gain a right to this water. The rough odds given for this zone, which are judgements and not measurements, are still low for holding out against outside control, because of the cost, the sea itself and the boarding rule, and recognition as a state is put at well under one percent.

combo-rented-sovereign.essay:
Some of what makes a country useful can be done by contract. A state holds legal powers that only states may exercise, such as registering ships, sponsoring seabed mining or filing for satellite slots. Nothing stops a state from hiring a private company to run the office. A community or company could therefore aim to get a state's powers working for it without being a state, by making a deal with a small government. This combines a recognised state's legal personality with private management. Unlike most ideas in this field, it has a long and successful record as a business running one state function, and it gives the operator no territory and no law of its own.

The classic case is Liberia's ship register. It was the idea of Edward Stettinius, a former US Secretary of State, who set up The Liberia Corporation in 1948 as a joint venture with the Liberian government. Under the deal, 25 percent of revenue went to the government, 10 percent to social programmes in Liberia and the rest to his corporation. The first ship was registered on 11 March 1949. Within 18 years Liberia had the world's largest register. Through two civil wars maritime funds reached about 70 percent of the government's revenue, and it has been described as one of the few legal sources of income for Charles Taylor's regime. Today the register is run by a company called LISCR and is reported to be managed from Virginia in the United States. In 2025 Liberia was again the largest by deadweight tonnage, with 424.1 million tonnes, about 17.4 percent of the world's total. The Marshall Islands started its own register in 1988, and its operator, International Registries, had its management buy it out in 1993.

Other functions followed. The Metals Company gained seabed exploration rights through subsidiaries sponsored by Nauru and Tonga, because a company needs a contract with the International Seabed Authority and a sponsoring state. Tongasat filed for satellite slots through Tonga, since only member states of the International Telecommunication Union can apply. Estonia sells company formation to e-residents worldwide. The Comoros sold nationality to stateless people in the Gulf, in a deal that led to a parliamentary inquiry into missing money. The pattern is settled in the sense that it exists and is legal in the host state, where its own law allows it.

The limits are these. The state keeps the power. A private registry runs on a contract, and the state can end it, as Charles Taylor's government showed when it signed a new contract with LISCR after taking power. The legal duties stay with the state. Under Article 94 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea a flag state must really control its ships, and under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty a state is responsible for what its private actors do in space. So a state that hires out its power remains answerable. If a licensee causes trouble, the state is the one other countries complain to, and it has every reason to cancel.

Then there is the meaning of the genuine link. Article 91 of the Law of the Sea treaty says there must be a genuine link between a flag state and its ships, repeating a 1958 rule that required a state to exercise jurisdiction and control effectively. A 1986 convention intended to strengthen this has not entered force as of 2026. So how little link is enough is open in practice, and much of world shipping sits on the answer. Whether a similar test applies to space licences or to company registers is also unsettled. Adrian Taghdiri wrote in a 2013 note that flags of convenience might arise for spacecraft, and he warned of harm from loose rules.

Suppose a community wants to run its own flag register this way. It signs a contract with a small state's government to manage a special register, for its own ships only. Its ships then fly a real flag and escape the problem of statelessness. Ports, insurers and classification societies check the register's reputation, and a poor one means more port inspections. A new government can cancel the deal and the country's parliament can question it. Radio licences follow the flag. Home countries of staff and owners keep their rules. All this is ordinary shipping law, up to the point where the register looks like a private state's. Reading the treaty, nothing seems to prohibit a state from serving one customer only. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea held in M/V Saiga (No. 2), on 1 July 1999 (paragraphs 82 to 86), that the genuine link rule does not set criteria by which other countries can challenge a ship's registration, and that a country with concerns should report them to the flag state. No case on a register with one customer is known.

A contract might try to reach further, to immigration, courts or criminal law. Próspera and the Dubai financial zone show that a state can hand over commercial law and courts by its own statute, and Honduras shows it can reverse that. Selling nationality has been tried, and the EU court in the Malta case called it commercialisation inside the EU. Each extension raises the political risk at home, and the host's voters may object, as Honduras's did.

As a way to run one state function for profit, this is the most proven idea in this group, and it does not produce a territory under the operator's own laws. The strongest version is a narrow, profitable, publicly disclosed contract with a stable small state to run one lawful function very well, with revenue going to that state's people. It gets the operator real legal effect anywhere the state's acts are honoured, including a flag, a sponsor or a slot. The operator gets no sovereignty. The state remains the sovereign and can end the deal.

venus-clouds.essay:
Venus is the planet next to Earth on the side nearer the Sun. Its surface is about 464 C, hotter than the melting point of lead, under an atmosphere pressing about 91 times as hard as Earth's air at sea level. Higher up, conditions change. About 50 to 55 kilometres above the ground, the temperature and air pressure come close to those on Earth. This has led engineers to propose living there in craft that float, without ever touching the ground. So a territory on Venus would mean a group of balloons or airships drifting in the clouds of another planet.

The physics explains the appeal. The atmosphere of Venus is mostly carbon dioxide, which is heavier than the mix of oxygen and nitrogen people breathe. Breathable air therefore floats there, in the same way that helium floats on Earth, with over 60 percent of the lifting power helium has on Earth. A balloon could hold the residents' own breathing air and be lifted by it. According to NASA's HAVOC study, at 55 kilometres the temperature is 27 C, the air pressure 0.5 bar (about half that at sea level on Earth) and gravity 8.73 metres per second squared, a little below Earth's. Figures from the NASA scientist Geoffrey Landis put about 50 kilometres at a pressure about the same as sea level on Earth, with temperatures of 0 to 50 C. A person going outside would need breathing air and protection from acid and some heat, and no pressure suit. A tear in the balloon would let gases mix slowly, leaving time for repairs, because the pressure is about equal on both sides. Landis argued that the atmosphere above would also shield against radiation about as well as Earth's does.

The difficulties are equally physical. The clouds contain sulfuric acid, so every outer surface must resist it. Winds at the cloud tops reach up to 95 metres per second, about 340 kilometres per hour, circling the planet about every four Earth days, and a floating city would travel with them, since tethering it would put stress on the structure. Hydrogen is very rare on Venus, which limits local water. Metals and other solid materials would have to be brought in or obtained some other way. The only human-made craft known to have floated there are the Soviet Union's Vega balloons, from 1985, and those small balloons lasted only days, until their batteries ran out.

The law is that of outer space generally. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, says in Article II that outer space, including the Moon and other natural bodies in space, cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Nobody therefore owns Venus or its air. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and countries answer for what their nationals do. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space or on a planet, moon or other natural body. Since nothing has been built there, no one has tested whether a balloon drifting in the air of Venus counts as a space object or as use of the planet. The treaty text speaks of objects launched into space and of natural bodies. A balloon launched from Earth and carrying its passengers fits those words reasonably well. A city built there from materials gathered on site raises a harder question that has no answer yet. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty does mention objects "landed or constructed on a celestial body", but only in the sentence saying that ownership of such objects is unaffected by where they are. Its sentence on legal power speaks of an object "launched into outer space". Reading the text, it seems the drafters had things built on a natural body in mind for ownership and left open who holds legal power over something built from local material.

Three proposals make up the record. In 1971 the Soviet engineer and science fiction writer Sergei Zhitomirsky proposed the Floating Islands of Venus, cities kept up some 50 or 60 kilometres high using technology from zeppelins and hot air balloons. He is not known to have claimed any part of Venus. In 2003 Landis presented his paper Colonization of Venus at a conference in Albuquerque. He argued that the only trouble with Venus is that the ground lies too far below the comfortable level, so settlers should live in the air. At the far extreme, aerostats, meaning craft that float like balloons, might cover the whole planet. In 2014 Dale Arney and Chris Jones, engineers at NASA's Langley Research Center, created HAVOC, the High Altitude Venus Operational Concept. It ran in five phases, from a robot airship 31 metres long to astronauts in orbit, a crew staying about 30 days in an airship 129 metres long, a one-year stay, and a permanent human presence in the atmosphere. Travel out would take 110 days and return 300, for 440 days in total. NASA later said it was an internal study for building analysis skills and never a real mission. It received no further funding and was cancelled by 2017. None of these proposals dealt with who would govern the residents.

Suppose a private group wants to build one floating station. Before anything else it needs a launching country, a licence and an entry on a register. In the United States, the licence comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance for harm to others of up to $500 million. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. That country then keeps legal power over the station and its staff, however far away they are. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. Contamination comes next. Article IX requires countries to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds, and the licensing country may apply that to a private crew.

Money is the next bump. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, so a year's food for one person, about 1,000 kilograms, would cost about $3.3 million to lift that far, and Venus is much farther. No private funding for this is known. Each resident needs about 0.84 kilograms of oxygen a day and much more in food and water. A breakdown would be serious, because a return trip takes months and there is no ground to land on. Medical care would be whatever is aboard. The Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, depends on other crews and countries being able to reach the spot, and none could for months. A crime aboard would fall under the registering country's law, and citizens would stay subject to their home country's rules, including US tax returns for Americans.

A common misunderstanding is that floating avoids the ban on occupying a planet. Article II says "by any other means", so a country or its licensed company gains no claim by floating. Another is that a floating city could meet the usual test of statehood, the Montevideo Convention of 1933, which asks for a defined territory. A craft blown around the planet by winds of 340 kilometres per hour has no fixed area, and no one may claim the air it moves through.

A project within the law would be a small research airship under one country's licence, with robots first, along the path HAVOC described. Distance would slow any outside control, which is why holding on once there is estimated at about 35 percent, while the chance of building at all is estimated at about 1 percent, and the chance of getting a territory under its own laws is much lower. In law it would stay a registered craft, the property of its owner, under the registering country.

combo-new-island-beyond-eez.essay:
A volcano could one day push a new island above the sea far from any country's waters. This is the rarest situation in this list and one of the most interesting in law, because it would be real natural land, which an artificial platform can never be. The idea combines new land, the high seas and the old rules on unclaimed territory, with or without a state acting as sponsor.

Some parts are settled. Article 121 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says an island is a naturally formed area of land, surrounded by water, above water at high tide. A volcanic island meets that test, so it would avoid the problem that sinks every platform. Rocks that cannot sustain human habitation or economic life have no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf (Article 121(3)), though they do have a territorial sea, the belt of up to 12 nautical miles. The old rule on acquiring empty land is also well established. In the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928 Max Huber held that discovery gives only a starting claim, which must be completed by actual and continuing display of state authority. In the Clipperton award of 1931 France kept an uninhabited island on the strength of its 1858 proclamation and notice, because the island was empty and no earlier owner was proved. These rulings concern countries, and writers generally treat acquisition of this kind as a method used by states.

Nearly all new islands rise inside some country's waters, and then there is no question. Graham Island off Sicily in 1831 drew Sicilian and British claims within weeks and then wore away. Iceland said Surtsey was Icelandic as soon as French journalists landed on it in 1963. Beyond every zone the case has never arisen in any court, so the following points are open, and writers say so. Pawel Czubik's recent study separates three cases, an island under a state's sovereignty, an island on the high seas, and an island in zones of limited rights, which he calls the most problematic. For islands that can be treated as res nullius, meaning belonging to no one, he asks whether acts by private persons with no authority from a state can extend a state's territory. Duncan Hollis, writing about a new island near Tonga in 2006, said an island outside national baselines might be open to competing claims by discovery and occupation, and he raised the idea of treating it as common heritage. He said private groups may have a stronger claim to private property in such land than to statehood, and that their claims to found a nation rarely succeed today. A 1978 comment by Jimmy Verner asked whether seabed claims, nearness, occupation or discovery could support ownership of new islands in the Pacific.

The treaty text pulls two ways. Article 89 bars claims to the high seas, and Article 137 bars claims to the seabed beyond national limits. Neither article mentions land above water. On one view new land is simply new territory that the old rules can reach. On the other, it is a piece of the common seabed that happens to break the surface, so Article 137 forbids taking it. Reading the text, it seems that the second view has some force for the summit's roots and less for the dry part. A further difficulty follows. A state that took such an island would gain a 12-mile belt of territorial sea and its seabed, which would be carved from what had been high seas and common seabed, and the treaty does not say how those rules fit together. No state has had to answer that.

With a sponsor, the path is clearer. Suppose a state acts quickly, lands officials and governs the place. Under Palmas and Clipperton it has a recognised method, and rival states would need a better claim. A founder working with such a state could then receive whatever charter that state's law allows. Article 121 would give it territory, and that territory would belong to the sponsor, so the founder would hold a concession. The old US Guano Islands Act of 1856 is the closest private route. It lets American citizens claim islands with guano deposits for the United States, provided they belong to no other government. Leicester Hemingway relied on it for his raft New Atlantis, which was no island, and storms destroyed it. It too gives the claim to the sponsoring country and no independence to the finder.

Without a sponsor, the group would have real land with nobody's title on it, and a claim to statehood stronger than any platform's, since the Montevideo tests ask for a defined territory. It would still need other states' recognition, and states have shown little interest in giving it. Tonga annexed the Minerva Reefs in 1972 to stop a private country, and any coastal or nearby state could do the same by sending a boat. The landing party has to arrive from a port, which has a government. The group's members are nationals of states, and their taxes and criminal law follow them. There is no title that a bank could lend against, unless a government recognises one.

The ground may also disappear. Graham Island lasted about six months, Zalzala Koh about three years, and the Hunga Tonga island was largely destroyed seven years after it formed in 2015. Surtsey lasted because hard lava capped its ash, and that took years of eruption while the island could not be lived on. A founder would have to wait through all of this, with no water and little soil.

The strongest version is a group with a ship waiting, sailing under a state that has agreed in advance to back the group and to grant it a charter if land appears. This would be a very long wait, since no one can forecast the event, and new islands almost always rise inside coastal zones. It is the one sea route in which the land itself would meet the legal definition of territory. The chance of such land appearing and lasting is close to nil, because the event is so rare and the land so unstable, and a private group's chance of holding it as its own territory under its own laws is also very low, because only a state can acquire it by occupation.

outer-moons.essay:
Beyond Mars and the asteroid belt lie the giant planets Jupiter and Saturn, each with many moons, and smaller worlds called dwarf planets, such as Ceres in the asteroid belt. Some of these bodies are large and hold huge amounts of ice. Writers and engineers have suggested them as settlement sites because they could supply water, fuel and building materials on the spot. All such plans are studies on paper. No crew has been sent under any of them, and nobody has carried people this far.

Each world poses different physical problems, so a few figures help. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has ice over a hidden ocean that may hold more than twice the water of all Earth's oceans. Its radiation is the main barrier, about 5.40 sieverts per day for an unshielded person, when about 5 sieverts over a few days is fatal. A sievert is a measure of radiation dose. Ganymede, another moon of Jupiter, receives about 0.08 sieverts per day and has gravity about 0.15 of Earth's. Callisto lies outside Jupiter's radiation belt, the zone of harmful radiation around the planet, and has gravity about 0.13 of Earth's. Titan, a moon of Saturn, has gravity 0.138 of Earth's, a thick atmosphere of nitrogen and methane, and lakes of hydrocarbons, but extreme cold and no free oxygen. Enceladus, also a moon of Saturn, has an underground ocean. A 2016 analysis of data from the Cassini spacecraft put the ice above it at 18 to 22 kilometres thick on average and less than 5 kilometres in the south polar region. Gravity this low has unknown effects on bone, muscle and children's growth.

The legal position is short and the same everywhere here. Nobody owns these worlds. They are natural bodies in space, so they fall under the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article II says they cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority, by using or occupying them, or by any other means. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country. Article VIII says the country that registers a craft keeps legal power over it and its crew, in space or on any natural body. The treaty text sets no distance limit on either rule. Since no craft has carried people this far, none of this has been tested. The Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with 17 members, also extends its ban on owning the surface to other bodies in the solar system, though only for those members.

Contamination is a further issue here. Article IX requires countries to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds. COSPAR, an international committee of space scientists, issues a policy on protecting other worlds, and its January 2026 version added a unified policy for icy worlds. Oceans under ice are places where scientists hope to look for life, so a mission to drill into Europa or Enceladus would expect close questions from its licensing country and from its national space agency. COSPAR's policy has no treaty force of its own and works through those agencies.

The published descriptions of these settlement plans do not discuss ownership or law at all. They are engineering studies. Robert Zubrin, an American aerospace engineer who founded the Mars Society, wrote in his 1999 book Entering Space that Titan was the best moon for a base. Stephen Gillett had written about Titan as a home for life in the magazine Analog in 1992. Titan's atmosphere could supply a gas for making breathing air, and water beneath the surface could yield oxygen. In 1997 the private Artemis Project drafted a plan to settle Europa, with igloos on the surface as bases for drilling, and possibly people living in air pockets inside the ice. Metals and minerals would have to be brought in, heavy shielding would be needed, and the plan was never carried out. In 2003 NASA's HOPE study, short for Revolutionary Concepts for Human Outer Planet Exploration, chose Callisto. A base there could make fuel for further exploration, and it has accessible water, silicate rock and metals. A crew's round trip was estimated at about 2 to 5 years, assuming major advances in propulsion. It stopped at the study stage.

The fourth case points to a different kind of settlement. In 2020 the Finnish space physicist Pekka Janhunen posted a preprint, a paper shared before formal publication, on a settlement in high orbit around Ceres. He chose Ceres for its nitrogen, which an Earth-like atmosphere requires. Spinning habitats joined to a disk-shaped frame would give the same gravity as Earth, mirrors would bring in sunlight, and a space elevator on Ceres would lift material cheaply. Density would stay at 500 people per square kilometre, on soil 1.5 metres deep. Each person would account for about 10 million kilograms of material. An orbiting structure of this kind would presumably be treated as a space object, though it would be built from Ceres materials and never launched from Earth. Who would register it is uncertain, because the Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects, speaks of objects launched into space. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty does mention objects "landed or constructed on a celestial body", but only in the sentence saying that ownership of such objects is unaffected by where they are. Its sentence on legal power speaks of an object "launched into outer space". Reading the text, it seems the drafters had things built on a natural body in mind for ownership and left open who holds legal power over something built from local material.

Suppose a private group tried. The first step would happen on Earth, as for any space mission. It would need a launching country, a licence and an entry on a register. In the United States the licence comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million, and the launching country stays liable for damage. Frequencies would need filing through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. These steps all happen before the group leaves, so the group cannot avoid them by distance.

The next bumps are the voyage and supplies. Radio messages would take many minutes each way, so no one could call for instructions in an emergency. Travel would take years, which would keep other states away and also make rescue impossible. The treaty's Article V asks astronauts of member countries to help each other, which is of little use when no one is close. A doctor, a surgeon, teachers and engineers would all need to be aboard. Nothing delivered from Earth would arrive soon, and a resident could not easily leave. Children born there would have no choice in the matter, and they would be growing up in a gravity whose effects are unknown. Their nationality would depend on their parents' home countries, since the treaty does not mention birth. Americans would still have US tax duties on paper, whatever their distance.

Common misunderstandings concern distance again. Being very far away does not end the registering country's legal power, because the treaty sets no limit. Being first on Titan does not create a claim to it, because Article II bars that and Article I keeps all areas open to everyone. A self-declared nation would still lack a defined territory, one of the four tests of statehood in the Montevideo Convention of 1933. Recognition is estimated at about 0.1 percent.

A plan that stays within the law would be a research base licensed by a treaty country, on a low-radiation world such as Callisto, as NASA's study suggested, and supplied by machines sent ahead. That study assumed major advances in propulsion. The chance of building is estimated at about 0.5 percent. Once a crew had arrived, distance would give them a fairly high practical chance of being left alone, estimated at about 40 percent, although the chance of getting a territory under their own laws is much lower. The same distance would make rescue impossible, and the law would continue to treat them as under the country that registered them.
